title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
authors: Yiyang Du,Yuxuan Kuang,Qitao Zhao,Yixuan Wang,Zhanqiu Guo,Yi Xu,Xin Li,Wenbin He,Liu Ren,Chenyan Xiong
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action’s outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.1
introduction:
Recent advances in robot foundation models follow two main paradigms: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), which adapt Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to output low-level robot actions, and World-Action Models (WAMs), which build upon video-generation world models. Despite building upon existing foundation models, both families still suffer from brittle out-of-distribution generalization [15, 56, 44] and limited long-horizon memory [12, 39]. Moreover, deploying VLAs and WAMs to new downstream tasks typically requires task-specific fine-tuning [21, 6, 35, 50], limiting their zero-shot adaptation.

Beyond these two paradigms, frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra [34] offer a promising alternative: they control robots directly via low-level numerical actions without relying on high-level primitives, show strong zero-shot generalization and working memory in robotic manipulation [55, 20, 22, 18], and outperform specialized VLAs and WAMs [55, 20, 47]. These results demonstrate the vast potential of leveraging frontier language model agents directly as generalist robot policies.

Existing evaluations assess these agents at the episode level, with binary success rates or aggregate task scores that show neither how an agent succeeds nor where it fails. In this paper, we provide a systematic, fine-grained investigation into the capabilities and limitations of frontier agents on direct robot control by analyzing their behavior at the action level. Evaluating an individual action can be ambiguous because robot manipulation is inherently multimodal [16, 38, 10]: since multiple distinct trajectories can validly advance the same task, whether an action succeeds depends on its intended sub-goal. We resolve this ambiguity by letting the policy agent state a local intent alongside each action, establishing a verifiable local contract for every action (Figure 1(a)). Conditioned on the global task goal, this local intent, and multi-view observations, our AgentRoboCritic framework determines whether each executed action succeeded and assigns a specific failure mode to every failed action. Using GPT-6 Astra as the critic, we annotate episodes across 12 robot manipulation benchmarks for further analysis.

Our analysis characterizes both the promising capabilities and the current limitations of frontier agents on direct robot control. On the capability side, frontier agents show three major strengths (Figure 1(b)). First, they recover from local execution failures in closed loop, unlike imitation-trained policies whose errors compound under covariate shift [37], and half of their successful episodes contain at least one failed action that the agent later corrects. Second, they show reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, executing actions that follow the target object, category, and sequential order specified in the local intent. Third, they achieve strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. On the limitation side, frontier agents face task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks, led by object acquisition and retention (Grasp) in general manipulation, spatial mating (Alignment) in tight-tolerance visuo-tactile tasks, and unintended collisions (Interference) in cluttered scenes. Recovery is also uneven across failure modes: Alignment failures are recovered less often than Grasp failures.

To validate the reliability of our automated annotations, we construct a 400-action human-annotated evaluation benchmark and demonstrate that GPT-6 Astra aligns closely with human judgments, while ablating local intent causes a sharp collapse in failure-mode attribution. Finally, to enable low-cost action-level critique for direct robot control, we curate an open-source dataset of 12,844 annotated actions and fine-tune an open-source critic VLM, Muse-Glimmer-30B, which approaches GPT-6 Astra on both action outcome and failure-mode accuracy (Figure 1(c)).

Our main contributions are as follows:

Intent-Grounded Action Critique Framework: We propose AgentRoboCritic, a framework that evaluates frontier language model agents on direct robot control at the action level by conditioning the critique on both global task objectives and the policy’s local intent.

Action-Level Analysis of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control: We go beyond episode-level success rates to establish frontier agents as a promising path toward generalist robot policies and to identify the physical execution bottlenecks that remain.

Open-Source Critique Dataset and Critic VLM: We curate and release an action-level critique dataset alongside a 400-action human-annotated test set, as well as a fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic VLM that enables accurate, low-cost failure analysis.

1. Intent-Grounded Action Critique Framework: We propose AgentRoboCritic, a framework that evaluates frontier language model agents on direct robot control at the action level by conditioning the critique on both global task objectives and the policy’s local intent.

2. Action-Level Analysis of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control: We go beyond episode-level success rates to establish frontier agents as a promising path toward generalist robot policies and to identify the physical execution bottlenecks that remain.

3. Open-Source Critique Dataset and Critic VLM: We curate and release an action-level critique dataset alongside a 400-action human-annotated test set, as well as a fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic VLM that enables accurate, low-cost failure analysis.

title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
authors: Onur Beker,A. René Geist,Michael Posa,Marc Toussaint,Justin Carpentier,Georg Martius
abstract:
Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics, or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact.
In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver’s role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.
introduction:
What exactly is a contact model? And what does it mean to formulate one using cone complementarity? Answering these questions requires taking a step back and asking a more fundamental question: where do contact forces come from?
The normal contact force arises from the short-range repulsion between atoms that are pushed close together. The frictional contact force arises from the interactions at the microscopic asperities where two surfaces actually touch, which adhere, deform, and interlock as the surfaces slide over each other. Contact is therefore a complex, multiscale effect, and a “mechanistic” approach that tries to numerically simulate these processes directly is intractable at the scale of robots.

Practical contact models used in robotics are therefore “phenomenological”: they reproduce the macroscopic phenomenon (“what contacts do”) without reproducing the underlying microscopic mechanism (“how contacts do it”). The first question any contact model must answer is thus: what do contacts do?
They do two things:
i) prevent intersections between surfaces that try to pass through each other, and
ii) dissipate energy between surfaces that try to slide on top of each other. All contact models, at their core, are therefore mathematical abstractions designed to produce these two effects in a way that makes theoretical analysis and numerical simulation tractable. And cone complementarity formulations of contact dynamics are a family of particularly elegant ways of doing so.

Aimed at doctoral students and early-career robotics researchers, this tutorial collates the most common mathematical formulations of contact dynamics based on cone complementarity conditions, along with the key techniques and insights used to solve the resulting problems numerically.
The material draws primarily from (Witkin and Baraff, 1997; Google DeepMind, 2022; Stewart, 2000; Acary et al., 2018; Andrews et al., 2022; Le Lidec et al., 2023; Carpentier et al., 2024; Tsounis et al., 2025; Castro et al., 2023; Lynch and Park, 2017; Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004), supplemented by the authors’ own derivations. Upon completing the tutorial, readers should be well prepared to explore the open-source implementations of widely used simulators (e.g., MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012), Bullet (Coumans, 2015), Drake (Tedrake and the Drake Team, 2019), Kamino (Tsounis et al., 2026), Simple (Carpentier et al., 2024), Newton (The Newton
Contributors, 2025)), or to extend their understanding beyond forward simulation by investigating the use of cone complementarity formulations of contact dynamics in optimal control and trajectory optimization (Mordatch et al., 2012; Posa et al., 2014; Manchester and Kuindersma, 2019; Toussaint et al., 2020; Tassa et al., 2012; Howell et al., 2022a; Pang et al., 2023).
To get the most out of the tutorial, readers will benefit from prior familiarity with rigid-body dynamics (Lynch and Park, 2017; Featherstone, 2014; Toussaint, ; Robotic Systems Lab, 2017; Kim, 2012; Tedrake, 2024), convex analysis (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004; Nesterov, 2018; Bertsekas, 2009; Parikh and Boyd, 2014), and numerical methods (Nocedal and Wright, 2006; Solomon, 2015; Strang, 2007).

Before delving into the subject at a mathematical level, let us briefly clarify the scope of the tutorial and point readers to complementary pedagogical resources on topics that are not covered.

Several existing resources cover material that overlaps with the contents of this tutorial. The SIGGRAPH course of Andrews, Erleben, and Ferguson (Andrews et al., 2022) is the closest in spirit. Written for computer graphics, it covers collision detection in detail, and focuses on linear complementarity formulations as well as penalty and barrier formulations used for deformable bodies; with a brief mention of cone complementarity formulations used in robotics. This tutorial is complementary: it is written for robotics, focuses on cone complementarity formulations, and provides very brief summaries of collision detection and linear-complementarity formulations (mostly derived from the SIGGRAPH course itself). Acary, Brémond, and Huber (Acary et al., 2018) survey the exact formulations of the frictional contact problem for a computational mechanics audience, and compare the solvers of Siconos numerically on a large benchmark collection. The present tutorial also covers the exact formulations (borrowing several of their mathematical constructions and terminology), and additionally discusses its convex relaxations that are commonly used in robotics. The monograph of Acary and Brogliato (Acary and Brogliato, 2008) and the review of Stewart (Stewart, 2000) treat the mathematical theory of nonsmooth dynamics and its time discretization in a depth and generality that go well beyond the scope of this tutorial. Le Lidec et al. (Le Lidec et al., 2023) provide a comparative analysis of the contact dynamics formulations and solution algorithms used by current robotics simulators, including numerical experiments and discussions on the physical artifacts of the convex relaxations. This tutorial instead provides the pedagogy around the same subject, with step-by-step mathematical derivations, as well as additional formulations and solution algorithms that are no longer commonly employed in the modern simulation landscape of today but do nevertheless provide important context. Finally, the MuJoCo documentation (Google DeepMind, 2022) and the paper introducing Drake’s SAP solver (Castro et al., 2023) present the mathematical formulations of these two simulators in detail, each within its own framework. This tutorial places both within a common family of transcriptions (i.e., the nonlinear least-squares transcription from Section 4), and presents self-contained mathematical derivations.

This tutorial focuses on what are commonly called the “discrete time-stepping” family of methods for simulating cone complementarity formulations of contact dynamics, which underpin most of the widely used simulators of today (Todorov et al., 2012; Coumans, 2015; Tedrake and the Drake Team, 2019; Carpentier et al., 2024; Tsounis et al., 2026). The theoretical foundations of these methods can be traced to Moreau’s seminal work in the 1980s on the “measure differential inclusion” framework (Moreau, 1983; Moreau, 1985; Moreau, 1988), followed by the development of “impulse-based theories” of contact dynamics (Brogliato, 1996; Glocker, 2001; Stewart, 2011). Their computational foundations in turn originate from the “nonsmooth contact dynamics” framework developed by Moreau and Jean in the 1990s (Moreau, 1988; Moreau, 1994; Jean, 1999), and the subsequent advances that shaped modern time-stepping methods (Stewart and Trinkle, 1996; Stewart, 1998; de Saxcé and Feng, 1991; de Saxcé and Feng, 1998; Glocker and Studer, 2005; Anitescu, 2006; Anitescu and Tasora, 2010; Tasora and Anitescu, 2011; Acary et al., 2011; Todorov et al., 2012; Todorov, 2014; Acary et al., 2018; Castro et al., 2023; Carpentier et al., 2024).

Before impulse-based theories and discrete time-stepping methods rose to prominence, the prevailing approach was to formulate cone complementarity models of contact dynamics in continuous time (Fourier, 1798; Ostrogradsky, 1838; Jellett, 1872; Painlevé, 1895; Mayer, 1899; Zermelo, 1899; Delassus, 1917; Signorini, 1959; Fichera, 1963; Moreau, 1966; Lötstedt, 1982). Computationally, these formulations were commonly paired with what are called the “event-driven” family of methods, perhaps most notably in the research program of Glocker and Pfeiffer (Glocker and Pfeiffer, 1993; Glocker and Pfeiffer, 1995; Pfeiffer and Glocker, 1996). This family of event-driven methods can provide greater accuracy by explicitly resolving the timing of contact events, but typically incur substantially higher computational costs, making them more prevalent in computational mechanics than in robotics, where time-stepping methods offer a more efficient alternative with accuracy often sufficient for simulation and control. The event-driven family is therefore beyond the scope of this tutorial, but we refer interested readers to the classical textbook by Glocker and Pfeiffer (Pfeiffer and Glocker, 1996).

Not all widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations of contact dynamics. In particular, linear complementarity formulations (Baraff, 1994; Stewart and Trinkle, 1996), position-based dynamics (Müller et al., 2007; Macklin et al., 2014; Macklin et al., 2016) as well as penalty and barrier-based formulations (Li et al., 2020; Ferguson et al., 2021) are widely used in computer graphics. As these approaches are already covered extensively in existing tutorials and surveys (Müller, 2021; Li et al., 2026a; Ferguson, 2023; Andrews et al., 2022; Bender et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2020; Witkin and Baraff, 1997), we refer the interested reader to this material. Similarly, compliant contact models such as the classical spring-damper based point-contact laws (Hertz, 1882; Hunt and Crossley, 1975) and the hydroelastic pressure-field model (Elandt et al., 2019), together with recent convex formulations and error-controlled integrators for such models (Castro et al., 2025; Kurtz and Castro, 2025) are out of scope for this tutorial.

The tutorial presents the material in pedagogical order instead of chronological. Rather than tracing the historical development of the theory, the exposition builds directly on its current state of the art, using modern terminology from convex optimization and numerical methods to explain the key results and their underlying principles.
Following background sections that introduce the necessary concepts from rigid-body dynamics (Section 2) and convex optimization with cone constraints (Section 3), the core material is organized under three main sections: Problem Formulation (Section 4), Numerical Methods (Section 5), and Comparative Analysis (Section 6). The tutorial then concludes with a discussion of future directions for the reader (Section 7), and a retrospective overview of the material. The former highlights possible paths for further exploration such as trajectory optimization and differentiable simulation, helping readers identify where to continue their learning journey now that they are equipped with a foundational understanding of cone complementarity formulations contact dynamics.

title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Kai Lu,Chenyang Ma,Ioannis Havoutis
abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at https://kl-research.github.io/pgx.
introduction:
Humanoid loco-manipulation for long-horizon tasks is central to embodied intelligence and generalist robotics, with applications in domestic assistance, healthcare, and industrial logistics. Yet even seemingly routine tasks in these domains demand complex, extended coordination between locomotion and manipulation. For instance, fetching a coffee or clearing a table interleaves walking, contact-rich manipulation, and precise object-part interaction over long action sequences. The challenge lies in jointly addressing three tightly coupled aspects: temporal structure, skill dynamics, and precise control, all of which must be grounded in physical interaction and integrated within a unified visuomotor control framework (see Fig. 1).

Traditional methods for loco-manipulation separate these concerns across modules: task and motion planning or behavior trees control timing [1, 2, 3], model-based whole-body control owns precision, and manipulation is realized by hand-designed motion primitives. These systems are transparent and precise, but every skill must be engineered for a specific object and scene, and contact-rich skills remain brittle.

Learning-based methods offer a more generalizable alternative: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] and learned whole-body controllers [10, 11, 12] acquire transferable manipulation skills and locomotion behaviors from data, reducing the need for task- or object-specific programming. However, learning and executing the entire long-horizon loco-manipulation task with a single policy introduces difficulties in maintaining task progress, coordinating reference frames, and handling highly imbalanced demonstrations. Without an explicit representation of task progress, visually similar observations from different stages can lead to incorrect skill execution [13]. Moreover, actions represented relative to the moving pelvis frame make precise manipulation difficult, since the action reference changes as the humanoid moves. Long-horizon demonstrations are also highly imbalanced: walking and low-motion segments dominate the trajectory, which can bias imitation learning toward conservative or near-static actions (e.g., standing still). Thus, these challenges remain major obstacles to reliable end-to-end long-horizon loco-manipulation, despite rapid progress in humanoid whole-body control [14, 11, 12] and VLAs.

To this end, we aim to establish a physically grounded framework bridging robot foundation models (i.e., VLAs) and structured robot planning and control. Our insight is that the aspects a flat VLA handles least reliably, deciding when and where to act, can often be resolved directly from physical quantities, whereas learning how to execute a skill is precisely where VLAs are most effective. PGX therefore uses physical structure to determine task progress, skill initiation, and spatial grounding, while leaving the execution of transferable manipulation skills to the VLA. By decoupling timing and world-frame precision from the learned policy, we hypothesize that the same foundation-model backbone can execute long-horizon loco-manipulation more reliably.

Building on this insight, we introduce PGX (Physically Grounded eXecution), a training-free execution framework that separates deciding when and where to act from learning how to act. Rather than modifying the VLA, introducing a learned planner to infer sub-tasks from images [15, 16, 17], or folding temporal structure into the policy itself [18, 19], PGX assigns task progression and spatial precision to physically grounded components while preserving the VLA as the manipulation skill executor. Specifically, PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers. 1) Timing: a predicate-gated finite state machine (FSM) maintains task progress and memory, representing each stage as a tuple of instruction, executor, guard predicate, timeout, and retry policy. 2) Skills: the VLA operates only within manipulation stages, while the execution layer re-establishes the starting conditions under which each skill was trained; failed guards trigger retries, and reverse transitions recover from prematurely entered stages. 3) Precision: world-coordinate locking (WCL) computes navigation goals from the current object pose, holds the base at its manipulation-entry position, and anchors precise contact targets in the world frame. In this way, physical structure governs task progression and spatial precision, allowing the VLA to focus on transferable manipulation dynamics.

We evaluate PGX in Isaac Lab Arena on three tasks (box transport, mug placement, and coffee fetching) and in a real-world coffee task using a Unitree G1 Humanoid Robot. We fine-tuned the state-of-the-art foundational VLA models π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.6 on collected human demonstrations. On coffee fetching, PGX improves the task success rate of a fine-tuned VLA from 35% to 80% with unchanged weights, and improves stage progression and success on all three tasks for both backbones. The real humanoid G1 experiment further demonstrates the effectiveness of the execution structure.

In summary, the main contributions of our work are:

We propose PGX, a physically grounded execution framework that incorporates VLA models with a predicate-gated state machine and a world-coordinate locking layer, improving long-horizon capability.

We develop predicate-gated stage sequencing with retry and reverse transitions, together with WCL components, and show that the decoupled layers supply structured robot behaviors and generalize across VLA backbones.

We evaluate the effectiveness of PGX on three simulated loco-manipulation tasks and on a real humanoid, where it turns near-failing flat policies into reliable long-horizon execution.

1. We propose PGX, a physically grounded execution framework that incorporates VLA models with a predicate-gated state machine and a world-coordinate locking layer, improving long-horizon capability.

2. We develop predicate-gated stage sequencing with retry and reverse transitions, together with WCL components, and show that the decoupled layers supply structured robot behaviors and generalize across VLA backbones.

3. We evaluate the effectiveness of PGX on three simulated loco-manipulation tasks and on a real humanoid, where it turns near-failing flat policies into reliable long-horizon execution.

title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
authors: Hao Vo,Taisei Hanyu,Yuki Ikebe,Pham Tri Quang,Sreevenkata Anjani Tishita Godavarthi,Nghi D. Q. Bui,Daniel Sonntag,Chase Rainwater,Duy Minh Ho Nguyen,Anh Nguyen,Ngan Le
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper–object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object’s mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.
introduction:
Physical understanding has widely recognized as a cornerstone of language-conditioned robotic manipulation systems [4, 56, 15, 41]. A broad spectrum of methods have emerged, ranging from hybrid frameworks [53, 28] to unified systems [41, 20, 63], from vision-language architectures [61, 2, 19] to multi-sensory models [57, 38], and from static methods [61, 2, 19, 43, 15, 44, 22, 21] to dynamic paradigm [62, 27, 31, 17, 49].

Despite this great progress, recent works predominantly focus on the intrinsic gripper–object contact, whether in standard manipulation tasks such as Pick-and-Place, Re-orientation, and Opening & Closing Articulated Objects [30, 37, 7, 60], or in contact-rich tasks such as Insertion, Fragile Grasping, and Wiping [12, 57, 16, 26, 18, 32, 11, 38, 45]. However, they largely overlook how the manipulators interacts with its surrounding environment (e.g., gravity, friction, inertia, aerodynamics, mass distribution, etc.), namely the newtonian mechanics underlying everyday physical interactions, which substantially limits their ability to reflect genuine physical intelligence.
To fill this gap, we recast language-conditioned robotic manipulation through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity [8], focusing on throwing-based object manipulation. In this setting, the manipulator must estimate the object’s physical properties, such as its mass, center of mass (CoM), and friction, and plan the forces and contacts needed to send the object to a target location outside its own kinematic workspace.
We introduce PhyDEX, a high-fidelity synthetic manipulation dataset comprising 35k trajectories across 9 throwing tasks and 100 scenes. It covers rigid, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects, as well as diverse destination types, with all physical properties randomized. PhyDEX is generated by a fully decoupled, autonomous simulation pipeline that separates asset specification, skill policies, task composition, and rendering. Each task is built by retrieving embodiments, scenes, and objects from an asset library and composing scripted skill policies into complete behaviors. This compositional design enables automatic generation of object-level annotations, physical randomization, and collision-aware motion plans, supporting systematic VLA validation through fine-tuning and closed-loop evaluation.

To evaluate the physical understanding of current policies, we select three representative policies: GR00T N1.7 [3] as a general-purpose policy, DynamicVLA [54] as a high-frequency policy, and ForceVLA [57] as a multi-sensory VLA. Our experiments show that current policies are not yet reliable for tasks requiring physical understanding, with average success rates below 10%. We further identify generalization and the probing of object physical properties as the main bottlenecks of current systems. To confirm that this trend holds beyond a single setup, we additionally conduct evaluations across multiple platforms, including a humanoid robot and real-world experiments.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We propose PhyDEX, a diverse and comprehensive dataset of nine throwing tasks for studying physical understanding in robot manipulation.

We propose PhyDEX, a diverse and comprehensive dataset of nine throwing tasks for studying physical understanding in robot manipulation.

We introduce a scalable construction pipeline that generates diverse, end-to-end data for throwing tasks.

We conduct extensive evaluations across multiple embodiments, including robot arms and humanoids, in both simulation and real-world experiments. Our results show that data scarcity and physical blindness are the main bottlenecks keeping current policies from performing reliably on physical understanding tasks.

1. We propose PhyDEX, a diverse and comprehensive dataset of nine throwing tasks for studying physical understanding in robot manipulation.

2. We introduce a scalable construction pipeline that generates diverse, end-to-end data for throwing tasks.

3. We conduct extensive evaluations across multiple embodiments, including robot arms and humanoids, in both simulation and real-world experiments. Our results show that data scarcity and physical blindness are the main bottlenecks keeping current policies from performing reliably on physical understanding tasks.

title: ACE-Brain-0.7: Learning Execution-Grounded Reasoning for Embodied Agents
authors: Yinhe Wang,Shijun Shi,Feng Pan,Tao Tao,Wei Mao,Jiangning Zhang,Zhiyao Ren,Yihang Jiao,Haoming Gu,Yunpeng Qing,Jiyu Guo,Zhi Hou,Dacheng Tao,Xiaogang Wang
abstract:
Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state.
We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision–language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation.
To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question–answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation.
These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes.
We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data.
Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5.
Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg.
Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states.
Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.
introduction:
Recent advances in embodied AI have equipped robots with a growing range of manipulation skills.
Completing complex, long-horizon tasks requires high-level reasoning that combines task goals with environmental observations to coordinate these skills, assess execution state, and select the next action.
Systems such as Hi Robot [1], π0.7\pi_{0.7} [2], and Gemini Robotics [3] demonstrate how vision–language models (VLMs) can support task planning, sub-task prediction, and execution supervision.
However, a plausible plan does not guarantee an accurate judgment of execution state.
Task knowledge tells a model which steps are usually required, but deciding when to advance requires observations of what has actually happened.
In Figure 1, the robot attempts to place the block in the bowl and opens the microwave door but fails to reach the bowl; at this state, issuing a placement or door-closing command would skip an unresolved step.
Recognizing this situation requires the model to relate the observed scene to the task’s progress and completion conditions.

We use execution-grounded reasoning to describe judgments that follow the observed progress and outcome of a task.
This motivates supervision that covers different stages of execution, including incomplete and failed attempts.
To learn this ability, we curate a training collection of 3.7 million question–answer pairs centered on task execution.
Specifically, we collect supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation, with questions posed at multiple moments and answers derived from step timelines, object states, and failure labels.
For newly annotated egocentric videos, we also retain the frames supporting each judgment.
We combine this collection with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data to fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B [4], obtaining ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B VLM that supports all three capabilities.

ACE-Brain-0.7 outperforms every evaluated open model on each of the six public task-reasoning benchmarks.
It also achieves the highest average scores among the evaluated models on both benchmark suites: 76.5 for task reasoning and 75.90 across seven spatial-grounding benchmarks.
On RoboBench [5], ACE-Brain-0.7 scores 52.1 on next-subtask prediction, exceeding 34.7 for GPT-6 Astra [6] and 39.0 for Claude Opus 5.5 [7].
To examine the contribution of the question–answer collection, we also compare Qwen3.5-9B with a task-only variant fine-tuned on this collection alone.
Experiments with controlled visual inputs indicate that the trained model benefits more from ordered visual history, while temporal question pairs test its judgments across different execution states.
On 114 pairs, the task-only model raises paired accuracy from 15.8 for Qwen3.5-9B to 54.4.

Our contributions are threefold:

A training collection of 3.7 million question–answer pairs and a data construction pipeline that derives execution-related supervision from human videos, robot episodes, and simulation, with egocentric video serving as a major data source.

ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B VLM that jointly supports spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation, achieving leading overall performance across the corresponding evaluations.

An empirical analysis of planning and execution judgments through capability-level comparisons, controlled visual inputs, temporal question pairs, and an ablation of egocentric supervision.

1. A training collection of 3.7 million question–answer pairs and a data construction pipeline that derives execution-related supervision from human videos, robot episodes, and simulation, with egocentric video serving as a major data source.

2. ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B VLM that jointly supports spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation, achieving leading overall performance across the corresponding evaluations.

3. An empirical analysis of planning and execution judgments through capability-level comparisons, controlled visual inputs, temporal question pairs, and an ablation of egocentric supervision.

title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
authors: Shibo Zhou,Tianqi Hong,Zheng Yan,He Yang
abstract:
Power electronics carries the energy transition, yet its hardware still improves at the speed of human hands: an
engineer must design, build, test and improve each new board. We present JARVIS, an embodied agent that does all
four by itself. JARVIS first knows its machines: for each one, it keeps a record of what the machine is, how to reach
it and what its limits are. It then scans its bench with a 3D scanner on its robot arm, obtains a panorama of the whole
bench and builds from it, on its own, an executable digital twin of the bench, in which the programs that drive the
real machines also run. In the twin, the agent rehearses the experiment before it uses any material: every motion of
the arm, the heating of the board, the duration of every step and the response of the circuit. One sentence typed on
a screen then starts the run. The agent builds the board on unmodified desktop machines. The arm carries the board and
changes the tool heads of a desktop PCB printer, which deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste and follows the
surface of the board as it prints. A pick-and-place machine sets the parts. The agent tests the board
hardware-in-the-loop on an OPAL-RT real-time simulator, with an oscilloscope as a second instrument, and
it checks every step of its work through its 3D scanner and the machines’ own cameras and sensors. Finally, it analyzes the
measured data, explains where and why the board departs from its design, and proposes the next design, which it draws
in KiCad and rehearses in the twin. On a 60 Hz notch filter of the kind used in the sensing chain of grid-connected
converters, JARVIS ran the experiment in 2 h 39 min with no human action, and the board
removed 50.6 dB at 60 Hz. It was the first run of the experiment: the agent resolved by itself the faults it
met on the way, and from the data and its own run it proposed improvements to the design and to the experiment. Rehearsal exposed five defects before any material was used, including a test
plan that would have rejected a correct board. A live display shows the bench at work, and a thinking screen shows what
the agent thinks. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the
physical design–build–test–learn loop for circuit boards.
introduction:
Power electronics sits between every energy source and every load. It feeds solar and wind power into the grid,
charges and drives electric vehicles, and supplies data centers. Its hardware improves through a loop. Engineers state
what a board must do, design it, build it, measure it and learn from the gap; then they go around again. Before a
board or a controller meets a real grid, the field verifies it hardware-in-the-loop (HIL). The real board is
connected to a real-time simulator, which produces the board’s input signals and records its response in real
time [1]. Every turn of this loop still passes through a human engineer. The engineer reads the
requirement, draws the schematic, lays out the board, carries it from machine to machine, wires it to the simulator
and interprets the result.

Language models have started to help with the design step. In power electronics, they choose modulation strategies and
converter parameters [2, 3], draft converter designs [4] and generate
schematics and board layouts from a requirement [5]. In other fields, large language model
(LLM) agents fix real software issues [6, 7], write hardware description
code [8, 9, 10] and design analog circuits [11].
Robots guided by language grasp, place and assemble objects [12, 13, 14, 15]. The physical part of the hardware loop, however, is still done by people. Each turn of the loop crosses
several machines, materials and instruments, and no autonomous system has handled all of them together.

Self-driving laboratories, in which robots run experiments that software chooses, show what closing such a loop
is worth. Guided by optimizers or by LLM agents, they have searched photocatalyst mixtures [16],
synthesized computationally predicted inorganic compounds [17], and planned and run chemical
reactions [18, 19]. They compress months of bench work into
days [20, 21]. Most of these systems vary the recipe of a fixed workflow: the steps
stay the same and only the quantities change. Even an agent that builds its own chemistry laboratory produces samples,
not devices that must first be designed [22]. Hardware asks for more, because a new circuit is a
new object. It changes the pattern to print, the paste to dispense, the parts to place, the way the board is contacted
and the test that judges it. Language-model tools for electronic and power-electronic design, on the other hand, stop at
simulation or the layout, and people still build and measure the board. What is missing is an agent that is engineer and
technician at once: one that designs a board, builds it on real machines, measures it, understands the result and
decides what to change.

We present JARVIS, an embodied agent that closes the design–build–test–learn loop for power-electronics hardware
(Fig. 1). Fig. 2 shows its bench, next to the twin that the agent built of it. JARVIS works in
four stages, and each stage builds on the one before.

It knows its machines. For every machine, the agent keeps a record of what the machine is, how to
connect to it, what its limits are, and what has worked or failed on it. Every fact in the record states its source.

It builds its own twin of the bench. A 3D scanner on the robot arm scans the bench from several directions.
The agent merges the views into a panorama of the whole bench and places the complete CAD model of every machine and
fixture (a holder for boards or tools) where the scan found it. The result is a digital twin of the bench.
The twin is executable: the programs that control and judge the real bench also run inside it.

It rehearses the experiment in the twin. From a need stated in plain language, the agent sets the
requirement, designs the circuit and the printed circuit board (PCB), and turns the design into programs for every
machine. It
then runs the whole build and test in the twin. The rehearsal covers the physical side of the experiment: the motion
of the arm, the heating of the board and its holder, the time of every step and the response of the circuit. The
agent fixes every defect it finds there.

It runs the experiment on the bench and learns from it. A six-axis arm, a desktop PCB printer and a
pick-and-place machine build the board. An OPAL-RT real-time simulator tests it hardware-in-the-loop. The agent then analyzes the
measured response, explains each departure from the design, and proposes the next design, which it draws and
rehearses.

Four principles make these stages work on a real bench. First, the agent operates machines as a skilled person does:
no machine’s hardware or firmware is changed. The arm changes the printer’s tool heads, and the agent operates the
printer’s own application as a person would click through it. Second, the agent checks its own work. Its 3D scanner
and the machines’ own cameras and sensors confirm every step, and no person inspects anything during a run. Third, every
physical action is accountable. Before each action, the agent writes its goal, plan, expected result and stopping
condition into an attempt ledger. After the action, it saves the full output as evidence and records what it learned.
A session is one continuous run of the agent, and the language model remembers nothing from earlier sessions.
The records therefore let any later session resume the work. Fourth, the work is visible. During a run, a live display
shows the bench and the data of every machine, and a thinking screen shows what the agent is thinking, in plain words.

Our benchmark is a 60 Hz notch filter. A grid-connected converter must measure small quantities next to the large
60 Hz fundamental of the grid, such as harmonics or a DC offset in its current. Its low-level sensor signals also pick
up 60 Hz hum. A 60 Hz notch filter removes the fundamental or the hum, so that the small quantity can be measured. The
requirement of such a filter is precise and its test is exact, so the behavior of the loop can be judged without doubt.
A person stated the need in plain words: a notch filter at signal level, as hardware. The agent set the requirement
itself: remove 60 Hz mains hum from a ±\pm10 V signal by at least 40 dB, with a flat passband. It designed the
circuit and the board in KiCad, and it ran the rehearsal of their build in the twin. The person read the agent’s plan and agreed
to it in one sentence typed on a screen, which started the run. In JARVIS, a person states the need and agrees to the
agent’s plan; the agreement is a safety step of this first stage, and once the system is mature, the need alone will
start the work. JARVIS then ran it to the end with no human
action, in 2 h 39 min: it surveyed the bench, built the board, tested it on the simulator, and pushed the
tested board out of its holder to load the next blank one. The board’s notch lay at 60.3 Hz, and it removed
50.6 dB at 60 Hz. From the measured response, the agent explained why the passband sagged at low frequency: the
filter network’s output impedance met the load on its output, and it proposed the next board, which it drew in KiCad and rehearsed in the twin. This was the first run of the
experiment. On the way, the agent met faults of the kinds common in computer and engineering practice and
resolved each by itself, and at the end it proposed improvements to both the board and the experiment, which a platform
that executes a fixed recipe does not do. Rehearsal in the twin
had caught defects before they could waste a board or cause a wrong verdict. In one, the planned frequency sweep would
have failed a correct board. In another, the pattern that the printer draws before each print to start the ink flowing
would have crossed the circuit.

Our contributions are:

Autonomous Hardware Loop for Power Electronics. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power
electronics, and for circuit boards in general, in which an agent closes the complete design–build–test–learn
loop. From a need stated in plain language, it sets the requirement, designs the circuit and the board, builds the
board on unmodified desktop machines, verifies it hardware-in-the-loop on the simulator, analyzes the measurement and turns it into the
next design.

An Executable Digital Twin Built by Scanning, for Physical Rehearsal. The agent scans its bench, merges
the views into a panorama and builds the twin on its own. The twin runs the bench’s own motion planners,
safety checks and physical models, so every multi-machine build is rehearsed from start to end, including its motion,
heat, time and circuit response, before it runs.

Embodied Machine Operation. One arm and one agent operate the printer, the pick-and-place machine and the
simulator without changing their hardware or firmware. The arm changes the printer’s tool heads, a task the
printer was never designed for, and exchanges boards by itself. The agent adapts the build to each board: it reasons
about the board’s surface at every stage, has it mapped so that the nozzle follows it, and decides how much
unevenness each stage may have.

Self-Checking, Accountable and Visible Autonomy. The agent confirms every step with its 3D scanner
and the machines’ own cameras and sensors, and measures the board with two instruments. An attempt ledger with a source label
on every fact makes every physical action auditable and resumable across sessions. Two screens show people what the
bench is doing and what the agent is thinking.

1. Autonomous Hardware Loop for Power Electronics. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power
electronics, and for circuit boards in general, in which an agent closes the complete design–build–test–learn
loop. From a need stated in plain language, it sets the requirement, designs the circuit and the board, builds the
board on unmodified desktop machines, verifies it hardware-in-the-loop on the simulator, analyzes the measurement and turns it into the
next design.

2. An Executable Digital Twin Built by Scanning, for Physical Rehearsal. The agent scans its bench, merges
the views into a panorama and builds the twin on its own. The twin runs the bench’s own motion planners,
safety checks and physical models, so every multi-machine build is rehearsed from start to end, including its motion,
heat, time and circuit response, before it runs.

3. Embodied Machine Operation. One arm and one agent operate the printer, the pick-and-place machine and the
simulator without changing their hardware or firmware. The arm changes the printer’s tool heads, a task the
printer was never designed for, and exchanges boards by itself. The agent adapts the build to each board: it reasons
about the board’s surface at every stage, has it mapped so that the nozzle follows it, and decides how much
unevenness each stage may have.

4. Self-Checking, Accountable and Visible Autonomy. The agent confirms every step with its 3D scanner
and the machines’ own cameras and sensors, and measures the board with two instruments. An attempt ledger with a source label
on every fact makes every physical action auditable and resumable across sessions. Two screens show people what the
bench is doing and what the agent is thinking.

title: An Open-Source ROS 2 Framework for Shared Control in Surgical Teleoperation: Integrating the Haply Inverse3 with the da Vinci Research Kit
authors: Balint Varga,Sebastian Fritz,Gergely Kiss,Kristof Takacs,Peter Galambos
abstract: Surgical teleoperation deprives surgeons of touch, forcing visual inference of tissue forces; the commercial platforms now restoring force feedback remain closed, preventing open research on haptic shared control. This paper provides a system-contribution: it presents an open-source, ROS 2-native framework that integrates the compact, three-degrees-of-freedom (3-DOF) Haply Inverse3 haptic device with the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). The framework includes a novel mapping strategy that combines 3-DOF translational device input with separately tracked VerseGrip orientation into 6-DOF patient-side manipulator commands. Two virtual-fixture-inspired guidance modes serve as reference implementations to evaluate the framework in a within-subjects user study on a teleoperated hot-wire benchmark task in simulation, and the architecture is further demonstrated on physical dVRK hardware. Relative to unassisted manual control, linear guidance significantly reduced both the number of wire contacts and the task completion time, whereas the progressive-stiffness guidance produced consistent but statistically non-significant trends in the same direction. Subjective ratings of workload, agency, and satisfaction showed favorable descriptive trends for the guidance modes. The results demonstrate the feasibility of haptic shared control with a compact device coupled to the dVRK and provide an openly available, reproducible platform for future research. They further suggest that simpler linear feedback may be more robust for inexperienced operators than more complex profiles.
introduction:
Robotic surgical systems such as the da Vinci platform have transformed minimally invasive surgery, but a fundamental limitation remains: the physical separation between surgeon and patient removes natural tactile and force feedback. Current clinical systems have therefore relied primarily on visual cues and learned motor strategies to regulate interaction forces [1, 2].
This sensory gap can increase applied forces, elevate the risk of tissue damage, and make it harder to discriminate tissue properties during manipulation [3, 4].
Although da Vinci 5 introduces force feedback, the platform remains closed, which limits experimental access to the feedback architecture, custom control designs, and alternative haptic rendering strategies.
Recent studies suggest that force feedback can reduce applied tissue forces and improve task performance, but the available evidence is still limited and does not yet isolate force feedback from all other platform changes in clinical use [5, 6, 7, 8].
Moreover, because human-in-the-loop control is a complex, multidimensional phenomenon, the design of effective haptic shared control strategies for surgical teleoperation remains an open question that requires further investigation [9, 10, 11].
In contrast, research platforms such as the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) provide the openness needed to investigate new control architectures and human-robot interaction concepts [12, 13].

Integrating haptic devices, such as the 3-DOF Haply Inverse3, with the 6-DOF dVRK requires combining secondary orientation sensing with translation and matching coordinate frames.
The primary goal of this work is the system integration itself: providing the research community with an open, ROS 2-native solution for using compact haptic devices with the dVRK. The novelty lies in the end-to-end integration of a compact 3-DOF haptic device with a da Vinci-derived teleoperation platform. The haptic shared-control evaluation presented in this paper serves as a means of validating this platform rather than as an end in itself; the evaluated feedback modes are intentionally simple implementations. The hot-wire task is used as a benchmark because it emphasizes path following, speed regulation, and collision avoidance, all of which are relevant to surgical teleoperation.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

We develop an open-source ROS 2 architecture that enables teleoperation between the Haply Inverse3 with the VerseGrip and the dVRK, including a specified mapping pipeline.

We implement two virtual-fixture-inspired guidance modes (linear and progressive-stiffness) as reference implementations within this framework, rendered under matched maximum forces.

We empirically evaluate human-in-the-loop performance in a controlled user study, showing improvement in both wire contacts and completion time under linear guidance, and demonstrate the transferability of the architecture to physical dVRK hardware.

title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yuzhi Huang,Jie Wu,Fanding Huang,Junchao Lin,Weichen Zhang,Ziyi Xiong,Yang Li,Zhengwei Xie,Zhimin Wang,Zhen Liu,Jiazhen Huang,Yuzheng Zhang,Yuche Liu,Hongyi Yang,Chen Tang,Shixiang Tang,Hakan Aktas,Adam Wu,Duo Wu,Kangye Ji,Shuzhao Xie,Huanan Liu,Weijue Bu,Chenxin Li,Xinyuan Wang,Tianyi Bai,Yinan Mao,Jiawei Wang,Minglei Li,Heng Yu,Ehsan Adeli,Minchen Li,Yong-Lu Li,Cengiz Öztireli,Huazhe Xu,Chao Yu,Jing Zhang,Shanghang Zhang,Weitao Zhou,Wenwu Zhu,Cheng Chi,Jingyan Jiang,Zhi Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
“Knowledge is the beginning of action and action is the completion of knowledge.” — Wang Yangming

The central ambition of embodied intelligence is to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability. Studies of human sensorimotor control indicate that adaptive and reliable manipulation involves reasoning over task-relevant information, executing physical actions precisely, and adapting behavior through environmental feedback [1, 2, 3]. In the cooking task of Fig. , a robot must remember which ingredient to add next, coordinate both arms to add the ingredient, and switch the stove from heating to keep-warm mode based on temperature feedback. These requirements motivate three capabilities. Mind decides what to do from earlier observations. Act produces the required physical effect in time. Mind-Action Composition closes the loop, so that remembered information guides each action and each physical outcome updates the next decision.

Recent embodied systems spanning multimodal agents [32], vision-language-action models (VLAs) [19, 20], world-action models (WAMs) [23, 26], and hybrid architectures [27, 28] have substantially advanced robotic manipulation. However, their capabilities in Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition remain poorly understood, which makes it difficult to identify capability bottlenecks and guide further development. Two limitations of existing embodied benchmarks [4, 6, 7, 8, 12] explain why. First, conventional benchmarks often assess cognitive reasoning and physical execution within the same tasks and report only whether a task succeeds [4, 5, 6], so a failure cannot be traced to Mind or Act. Second, although recent benchmarks have introduced finer-grained diagnostics and separate assessments of reasoning and physical execution [8, 11, 12, 13], they rarely evaluate Mind-Action Composition, particularly whether physical outcomes can effectively inform subsequent decisions. Closing this gap requires tasks that stress one capability while keeping the others present but easy, a judgment of composition based on verified physical outcomes, and a comparison of systems with different action interfaces and inference speeds on equal terms.

To this end, we introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark for Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition in robotic manipulation (Fig. ). Its 30 tasks come from five real-world application domains and are organized into three views of ten tasks each, covering 12 capability categories. Each view emphasizes one demand by design. Mind tasks keep physical operations simple, Act tasks state the required operation explicitly, and Mind2Act tasks chain dependent operations so that each physical outcome decides what comes next. Success is judged from physical predicates on the environment, and the evaluator records stages and events within each episode. Each task has three difficulty levels that raise its demands while keeping the objective fixed. Each level runs in a Clean and a Random scene, which share the same instance but differ in clutter, materials and lighting (180 configurations in total). Agents and end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and 4,500 demonstrations (75.8 hours) are provided for fine-tuning end-to-end policies. A diagnosis harness combines rule-based analysis of the evaluator’s stage and event records with an LLM judge to attribute each failed episode of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition. It summarizes each of these systems in a per-model report called a model profile card (Fig. 5; Appendix E.4).

Our evaluation on Mind2Act World reveals a clear pattern. Existing architectures are uneven across Mind and Act, yet all struggle with Mind-Action Composition. The strongest agent retains task state well but struggles to sustain contact, and its timed successes are measured with a simulator that pauses during inference. End-to-end policies respond within a fraction of a second and execute practiced motions, but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization. Notably, on Mind2Act, the strongest system succeeds in only 12.0% of episodes, far below its 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Competence in either capability therefore does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks.

The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition.

We develop a diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to Mind, Act, or Mind-Action Composition. The harness also summarizes three representative models in model profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies.

We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. Our results show that systems differ in which of Mind and Act is weaker, and that all of them struggle with Mind-Action Composition.

1. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition.

2. We develop a diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to Mind, Act, or Mind-Action Composition. The harness also summarizes three representative models in model profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies.

3. We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. Our results show that systems differ in which of Mind and Act is weaker, and that all of them struggle with Mind-Action Composition.

title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
authors: EngineAI
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces.
Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale.
We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills.
Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert.
We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert.
Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks.
After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and π0.5\pi_{0.5} in both individual and long-horizon evaluations.
The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.
introduction:
Humanoid robots could help people with a wide range of tasks in homes and workplaces.
Many require whole-body loco-manipulation, in which the robot coordinates its steps and posture with its hand movements [17, 24].
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [5, 16, 31] and world action models [47, 22, 48] have shown that robots can learn diverse manipulation skills from demonstrations.
For humanoids, however, the cost of whole-body teleoperation limits the range of tasks and environments represented in robot demonstrations [13, 49].

Human experience of everyday activity offers a more scalable alternative to robot teleoperation.
Recent work draws on the variety of activities and environments in these videos [46, 43] to pretrain manipulation policies [41, 52, 23].
Despite this diversity, visual observations alone provide no explicit targets for whole-body motion.
Prior work therefore retargets recorded human motion to obtain robot action targets [7, 21].
However, differences in body proportions and joint structure can cause the resulting postures and hand trajectories to deviate from those in the human demonstration [2].
These deviations motivate retaining the original human motion as a training signal alongside the retargeted robot actions.
Using that signal at scale requires egocentric video paired with synchronized whole-body motion across diverse tasks and environments.
Yet many large egocentric datasets provide video alone or primarily track the head and hands [11, 15], while datasets such as Nymeria [28] offer only a few hundred hours of paired recordings.

We address this data gap with Awaken-Human, a dataset for humanoid pretraining that pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion.
Collected under a common protocol using lightweight wearable sensors, the demonstrations cover more than 100 skills across homes, workplaces, retail spaces, and storage areas.
We reconstruct 3D hand motion from the video and annotate the demonstrations with subtask descriptions and frame-level depth maps.
For each demonstration, we retain the original human trajectory alongside the corresponding retargeted robot actions.

Building on Awaken-Human, we introduce Awaken-HI, a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation.
By predicting human motion alongside retargeted robot actions, its shared action expert receives direct supervision from the original human trajectories.
During pretraining, the expert also predicts camera-frame wrist poses, while separate heads estimate current and future depth and describe the current subtask.
We then post-train the policy on approximately 150 hours of T800 teleoperation data using the same robot action interface.

We observe that Awaken-HI’s robot action prediction error on held-out data follows an empirical scaling law, decreasing as the pretraining set grows from 5,000 to 50,000 hours of human demonstrations.
With the same T800 demonstrations for post-training, more human pretraining data also raises the policy’s mean success rate on three household tasks.
Controlled ablations show that adding human motion supervision reduces action prediction error and improves real-robot task success compared with pretraining on retargeted actions alone.
After full-corpus pretraining, we post-train Awaken-HI on the same T800 demonstrations used for GR00T N1.7 [31] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [16].
Awaken-HI outperforms both baselines on all eight individual loco-manipulation tasks, averaging 93.75% success.
It retains this advantage on long-horizon industrial and household tasks.
The policy also follows instructions that pair familiar objects and destinations in new ways and applies a learned manipulation skill to objects unseen during robot post-training.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce Awaken-HI, a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and robot actions through a shared action expert.

We build Awaken-Human, a dataset pairing 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion across diverse tasks and environments.

We find that as human pretraining data grows, action prediction error decreases according to an empirical scaling law and real-robot success rates rise. Awaken-HI also generalizes to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations and to objects unseen during robot post-training.

1. We introduce Awaken-HI, a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and robot actions through a shared action expert.

2. We build Awaken-Human, a dataset pairing 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion across diverse tasks and environments.

3. We find that as human pretraining data grows, action prediction error decreases according to an empirical scaling law and real-robot success rates rise. Awaken-HI also generalizes to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations and to objects unseen during robot post-training.

title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
authors: Weile Li,Yunfan Lou,Muqing Shi,Zihao Zhang,Zhenbiao Huang,Boxian Yao,Xiyu Zhu,Zhibo Pang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robotic manipulation [5, 19, 4, 27]. Building on pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), VLA models learn to predict robot actions from visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive states through imitation learning [3]. Nevertheless, contact-rich manipulation remains challenging, as critical contact events, such as incipient slip and jamming during insertion, are often difficult to infer from external visual observations. To capture contact events, recent efforts augment VLA models with tactile observations [40, 16, 38, 44, 26, 42, 11, 2, 22], typically acquired by vision-based tactile sensors such as GelSight [41] and DIGIT [20], which capture the deformation of a soft gel.

Existing visuo-tactile policies incorporate tactile observations as additional inputs [16, 32, 40, 43, 49], predict future tactile signals [9, 13, 33, 38, 46], or emphasize tactile changes during training [10, 25, 36, 37, 45] (Fig. 1c). However, incorporating tactile inputs yields inconsistent gains and can even reduce the success rate relative to the same VLA without tactile inputs [40, 44]. Moreover, we apply a tactile-off test, which removes tactile input at test time, and find that the success rates of some existing policies change little, indicating limited reliance on tactile information (Sec. 4.4). We attribute the inconsistent gains and the limited reliance to the nature of the tactile signal, since a tactile sensor measures how the contact responds to the robot’s own actions. Consequently, given the initial tactile observation, a substantial portion of the subsequent tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 1a). As an input, the predictable portion is largely redundant, and adding an input modality can even degrade performance [34]. When future tactile signals are the prediction target, the predictable portion makes up most of the target, so the prediction loss is dominated by changes that vision and executed actions already explain. Weighting the loss by the magnitude of tactile change does not help, since the largest changes are often the predictable ones (Fig. 4). A central question arises: How can the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain be isolated and used to guide VLA policy learning?

To answer this question, we propose TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain as the supervision signal for VLA training. Inspired by the notion of innovation in estimation theory [18, 17], we define tactile innovation as the residual tactile change after accounting for the initial tactile observation, visual observations, and executed actions. Three properties of tactile innovation determine the design of TacInno. First, tactile innovation is conditional on visual observations and executed actions. We therefore introduce the TacInno tokenizer, which learns a compact discrete code as a proxy for tactile innovation and conditions both its encoder and decoder on the corresponding visual observations and executed actions, so that the code retains the contact dynamics that the two conditions cannot explain (Fig. 1b). Second, tactile innovation is dynamic, arising from transient contact events, such as incipient slip, that span several control steps. The tokenizer therefore encodes a short sequence of tactile observations with causal temporal attention rather than a single pair of frames. Third, tactile innovation lies in the future and is unavailable when the policy acts. We therefore train TacInno-VLA to predict the code from current observations as an auxiliary objective, supervising the tactile representations used for action prediction. The code serves only as a training target, and the tokenizer and auxiliary prediction heads are removed at deployment.

We evaluate TacInno on six contact-rich tasks from the UniVTAC benchmark [8] and four real-world tasks using a Franka FR3 robot equipped with a vision-based tactile sensor. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% in simulation and 70.5% in the real world, the highest among the evaluated visuo-tactile policies. Ablation studies verify the contribution of each design, and the tactile-off test confirms that TacInno-VLA relies on tactile input.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

With the tactile-off test, we show that some existing visuo-tactile policies rely little on tactile input, attribute the limited reliance to the redundancy of the tactile signal, and propose to separate the tactile change that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation.

We propose TacInno, which encodes tactile innovation into a discrete code with a conditional multi-frame tokenizer and uses the code solely as an auxiliary training target, adding no module for the code at deployment.

TacInno-VLA outperforms the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points in average success rate in simulation and the real world, respectively. The success rate of TacInno-VLA drops from 88% to 0% on Lift Can under the tactile-off test and by 21 percentage points on the lifting tasks when the code encodes the entire tactile change.

1. With the tactile-off test, we show that some existing visuo-tactile policies rely little on tactile input, attribute the limited reliance to the redundancy of the tactile signal, and propose to separate the tactile change that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation.

2. We propose TacInno, which encodes tactile innovation into a discrete code with a conditional multi-frame tokenizer and uses the code solely as an auxiliary training target, adding no module for the code at deployment.

3. TacInno-VLA outperforms the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points in average success rate in simulation and the real world, respectively. The success rate of TacInno-VLA drops from 88% to 0% on Lift Can under the tactile-off test and by 21 percentage points on the lifting tasks when the code encodes the entire tactile change.
