title: SpecFlow: Flow Matching in the Acceleration Spectrum for Multi-Agent Trajectory Forecasting
authors: Ziyang Xu,Peng Han,Hai Zhou
abstract: Multimodal trajectory forecasting must cover diverse future behaviors without sacrificing dynamical coherence. Most generative forecasters evolve frame-wise positions directly, leaving the relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration implicit. We present SpecFlow, a conditional flow-matching framework that treats the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients of future accelerations as its generative state. SpecFlow learns a transport from Gaussian noise to acceleration spectra and reconstructs velocity and position through fixed analytical integration initialized by the last observed state. A joint phase-space objective supervises all three kinematic levels. To represent destination uncertainty without future information, an endpoint predictor produces candidate destinations and confidence scores solely from observed context, and the highest-confidence candidate conditions the spectral denoiser. Alternating attention over trajectory hypotheses and agents captures multimodality and interaction. Under best-of-20 evaluation, SpecFlow achieves average minADE/minFDE of 0.15/0.22 on ETH/UCY, 0.69/0.86 at four seconds on NBA, and 7.38/11.57 on SDD. It establishes state-of-the-art results across all five ETH/UCY scenes and achieves the lowest four-second ADE on NBA with a tied-best FDE, while remaining competitive on SDD. Together, these results demonstrate that acceleration-spectrum flow matching provides an effective structured generative state across smooth pedestrian motion, coordinated multi-agent sports dynamics, and heterogeneous outdoor trajectories. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
authors: Yuxi Zheng,Yueqian Lin,Yudong Liu,Zijia Tang,Junyu Pan,Yiheng Wang,Hai Helen Li,Yiran Chen
abstract:
Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon.
In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output.
We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks.
The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network.
The endpoints do not fit the sink profile.
Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers.
On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4 points, and replacing their value directions with those of another observation lowers it by 3.2 to 7.2 points across three donors, whereas the same replacement on two non-endpoint tokens in the executed prefix lowers it by 28.4 points.
The token that does fit the sink profile on mass and value norm is the prefix BOS; on this checkpoint, zeroing its value raises success in two paired runs, by +13.2+13.2 points (95% CI [+7.0,+19.4][+7.0,+19.4]) and +6.0+6.0 points ([+0.2,+11.8][+0.2,+11.8]).
Inside the action chunk, a relative-offset routing profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps closed-loop success on three held-out tasks (42.7% against a 38.7% baseline), while uniform or shuffled routing drops success to 3–4%.
High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does.
introduction:
Flow-based vision-language-action policies denoise a chunk of continuous actions [3, 2].
In the action expert of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, each action query attends, at each denoising step, to a multimodal prefix and to all action tokens.
Wang et al. [17] observe that the first and last action tokens receive high incoming attention, call them radial action sinks, propose that they anchor temporal consistency across chunks, and use them to set an adaptive execution horizon.

The word sink carries a specific profile from language models: one token receives much of the attention, its value is small, and reading it changes the output little [8, 1].
If the endpoints had that profile, attention on them would park probability mass rather than carry action information.
Wang et al. make no small-value claim; the name alone invites this reading.
We therefore ask three questions about the endpoints and the tokens around them.
Where does the endpoint mass come from?
Do the endpoint values behave like a sink’s?
If not, which token does, and what keeps the action tokens distinct from each other?
We do not test the horizon rule of [17]; our results bear on how its anchors should be described, not on whether the rule works.

We answer these questions with paired interventions in the action expert of π0.5\pi_{0.5} on RoboCasa [11].
Each intervention and its baseline share the observation and the initial noise, and every closed-loop comparison is paired with the baseline of the same execution.

We find:

Endpoint mass is positional. Current-layer RoPE produces it in shallow layers and upstream action-token RoPE in deeper layers; removing the relevant rotations returns it to the uniform reference at high and mid noise (Section 4).

Endpoint values are not a null sink, and success is far less sensitive to them than to interior values. Their norms and gated outputs are typical or larger. Masking or zeroing them changes closed-loop success by less than 4 points and replacing them by 3 to 7 points, while replacing two executed non-endpoint tokens lowers it by 25 to 28 points (Section 5).

The sink-like token is the prefix BOS. It has high mass and a small, shared value; on this checkpoint, zeroing that value raises success by +13.2+13.2 and +6.0+6.0 points in two runs (Section 5).

Action routing follows a relative-offset profile. A shared profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps success on three held-out tasks, while routings that break the offset structure drop success to 3–4% (Section 6).

title: Alignment Drives Reuse: Learning Generalizable Robot-Use Agents from Heterogeneous Experience
authors: Ziyue Wang,Yaopeng Yang,Liyi Zhou
abstract:
Vision-language models demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains.
However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging.
Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric
conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across
benchmarks and hardware.
We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous
interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared
skillset for robot manipulation?
We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation
skills by aligning heterogeneous settings.
Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent
coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots.
It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing
interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration
policy that guides their selection and composition, without any
demonstrations or model weight updates.
We interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700
learning rollouts per agent model.
During training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and
tasks by 9–28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8–13.3 on
RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1–14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1–3).
After training, with the learned skills frozen, UniCraft demonstrates zero-shot
transfer across 4 new robot embodiments and 5 additional agent models on
robosuite and RoboDojo.
introduction:
Large language models and vision-language models have
demonstrated broad generalization across language, image, and video
tasks [4, 1].
Natural language and images provide a unified interface for representing
information and specifying tasks across domains.
Aligning heterogeneous data through this shared interface supports training
at scale on diverse sources, allowing models to acquire knowledge that
extends to new concepts, instructions, and reasoning
tasks [12, 16].
At inference, the same interface enables zero-shot transfer to new tasks without
task-specific examples or parameter updates [43, 41, 25].

However, comparable generalization in robotics remains challenging.
One of the main reasons is heterogeneity (Figure 1(a)).
Robot embodiments differ in their kinematics, observation
spaces, and action representations; even the same numerical action can
produce different physical effects depending on the robot and its
controller [33, 47].
These embodiment differences also shape how interaction experience is
collected and represented, while datasets introduce further differences in
coordinate conventions and annotation practices [23, 47].
These differences fragment experience across platforms, making it costly to
collect and difficult to transfer to new environments and embodiments.
These challenges also affect vision-language-action models, which extend pretrained
vision-language models to robot control by learning to predict actions from task-specific
demonstrations [53, 23, 3, 2, 49].
Their improvements on manipulation benchmarks do not consistently translate
into generalization beyond training conditions: changes in scenes,
instructions, or embodiments can cause sharp performance
drops [13, 47, 50].
Qwen-RobotManip advocates aligning heterogeneous manipulation data in
representation, motion, and behavior before VLA
training [47].

Another line of work learns and evolves robot control policies through
iterative interaction with the environment, reducing reliance on
task-specific trajectory
demonstrations [7, 17, 27, 29, 48].
In this setting, large language models or vision-language models write executable policy code and
continually revise it using interaction
feedback [26, 29, 48].
Successful executions and validated repairs are distilled into programmatic skills,
accumulating cross-task knowledge and enabling agents to solve diverse tasks through skill composition. [17, 29, 48].
This line of work represents a pragmatic middle ground between learning
from demonstrations in predefined settings and open-ended continual learning.
Its demonstrated scope, however, remains bounded by task definitions,
hardware configurations, and benchmark suites.
For example, GaP formulates policy evolution for variational automation
tasks, where a specified task is repeated within a fixed workcell with
bounded shape and pose variations [7].
SHAPER evaluates evolved skills under fixed execution interfaces, leaving
cross-embodiment transfer underexplored [42].
Skill2Real learns programmatic skills separately on LIBERO-90 and
robosuite [17].
These boundaries and misalignments constrain the experience generalization across tasks, scenarios and embodiments.
Naturally, they motivate three research questions.
(i) Can alignment enable unified learning of manipulation skills from
interaction across heterogeneous tasks, benchmarks, and embodiments?
(ii) If so, does such learning improve generalization to unseen tasks and scenarios?
(iii) Can the learned skills also transfer to unseen benchmarks and new embodiments?

Inspired by the alignment first, then scale
principle [47], we present UniCraft, a unified framework
designed to align heterogeneous settings (e.g., embodiments, environments,
and benchmark cases) for learning robot manipulation skills through
iterative interactions without trajectory demonstrations or updates to model weights.
We realize this principle by introducing
(i) a unified environment representation that describes observed scene
entities as typed Objects and exposes robot and camera capabilities
through a shared Python package;
(ii) composable skills that use reusable library functions
and declare the action interfaces required for execution, with adapters
providing their hardware-specific implementations;
(iii) a learnable orchestration policy that guides the agent model to write
and execute programs in response to observations and rollout outcomes; and
(iv) a canonical case representation that consistently specifies task
instructions and success conditions, embodiments, scenes, and initial
states across various benchmarks.
During the skill learning stage, mixed rollouts of these cases provide
aggregated feedback for jointly optimizing the shared programmatic
components and the orchestration policy.
This alignment enables each agent model to learn one shared repository from
180 tasks across LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, covering six
robot embodiments. Learning interleaves these tasks and embodiments,
yielding 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model
(Figure 1(b)). UniCraft demonstrates improved generalization
across 66 unseen-scenario cases and 36 held-out tasks with continued refinement,
as well as zero-shot transfer capability to four
new robot embodiments and the unseen robosuite [52] and
RoboDojo [9] benchmarks. Our main contributions are:

Methodology. We introduce UniCraft, which aligns execution
interfaces and learning cases, enabling joint learning and refinement of
one shared skillset and its orchestration policy across benchmarks and embodiments.

Interleaved training. We interleave interaction experience
from 300 task–embodiment pairs spanning 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments
to learn one shared skillset per agent model for reuse across heterogeneous settings.

Generalization. We demonstrate improved generalization
across 3 agent models over 3 consecutive training epochs. From the first
to the third epoch, pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks
increases by 9–28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8–13.3 on RoboTwin,
and 3.1–14.4 on RoboCasa365.

Zero-shot transfer. We show that UniCraft can transfer
zero-shot across 4 new robot embodiments, 2 unseen benchmarks, and 5
additional agent models.

1. Methodology. We introduce UniCraft, which aligns execution
interfaces and learning cases, enabling joint learning and refinement of
one shared skillset and its orchestration policy across benchmarks and embodiments.

2. Interleaved training. We interleave interaction experience
from 300 task–embodiment pairs spanning 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments
to learn one shared skillset per agent model for reuse across heterogeneous settings.

3. Generalization. We demonstrate improved generalization
across 3 agent models over 3 consecutive training epochs. From the first
to the third epoch, pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks
increases by 9–28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8–13.3 on RoboTwin,
and 3.1–14.4 on RoboCasa365.

4. Zero-shot transfer. We show that UniCraft can transfer
zero-shot across 4 new robot embodiments, 2 unseen benchmarks, and 5
additional agent models.

title: PUPPET: Physical-Unified Platform for Presence, Embodiment, and Teleoperation
authors: Mahika Vats,Milan Groshev,Carlos Gomez Cubero,Eduardo Castelló Ferrer
abstract: Remote access to robotics hardware does not by itself guarantee usable experimental data. A teleoperated trial can complete the task and still produce an incomplete or inconsistent record. PUPPET aims to solve this problem by presenting a cyber-physical framework that opens a physical robotics laboratory through a continuously synchronized VR replica of the robot, stranding environment, and task objects. In addition, PUPPET integrates a trial validation pipeline built into the experimental workflow. We evaluated PUPPET in a within-subject study with 30 participants, who performed the same table-to-shelf object-transfer task in person, through 2D teleoperation, and through PUPPET. VR reduced post-learning completion time by 27.7% over 2D (68.7 s vs. 95.0 s), statistically indistinguishable from in-person execution (72.1 s). It also produced more validation-ready (85.6% vs. 66.0%) and intervention-free (89.7% vs. 67.2%) trials. With PUPPET we show that modality shapes the remote task performance and the reusability of the resulting experimental record.
introduction:
Recent advances in physical AI increasingly depend on real-world interaction and the collection of physical experimental data [1]. As robotic systems expand across healthcare, industrial automation, logistics, domestic assistance, and collaborative applications [2, 3], access to the underlying infrastructure remains a major bottleneck. Robots and laboratory setups are expensive, geographically fixed, and difficult to replicate. Conducting and repeating real-robot experiments is therefore still strongly tied to physical presence in a laboratory.

Remote laboratories, digital twins, and immersive teleoperation systems have reduced this barrier by making physical robots accessible over distance [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. These platforms are mainly designed for algorithmic execution, benchmarking, education, or constrained remote interaction. [5, 6, 10].
Conventional 2D teleoperation provides remote access but limits spatial awareness, requiring users to reconstruct the workspace from separate camera views. More recently, VR and XR systems have enabled more immersive robot control and large-scale demonstration collection  [11, 12, 13, 14]. Despite these advances, existing platforms are still primarily evaluated in terms of task performance, interface usability, or control quality. What remains unexplored is whether the mode of access to a physical laboratory also affects the quality and usability of the experimental data produced.

Our work addresses several questions: Can immersive VR serve as an access layer to a physical robotics laboratory to record experimental data that is complete, consistent, and supports reuse? Does an embodied virtual environment change how users experience and manage a real-robot experiment?

In this work, we present PUPPET (Physical-Unified Platform for Presence, Embodiment, and Teleoperation), a cyber-physical framework designed around the observation that successful teleoperation is not necessarily the same as successful experimentation. For instance, a remotely controlled trial may complete the task but still produce an incomplete, inconsistent, or unusable data. PUPPET addresses this by providing access to a physical robotics laboratory through a synchronized VR environment that integrates the robot, task objects, workspace, and experimental context within the same virtual space. Data collection and validation are built into the workflow, so that each trial can be assessed by task outcome and whether the resulting data is complete, consistent, and supports reuse.

We evaluated PUPPET through a within-subject user study with 30 participants, in which each participant performed the same mobile manipulation task on a PAL Robotics TIAGo robot [15] under three conditions: in-person, conventional 2D, and VR-based access. By keeping the robot, task, and physical setup fixed across conditions, the study isolates the effect of the access modality itself. Each condition includes repeated trials, allowing us to examine both task execution and learning across attempts. The evaluation addresses task effectiveness, reliability of the experimental record, and user experience.

Our results show that, after the initial learning trial, VR reduced mean completion time by 27.7% relative to 2D teleoperation (68.66 s vs. 94.96 s), while remaining similar to the in-person execution time (72.10 s) and maintaining the same task success. For experimental reliability, VR produced more intervention-free trials than 2D (89.7% vs. 67.2%) and more validation-ready trials (85.6% vs. 66.0%). For user experience, VR significantly reduced workload (2.26 vs. 2.81), increased SUS usability scores (3.78 vs. 2.43) and increased task confidence (4.43 vs. 3.50) relative to 2D teleoperation.
In summary, the contributions of our work are:

A cyber-physical virtual laboratory that provides immersive access to a real robotics experiment by synchronizing the robot, workspace, and task-relevant objects in a continuously updated VR environment.

A cyber-physical virtual laboratory that provides immersive access to a real robotics experiment by synchronizing the robot, workspace, and task-relevant objects in a continuously updated VR environment.

An integrated validation pipeline that assesses whether each remotely conducted trial produces a complete, consistent, and reusable experimental record.

A controlled within-subject study comparing in-person, 2D, and VR-based access across repeated trials, evaluating task effectiveness, experimental reliability, and user experience.

1. A cyber-physical virtual laboratory that provides immersive access to a real robotics experiment by synchronizing the robot, workspace, and task-relevant objects in a continuously updated VR environment.

2. An integrated validation pipeline that assesses whether each remotely conducted trial produces a complete, consistent, and reusable experimental record.

3. A controlled within-subject study comparing in-person, 2D, and VR-based access across repeated trials, evaluating task effectiveness, experimental reliability, and user experience.

title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
authors: Zilang Cen,Chao Tang,Fangcheng Liu,Weishi Mi,Wei Hao,JiaYu Xu,Dehao Huang,Yehui Tang,Xiaohui Cui,Tingguang Li,Xiaoyuan Zhang
abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
introduction:
Long-horizon robot manipulation requires both reliable execution and effective planning. A robot must carry out individual subtasks, assess their outcomes, and determine which goal to pursue next. Visuomotor policies, such as VLAs [9] and WAMs [22], provide action execution capability, but successful long-horizon manipulation also requires coordinating these actions with task-level decisions.

Recently, agentic robot control approaches such as GPT-as-Policy [18] and Harness VLA [25] introduce multimodal reasoning agents to interpret task context, coordinate subtasks, and guide recovery. However, repeated agent calls incur substantial token costs and inference latency [17, 11]. These costs accumulate as the agent repeatedly processes visual observations and execution history. When execution must wait for its decisions, agent intervention becomes a bottleneck even during routine behavior that the policy can handle independently. The challenge is therefore to determine when agent intervention is needed and how it should guide execution repair and plan revision, without repeatedly querying the agent itself.

To address this challenge, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor integrates stage-aware visual context with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate active subtask progress, predict transition requests, and propose next goals. Progress anomalies, transition requests, and critical contact events in candidate actions selectively trigger agent review. Using shared task and execution context, the agent can authorize continued policy execution, shorten or refine candidate actions, take over subtask execution, or revise the proposed next goal. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions. This design allows routine execution to remain with the policy while directing agent reasoning toward decisions that require further assessment or correction.

We evaluate RoC on both simulated and real-world tasks, assessing task success and token consumption. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Three long-horizon tasks on the SO-ARM101 platform further demonstrate the effectiveness of RoC in real-world settings.

To summarize, our main contributions are twofold:

We propose RoC, an efficient agentic robot control framework for long-horizon manipulation that couples monitor-triggered agent review with coordinated execution repair and plan revision.

We develop an online task-state monitor that serves as a plug-in module to guide selective agent intervention, reducing redundant agent calls and reasoning overhead.

2. We develop an online task-state monitor that serves as a plug-in module to guide selective agent intervention, reducing redundant agent calls and reasoning overhead.

title: Exposure-Aware Informative Path Planning Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi,Yihui Mao,James W. Cross,Kyle Volle,Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
abstract: This paper addresses the finite-budget exposure-aware informative path planning (IPP) problem for a fleet of mobile sensing agents. The agents map an unknown scalar field while limiting exposure to high field intensity. Existing IPP methods optimize informativeness under motion or resource constraints, but do not address field exposure constraints. We formulate exposure-aware IPP (EA-IPP) as a scalarized bi-objective belief-state Markov decision process that trades the normalized Gaussian-process (GP) information gain against a normalized measurement-derived fleet exposure index. A parameter-shared proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework with decentralized actors and a centralized fleet critic is trained offline and evaluated on unseen fields. Across the radar, plume, and wildfire field families, the EA-IPP agent achieves the lowest GP reconstruction RMSE among the evaluated baselines while retaining D-optimal information within 10%10\% of the non-learning information baseline. The minimum field exposure is approximately 34.6%34.6\%, 20.1%20.1\%, and 27%27\% below the non-exposure-aware baseline for radar, plume, and wildfire, respectively.
introduction:
Autonomous robots are useful tools for mapping spatial phenomena such as pollutant concentrations, radiological dose rates, water-quality indicators, thermal fields, biological abundance, and electromagnetic fields [18, 12]. Robot trajectories must be planned to visit informative measurement locations while respecting the operational limitations of the robot [7]. In applications where exposure to the field is detrimental, the fleet must select a sequence of measurement locations that improves field map accuracy while limiting field exposure under finite energy or time budgets [18, 2].

Information maximization under motion and resource constraints is studied under the moniker of informative path planning (IPP) [3, 7]. Existing IPP methods include combinatorial and sampling-based planning, trajectory and Bayesian optimization, and receding-horizon planning [7, 2, 6, 10]. In adaptive IPP, each measurement updates the field belief, changing the estimated informativeness of future measurement locations. These estimates are then incorporated into sampling-, optimization-, or learning-based planners through online or receding-horizon replanning [6, 11]. A probabilistic belief, such as a Gaussian process (GP), is therefore central to adaptive IPP [15]. Bayesian active design can select measurements from predictive uncertainty [9], while GP experimental design uses A- and D-optimality to reduce posterior uncertainty through trace- and determinant-based criteria, respectively [4, 8].

Covariance-based information criteria depend on measurement locations, not field measurements. Consequently, two measurement locations can provide comparable uncertainty reduction while inducing different exposure. The information-exposure trade-off considered in this paper requires an objective that jointly accounts for posterior uncertainty reduction and the exposed field intensity. The GP posterior covariance identifies locations where additional measurements can reduce model uncertainty, whereas the posterior field prediction identifies which future measurements are likely to induce high field exposure.

In cases where the GP is updated after each measurement, and each action affects future fleet configurations and trajectories, EA-IPP is a finite-horizon sequential decision problem. A reinforcement learning (RL) feedback policy is therefore trained offline to map the current belief and fleet state to the next action, avoiding long-horizon action-sequence search at deployment [11].

Yanes Luis et al. considered multi-agent ASV patrolling using deep Q-learning [21], and later incorporated local GP mean and uncertainty estimates into multi-agent DRL for information gathering [22]. These approaches optimize coverage or information gain, but do not account for cumulative exposure to the measured field. Related safe-RL methods address risk through constrained objectives or safety mechanisms [5, 1], but are not formulated around the joint information–exposure objective considered here.

Constrained Bayesian optimization methods restrict motion actions to regions satisfying prescribed safety constraints [19, 20], while related safe GP approaches estimate unsafe sets and redirect candidate locations to the estimated safe region [13, 14]. These methods require a prescribed safety threshold to define the feasible set, whereas exposure-aware planning can instead trade information value against increasing field intensity without imposing a cutoff threshold.

In this work, exposure is traded against information acquisition through a hedging parameter λ∈[0,1]⊂ℝ\lambda\in[0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}, so high-intensity regions remain admissible to gain information value while incurring an exposure penalty. Finite-budget multi-agent IPP is formulated as a multi-objective belief-state Markov decision process (MDP), and an RL policy is trained offline on simulated fields for evaluation on unseen fields without requiring long-horizon combinatorial search. The contributions are as follows.

The formulation of an exposure-aware belief-state MDP for finite-budget IPP that couples covariance-based information acquisition with field exposure.

A reward design in which λ\lambda provides a mission-level trade-off between information gain and exposure.

The information-seeking PPO policy achieves lower RMSE than the evaluated information-driven baselines, while exposure weighting reduces exposure relative to information-seeking PPO.

title: LocoMuJoCo: A Comprehensive Imitation Learning Benchmark for Whole-Body Control
authors: Firas Al-Hafez,Davide Tateo,Oleg Kaidanov,Aditya Bhatt,Artur Zelik,Zhengyi Luo,Jan Peters
abstract:
LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL)and
reinforcement learning (RL)on whole-body control. The library couples
MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API,
exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped
embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for
every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1.
A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes,
terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while
compact JAX implementations of many RLand ILalgorithms
provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion
loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design,
the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage
example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at
https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.
introduction:
Humanoid robots have advanced rapidly in recent years, and improvements
in hardware have made the sim-to-real transfer of
learned controllers increasingly practical. Because humans and humanoid
robots share broadly similar embodiments, human motion data provide an
abundant source of training demonstrations. Despite this
progress, the imitation learning (IL)/reinforcement learning (RL)benchmarking landscape
remains fragmented across single-robot codebases, manipulation-only suites,
and toy locomotion tasks, forcing researchers to re-implement data pipelines,
retargeting methods, simulators, and evaluation metrics whenever they change
embodiments.

The first version of LocoMuJoCo (Al-Hafez et al., 2023b) paired realistic
humanoid models with motion-capture datasets and a common evaluation
protocol, but ran on CPU MuJoCo only. Version 1.0 rebuilt the library
around JAX, adding a GPU-parallel MJX backend, the retargeting pipeline,
many new embodiments, and JAX implementations of RLand ILalgorithms. The current version adds an optional MjWarp backend,
further algorithms, and the companion
loco-mujoco-real sim-to-real deployment pipeline.

title: I See You: Initial Multi-Robot LiDAR Registration with Mutual-Observation Checks
authors: Jonathan Lichtenfeld,Oskar von Stryk
comment: Accepted final version. IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR), Incheon, South Korea, November 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Compared to single-robot deployments, multi-robot teams can significantly improve search-and-rescue (SAR) mission success by covering large areas in parallel.
To collaborate effectively, these robots must be registered in a common reference frame.
Standard registration methods typically rely on external infrastructure or significant map overlap, but real deployments require infrastructure-free, stationary initial alignment for immediate operation.
While global LiDAR point cloud registration addresses this, existing single-scan methods often fail silently in aliased or degenerate environments.
Approaches scaling beyond two agents also remain rarely evaluated in real-world scenarios.
We propose a centralized, deployment-ready framework for pre-mission multi-robot registration.
Our system performs pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment and actively rejects impossible pose hypotheses via deterministic plausibility checks.
We validate the framework on a real-world custom dataset of four synchronized robots in various environments with ground truth.
The checks reject more than a third of the incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting less than 1% of the correct ones, and reduce the number of team registrations with a wrong robot pose by 38%.
Dataset and code are publicly available.
introduction:
Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) accelerate search and rescue (SAR) operations by covering large disaster sites in parallel [1, 2].
To coordinate safely, these robots rely on multi-robot simultaneous localization and mapping (MR-SLAM).
While MR-SLAM is a rapidly advancing field, unconditionally deploying these systems in unstructured, ad-hoc disaster zones remains a severe practical challenge.
A fundamental prerequisite for such missions is initial inter-robot registration:
before any collaborative mapping can begin, every robot must establish its pose within a shared reference frame (Fig. 1).

Some MR-SLAM frameworks require a coarse initial relative pose [2]. Others attempt to build the shared frame as the robots cross paths during exploration [3, 4, 5].
Yet, immediate alignment is an important requirement for field deployments.
Operators need a unified view to safely coordinate the initial rollout, and downstream SLAM algorithms benefit from a solid starting estimate to prevent early divergence.
Standard workarounds bridge this gap using manual calibration, external infrastructure, or GNSS.
In ad-hoc, unstructured environments, these dependencies introduce critical single points of failure.

We address the common deployment scenario where robots launch from a co-located staging area.
If their sensor fields of view (FOV) overlap, we can establish the initial reference frame immediately.
We scope our approach strictly to gravity-aligned LiDAR data, as LiDAR provides accurate 3D geometry and serves as the primary exteroceptive sensor for modern SAR UGVs.

However, raw point cloud registration remains highly vulnerable to real-world deployment conditions.
Sparse FOV overlap, dense vegetation, or structurally repetitive architecture can easily confuse global solvers.
In these scenarios, algorithms may output completely incorrect poses with high mathematical confidence.
Because standard optimization cannot independently distinguish a physically feasible alignment from an impossible one, these results should not be directly trusted.
A deployable system requires strict plausibility checks to actively reject physically impossible alignments before the mission begins.

We present a centralized, infrastructure-free framework to achieve robust pre-mission registration between multiple UGVs using LiDAR. Our primary contributions are:

A registration framework combining global point cloud alignment with deterministic physical plausibility checks to actively reject geometrically impossible hypotheses.

Real-world evaluation across diverse indoor and outdoor scenarios with a heterogeneous UGV team, demonstrating the prevention of critical pre-mission misalignments.

An open-source framework implementation accompanied by a synchronized multi-robot LiDAR dataset with ground truth: https://tu-darmstadt-ros-pkg.github.io/i-see-you-registration.

1. A registration framework combining global point cloud alignment with deterministic physical plausibility checks to actively reject geometrically impossible hypotheses.

2. Real-world evaluation across diverse indoor and outdoor scenarios with a heterogeneous UGV team, demonstrating the prevention of critical pre-mission misalignments.

3. An open-source framework implementation accompanied by a synchronized multi-robot LiDAR dataset with ground truth: https://tu-darmstadt-ros-pkg.github.io/i-see-you-registration.

title: FastRoverVLA: Fast Vision-Language-Action Execution for Off-Road Autonomous Driving
authors: Changtao Zhao,Yingxue Guan,Li Wang,Shijie Zhao,Yuhang Zhang,Shengkai Zhang,Qing Wang,Ziying Song
abstract: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed–curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.
introduction:
Off-road driving requires motion decisions in environments without fixed lane structure, where surface conditions, visibility, and feasible routes can change within a journey [1, 2, 3]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language-based reasoning to numerical actions or trajectories [4, 5, 6, 7]. Their outputs must also accommodate the vehicle motion that follows prediction. A scene-conditioned plan can remain relevant across several trajectory updates, while its speed and curvature commands require continued adjustment to the measured state.

Coupling every trajectory update to a new prediction repeatedly invokes multimodal inference [8, 9, 10, 11]. Efficient encoders and inference pipelines reduce the cost of individual calls [12, 13], while slow–fast systems combine expensive reasoning with a faster planning path [6, 14]. Action-chunk methods address continuity between predicted sequences through temporal aggregation, constrained generation, or learned correction [15, 16, 17]. These developments leave a specific execution problem at the decoded-action interface: retaining the motion corrections accumulated after a plan has been generated, without another learned planner or access to the generative sampler.

A retained plan must account for two changes during reuse: commands are consumed as time advances, and measured motion changes the state to which the remaining commands must be matched. Direct replay advances the sequence without resolving this state mismatch. Realigning the original plan at each update incorporates current motion but discards previous corrections. Carrying the corrected remainder into the next update preserves both the unconsumed actions and the motion corrections retained in them (Fig. 1).

FastRoverVLA decouples visual plan generation from recurrent execution around a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and a deterministic action adapter. The name combines “Fast” for reduced VLM inference demand, “Rover” for off-road driving, and “VLA” for vision-language-action planning. Visual inference refreshes the action buffer, while recurrent execution maintains motion-conditioned trajectories between refreshes. Each update aligns the retained speed–curvature actions with measured ego motion, generates a local trajectory, consumes the current action, and writes the corrected remainder back to the buffer. A bounded rule uses variation within the refreshed plan to assign its reuse budget. The resulting interface separates visual plan generation from motion-conditioned trajectory updates without modifying the backbone or training an auxiliary driving policy.

Evaluation on ORAD-3D [3] and RELLIS-3D [1] separates three questions: whether decoded plans benefit from persistent correction, whether visual initialization adds information beyond motion history, and whether sparse refresh reduces measured inference demand. Shared-prediction controls isolate the maintenance operations; motion-only and matched-image controls examine initialization. Backbone transfer, disjoint-sequence evaluation, and a past-only heading check test the stability of the execution effect. Independent real-request runs measure its computational consequence under serial replay.

The main contributions are:

FastRoverVLA introduces an action-level execution interface for off-road VLA planning. Maintaining a decoded plan as a recurrent state separates visual prediction from motion adaptation, allowing local trajectory updates between model requests without an additional learned driving policy.

The interface combines state alignment, action consumption, and correction write-back to preserve measured-motion updates in the retained plan. A bounded refresh rule assigns reuse budgets from normalized action variation, controlling inference demand through the same decoded-action representation.

Controlled replay and independent real-request evaluation cover two datasets and four backbones. In real-request evaluation, Qwen3-VL reduces 3 s FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% relative to every-update execution, while serial request-processing cost falls by factors of 16.6 and 20.8, respectively.

1. FastRoverVLA introduces an action-level execution interface for off-road VLA planning. Maintaining a decoded plan as a recurrent state separates visual prediction from motion adaptation, allowing local trajectory updates between model requests without an additional learned driving policy.

2. The interface combines state alignment, action consumption, and correction write-back to preserve measured-motion updates in the retained plan. A bounded refresh rule assigns reuse budgets from normalized action variation, controlling inference demand through the same decoded-action representation.

3. Controlled replay and independent real-request evaluation cover two datasets and four backbones. In real-request evaluation, Qwen3-VL reduces 3 s FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% relative to every-update execution, while serial request-processing cost falls by factors of 16.6 and 20.8, respectively.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
authors: Zheyuan Liu,Chuhan Wang,Jinduo Guo,Yue Huang,Xiangchi Yuan,Ningshan Ma,Meng Jiang
comment: A two-stage pipeline that teaches VLAs to stop prohibited tasks safely while preserving permitted skills
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot’s other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.11

introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025b; Qu et al., 2025), building on robot demonstration learning (Brohan et al., 2023) and multimodal task grounding (Driess et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023). Generalist policies extend these capabilities across robot platforms and unfamiliar environments (Ghosh et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a), while action-sequence prediction and efficient fine-tuning improve manipulation performance (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025a; Cui et al., 2026a). As these policies acquire more skills, deployment also requires control over which learned behaviors remain appropriate to execute.

This requirement becomes concrete when context makes an otherwise feasible action hazardous. Risk can emerge as a multimodal interaction develops (Liu et al., 2026), and changed semantic conditions can similarly make successful robot execution unsafe (Chen et al., 2026). VLAs may also act without meaningful instructions (Jang et al., 2026), while adversarial prompts and poisoned training data can induce harmful or attacker-chosen behaviors (Robey et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). Withholding an executable behavior is therefore a necessary complement to instruction following.

Planning methods support this control through robot affordances (Ichter et al., 2023), uncertainty-based requests for help (Ren et al., 2023), and contextual safety specifications (Ravichandran et al., 2026). At the policy level, constrained learning (Zhang et al., 2025) and refusal demonstrations (Chen et al., 2026) teach safer responses. Selective unlearning offers another route by reducing unwanted behavior while preserving useful capabilities in language models (Yao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024) and VLAs (Ranjan and Polyzou, 2026; Wang et al., 2026).

Since earlier actions determine later observations in sequential control (Ross et al., 2011), evaluation from initial states can leave intermediate states untested when an edited policy stops before reaching them. We examine these states by transferring control from the original policy during execution. This reveals a failure to stop ongoing tasks, as several policies that suppress completion from initial states still complete the prohibited task after takeover. Even when it remains unfinished, unsafe alternative responses arise, including dropping a held bottle (Figure 1). Dropping and holding both prevent placement but have different physical consequences. These observations, developed in Section 2, motivate the following research question.

Addressing this requires models to suppress prohibited behavior across execution states and produce an alternative response suited to the robot’s current state.
To meet these requirements, we propose State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative. Its two-stage design combines Fallback Target Construction, which assigns holding targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, with Joint Policy Adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. By learning an explicit fallback across execution states, SAFI enables the robot to stop prohibited tasks with a holding response while preserving its other skills. Our main contributions are as follows.

We identify failures to stop ongoing tasks and unsafe alternative responses in VLAs through an intermediate-state takeover evaluation that jointly examines prohibited execution and physical events.

We propose SAFI, a two-stage framework that constructs fallback targets from prohibited-task demonstrations and jointly optimizes fallback and retained-task imitation to suppress prohibited behavior and learn an appropriate alternative response while preserving permitted skills.

We evaluate SAFI across multiple LIBERO task suites and a BadLIBERO backdoor setting. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI achieves low prohibited-task completion rates after takeover with no recorded drops or falls, while preserving performance on retained tasks.

title: EmbodyAgent: Post-Training Embodied VLM Agents via Distillation, SFT, and RL
authors: Wei Dai,Jinkun Liu,Jiayi Chen,Han Liu,Wenbo Ding,Shaolun Huang
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces[15, 46]. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are typically accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework for embodied VLM agents built around three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher model—requiring no teacher weights or internal signals—under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success predicates; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills these explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders kept trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage using a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share a single primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, requiring no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks[26]—disjoint initial-state splits, greedy decoding at test time, and training-only safeguards—held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while RL training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per test episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish the failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.
introduction:
Closed-loop robot manipulation demands tight coordination between perception, planning, and control: an agent must decide how to structure control commands over time, when acquiring a fresh observation warrants another model turn, and how to recover when execution diverges from expectation. Recent robot-use agent (RUA) systems [15, 46, 7] demonstrate that vision-language models (VLMs) can supply this coordination directly through tool use [49, 36, 30, 23, 6], extending the interaction paradigm of digital computer-use agents [1, 38] to physical environments. Yet equipping an open-weight VLM with reliable closed-loop manipulation capability is not a prompting problem—it is a full-pipeline post-training problem. Off-the-shelf open VLMs fail completely under interactive control contracts (0/100 held-out tasks for an untrained 9B model); frontier models capable of solving these tasks zero-shot are often accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights, hidden states, or token logits; and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher trajectories alone stalls early (14/100) because an imitated policy encounters its own execution histories, errors, and observations at test time rather than the teacher’s.

To close this end-to-end gap, we build EmbodyAgent, a complete post-training stack for embodied VLM agents organized as three successive pipelines:

Black-box strong-teacher data synthesis. A frontier VLM teacher interacts with the environment strictly as a black-box agent through the tool harness—requiring zero access to teacher weights or logits. Our synthesis pipeline enforces structured reasoning before every code output and filters episodes by environment success predicates, turning raw black-box rollouts into clean multimodal training trajectories.

Multimodal SFT distillation. An open-weight 9B VLM student is distilled on the synthesized explanation-and-program targets with both its vision encoder and language backbone kept trainable. This stage eliminates cold-start format failures and grounds visual observations into executable control loops and observation requests.

Online outcome-based RL. Starting from the SFT checkpoint with no teacher in the loop, group-relative reinforcement learning optimizes the student VLM directly on its own sampled episodes using a runtime-error-penalized success reward. Online optimization overcomes imitation distribution shift and substantially improves both task success and multi-turn decision efficiency.

All three pipelines are unified by a single think-then-code policy representation over one Python execution tool (execute_python). Unlike prior code-as-policy agents [24, 2] that compose a hand-engineered library of manipulation primitives, EmbodyAgent exposes only two raw runtime operations: env.observation(), which returns primary and wrist camera images together with robot proprioception, and env.action(a), which advances one simulator control step with a∈[−1,1]7a\in[-1,1]^{7}. At every turn, the VLM is required to emit a chain-of-thought explanation planning loop structure, step batching, and observation timing, followed by an executable Python program. Because the policy lives entirely within a standard multimodal text-and-code interface—with no external action decoder and no pre-defined primitives—black-box synthesis, SFT, and RL operate over the exact same output contract without any cross-stage representation shift.

We validate the complete pipeline on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks [26] under a strictly separated evaluation protocol: per-task initial states are partitioned into disjoint train, validation, and test splits; Stage 1 synthesizes 100 successful episodes (1,475 targets) from the black-box teacher Astra Medium on train states; Stage 2 distills Qwen3.5-9B [41] across vision and language parameters; and Stage 3 runs temperature-one group-relative RL on train and validation states while evaluating greedily on all 100 held-out test states after every round under full episode budgets and zero test-time safeguards. Across this progression, held-out success advances from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after 64 rounds of RL), while RL training rollout success rises from 8.4% to 87.7% with all ten tasks improving. Simultaneously, Stage 3 RL sharpens the VLM’s execution efficiency, compressing median model calls per test episode from 36 (SFT) to 11 and yielding a self-contained 9B VLM that executes locally with no ongoing reliance on the black-box teacher.

Executing outcome-based RL over multi-turn code generation also surfaces a failure mode absent from fixed-action policies: a self-reinforcing runtime-error loop in which execution tracebacks enter the multimodal history that subsequent turns condition on, allowing error-prone patterns to amplify before recovery. We show that aggregate success rate lags this pathology and establish a per-round failure-category monitoring and sampling-only curation protocol that restores healthy optimization without altering evaluation.

Our contributions are threefold:

A full-pipeline Embodied Agent post-training stack. An end-to-end framework integrating weight-free black-box teacher data synthesis, multimodal SFT distillation, and online outcome-based RL that trains an open-weight 9B VLM from 0/100 to 14/100 to 84/100 across ten LIBERO Spatial tasks.

A unified think-then-code interface across stages. A single primitive-free execution contract (env.observation(), env.action(a)) shared verbatim by synthesis, SFT, and RL, turning action composition and observation scheduling into explicit VLM learning targets with no action decoder or cross-stage mismatch.

Diagnosis and stabilization of executable-code RL. Identification of a self-reinforcing runtime-error loop induced by outcome optimization over execution feedback, paired with failure-category monitoring and training-side safeguards that stabilize RL without contaminating test evaluation.

title: Planning to Stop: Factored Certification and Terminal Repair for Noncircular Robots
authors: Runtian Zheng,Congpeng Zhang,Ying Liu
abstract: Tight-space navigation requires a robot to clear obstacles and stop inside its goal despite uncertainty. We present GeoDiff, a motion-program planner coupling original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, and factored proof compilation. An exact feasible-translation characterization guides repair; request-local reuse reduces repeated geometric work. We establish conditions for compiler equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness. Across 11,440 floorplan-derived jobs, GeoDiff certifies 61/139 tasks at 5-cm tolerance within 15 s, versus 44/139 for the stop-set baseline. The strongest observed external certificate adapter certifies 13/139 tasks from 119/139 native routes, separating route availability from certification. On tasks derived from public BARN maps, GeoDiff certifies 202/270 at 5-cm tolerance for a Jackal-shaped body, versus 3/270 for the portal baseline. Development analyses distinguish emitter savings from solver coverage, and 1,420 route-tracking episodes characterize the execution interface. These results show how terminal reasoning and proof reuse increase finite-budget certification coverage while preserving the original physical task and goal.
introduction:
A robot can negotiate a doorway yet fail to stop inside the space reserved for it. For a noncircular body, a turn changes whole-body clearance; tracking and braking uncertainty spread the possible stopping states. When clearance and terminal tolerance approach the size of those uncertainties, reaching a nominal endpoint is only part of the planning problem. The planner must construct a motion whose complete stopping enclosure fits inside the requested goal.

This requirement also changes how computation should be spent. Route generation, terminal maneuvers, and geometric verification share a finite planning budget. A geometrically plausible route may consume that budget without yielding an acceptable stopping program. Conversely, a candidate that narrowly fails its terminal condition may contain precisely the information needed for an inexpensive repair. The central question is therefore: how should search use geometric failure evidence and repeated verification work to produce more certified stopping motions under a fixed deadline?

We address this question with GeoDiff, a planner organized around a single original-task acceptance relation (Fig. 1). The physical checker establishes whole-body motion and authorized braking obligations. A separate postcondition checks the conservative stopped-state enclosure against the original goal. Eligible terminal failures provide task-bound witnesses for bounded tail adjustments. Every adjusted candidate returns to the same verifier. Request-local factoring reuses identical geometric expressions so that overlapping proof obligations require less repeated computation.

The contribution builds on robust reach–avoid planning, tracking-error bounds, and feedback motion libraries Chung et al. [2024], Chung et al. [2025], Chen et al. [2021], Majumdar and Tedrake [2017]. Its distinctive object is the certifiable motion program under a deadline: terminal geometry determines which repairs are worth proposing, and proof structure determines which computations can be reused. This coupling connects the stopping specification to both candidate generation and compiler organization.

The paper develops three results. First, it formulates original-goal stopping and derives the exact feasible translation set for a fixed terminal enclosure, including label-dependent repair margins. Second, it establishes the invariants for exact request-local factoring and for transferring accepted finite programs to contract-faithful execution. Third, it evaluates the resulting certification coverage over 11,440 CUBI-DT jobs, reports native-route and certificate endpoints separately, and examines the mechanisms with development analyses and a route-tracking panel. The complete configuration is denoted GeoDiff; factored_bt is its experiment identifier.

title: One View, One Action: Spatially Generalizable VLAs through Observation-Aligned Experts and Cross Graph Consistency
authors: Jinxi Liu,Ruifeng Zhai,Hao Liu,Guangrun Wang
abstract:
Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view’s camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames.
Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs’ base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference.
Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models transfer visual and semantic knowledge from large-scale pretrained vision-language models to robotic control, achieving substantial progress in language-conditioned manipulation [46, 3, 4, 19, 5, 31, 34].
However, reliable manipulation also requires spatial generalization: the ability to generate appropriate actions across changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. Viewpoint shifts alter the visual appearance of scenes and robot motion [23], whereas variations in the robot’s state may require different motion trajectories to accomplish the same task. Yet existing benchmarks reveal substantial performance degradation under both types of shifts, highlighting the persistent challenge of spatial generalization [11, 45, 9, 29, 32].

Action representation provides a useful perspective on this spatial generalization challenge. The same physical robot motion can have different numerical representations across coordinate frames [42, 43, 22]. Figure 1(a) illustrates this for a single end-effector movement: its displacement components differ when expressed in the robot base coordinates and in each camera’s coordinates. Yet multi-view VLAs typically combine observations from multiple cameras while receiving action supervision only in the robot base frame [18], requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions [42, 16]. Consequently, the learned correspondence may become tied to spatial configurations encountered during training, limiting generalization to unseen camera viewpoints and robot initial states [39, 36, 12].
Prior work has explored camera-frame action prediction [42, 22] and explicit camera-geometry conditioning [17] to improve this spatial correspondence. These studies highlight the importance of reference-frame choice and camera geometry in action learning. This motivates jointly leveraging action supervision from all available views to improve the spatial generalization of the base-frame policy. As shown in Figure 1(b), we introduce camera-frame action supervision for each view while retaining the original base-frame supervision.

We introduce One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), a framework for learning observation-aligned actions. Its organizing principle is to predict actions expressed in the corresponding camera frame for each view. Specifically, we transform demonstration actions and robot states into each camera frame using known coordinate transformations. For each view, the model predicts actions in the corresponding frame, conditioned on the associated image and robot state expressed in that frame. In this way, the same physical motion provides diverse, observation-aligned action supervision across views, allowing each view to contribute to learning the base-frame policy not only through visual observations but also through its corresponding action prediction task.
This encourages the policy to rely less on observation–action correspondences specific to the training configurations.

We instantiate OVOA-VLA with a Mixture of Transformers [25], comprising a view-specific action expert for each input view and a base-frame expert. Each view-specific expert directly attends to visual tokens from its corresponding view, receives robot state expressed in that camera frame, and predicts actions in the same frame. The base expert uses all visual inputs and the base-frame robot state, while retaining the original base-frame action supervision.
We jointly train these experts under two complementary directed attention graphs. In the base-to-reference graph, the view-specific experts attend to action features from the base expert; in the reference-to-base graph, the base expert attends to action features from the view-specific experts. During training, we perform a forward pass under each graph for the same sample, with both passes sharing model parameters and receiving demonstrated-action supervision. Since both base-frame predictions correspond to the same action target, we introduce Cross Graph Consistency (CGC) to encourage agreement between them. Our model supports two inference modes: full inference uses the reference-to-base graph, while base-only inference uses the base-to-reference graph, where the base expert does not attend to the view-specific experts and thus permits their removal.

OVOA-VLA demonstrates strong performance across multiple simulation benchmarks [26, 11, 28, 41]. Full inference achieves average success rates of 98.7% and 88.1% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. On LIBERO-Plus, it improves success rates from 66.2% to 75.4% under camera viewpoint perturbations and from 67.2% to 88.4% under robot initialization perturbations, compared with π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Base-only inference achieves 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating that the gains persist without view-specific experts.
In real-world evaluations on a Franka Research 3 robot, base-only inference outperforms π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 5.0 percentage points in average success rate across six in-distribution tasks and raises the average success rate from 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
Our main contributions are as follows:

Observation-aligned action learning. We introduce OVOA-VLA, which jointly learns camera-frame actions from diverse, observation-aligned supervision derived from the same demonstration, improving base-frame policy generalization.

Complementary expert training. We design two complementary directed attention graphs to model both interaction directions between the base and view-specific experts, with CGC encouraging consistent base-frame predictions across graphs for the same sample.

Two inference modes. Our model supports full inference with the reference-to-base graph and base-only inference with the base-to-reference graph, where the base expert is independent of the view-specific experts.

Experimental validation. Experiments across four simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts.

1. Observation-aligned action learning. We introduce OVOA-VLA, which jointly learns camera-frame actions from diverse, observation-aligned supervision derived from the same demonstration, improving base-frame policy generalization.

2. Complementary expert training. We design two complementary directed attention graphs to model both interaction directions between the base and view-specific experts, with CGC encouraging consistent base-frame predictions across graphs for the same sample.

3. Two inference modes. Our model supports full inference with the reference-to-base graph and base-only inference with the base-to-reference graph, where the base expert is independent of the view-specific experts.

4. Experimental validation. Experiments across four simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts.

title: A Practical Proprioceptive Data Collection Utility for the Unitree GO1
authors: Jack Anders Smitterberg,Tan Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
The Unitree Go1 is a widely used platform for legged robotics
research, yet collecting proprioceptive data from it is unnecessarily
difficult: the Unitree SDK is sparsely documented, and ROS1 (Robot Operating System), the Go1’s
native middleware, is fully deprecated. We present an open-source
graphical utility that enables researchers to reliably record
proprioceptive data from the Go1, including joint states, IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) readings,
foot force sensor data, and gyroscope measurements, without requiring
ROS expertise. The tool provides a simple GUI (Graphical User Interface) for starting, stopping,
and labeling recordings in real time. The contribution of this paper is the collection utility. We characterize the
acquisition quality of 51 recordings collected with it, including the achieved
sampling rate and repeated samples. As a secondary, deliberately modest check that
the data is useful, we train a terrain classifier on it. The results are weak: a
Temporal Convolutional Network reaches about 38% accuracy on held-out recordings
across ten terrain classes (10% would be chance), and a window-level split that
ignores recording boundaries inflates the same measurement to about 99%. We
report this as a demonstration that the logged signals carry terrain information,
not as a competitive classifier. The utility is designed to lower the barrier to
collecting Go1 proprioceptive data without ROS.
introduction:
The Unitree Go1 [1] is a widely deployed quadrupedal
robot platform used by academic laboratories and hobbyists for legged
locomotion research. The Go1 remains attractive due to its low cost,
variety of sensors, ample onboard compute, and open-source nature. Continued research interest in the platform is evidenced by recent work on benchmarking locomotion controllers [2], state estimation [3], and novel sensing modalities [4].

Working with the Go1 in practice, however, presents significant
challenges. The official Unitree SDK is insufficiently
documented [5], and the Go1’s native middleware
is ROS1, which has reached end-of-life [6]. Unitree’s ROS1
package recommends Ubuntu 18.04 and ROS Melodic, both of which are
past end-of-life. The combination of an insufficiently documented SDK, unsupported software, and a deprecated middleware creates a steep barrier to entry for researchers who simply wish to collect data from the robot.

Prior work has demonstrated the value of proprioceptive sensing for legged robot tasks including terrain classification [7, 8] and obstacle estimation [9],
but to the best of our knowledge no generalized, easy-to-use
proprioceptive data collection framework has been released for this platform.

This paper presents an open-source, GUI-based utility that allows any researcher to collect labeled proprioceptive data from the Unitree Go1 without requiring ROS knowledge or deep familiarity with the Unitree SDK. The tool records joint states, IMU data, gyroscope data, and foot force sensor data, exporting structured CSV files suitable for direct use in machine learning pipelines. The focus of this paper is the utility, not the classifier. To show that the logged data is useful, we collect a multi-terrain dataset and train a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) [10] for terrain classification. This is a demonstration only, and its results are weak. We report accuracy on held-out recordings (about 38% over ten classes, against 10% chance) next to the much higher window-level accuracy (about 99%) that results when recording boundaries are ignored, and we characterize the acquisition quality of the logs, including the achieved sampling rate. The utility is released under the MIT License at https://github.com/RoLACLab/go1-proprioceptive-logger.
