title: Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion
authors: Yefim Nudelman,Dor Atzmon,Tom Tirer
abstract: Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) requires trajectories that avoid environmental obstacles and collisions between robots in a shared workspace. Diffusion-based planners often address obstacle avoidance through sampling-time guidance, while some conditioned approaches aggregate map geometry into a global representation. We present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a map-conditioned trajectory generator for multi-robot planning. SCTD retains multiple position-aware occupancy tokens accessed through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net, with hard endpoint inpainting enforcing start and goal states. One model trained on single-robot demonstrations across procedural environments generates obstacle-aware trajectories without sampling-time obstacle-cost guidance. High-level Conflict-Based Search (CBS) coordinates these trajectories through constrained replanning, retaining inter-agent guidance during sampling and reusing the model across workspace layouts and team sizes. Experiments assess single-robot success and trajectory quality, generalization to unfamiliar layouts with added obstacles, and coordinated multi-robot planning. On 15,000 held-out tasks, SCTD achieves higher success than the evaluated guided diffusion baseline, with the largest gains on hard-detour tasks, while trajectory-quality comparisons show smoother trajectories. Conditioning ablations show higher success with spatial tokens than with a global map embedding, and map-replacement tests demonstrate dependence on the supplied geometry. The resulting multi-robot system achieves higher team success than the compared diffusion baselines, with experiments covering teams of up to 15 robots.
introduction:
Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) is a fundamental challenge in robotics,
requiring teams of robots to move through a shared continuous workspace while avoiding
environmental obstacles and one another. Applications such as automated warehouses require
individual routes to account for workspace geometry while remaining compatible with the motions
of other robots. This coupling makes planning computationally challenging
as the team size and complexity of the workspace increase. Obstacle layouts also vary across tasks, requiring planners to adapt their routes to changing workspace geometry. One approach to this complexity is to formulate a discrete abstraction of MRMP
as Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF), representing configurations and transitions on a graph,
typically in discrete timesteps  [19]. MAPF methods such as Conflict-Based Search (CBS) separate coordination from individual path planning: a high-level search resolves conflicts by
imposing constraints, while low-level planners revise affected agents’ paths [15].
Within this decomposition, coordination repeatedly requests individual paths under updated
constraints. Extending this structure to continuous-space planning therefore motivates studying
low-level generators that account for the current workspace geometry while supplying trajectories
for individual sampling and replanning [14].

Diffusion models [16, 17, 5, 18] offer a learned approach to low-level trajectory generation
by modeling distributions over complete trajectories and generating samples through iterative
denoising [8]. Motion Planning Diffusion [3] (MPD)
develops this approach for robot motion planning, learning trajectory priors
from demonstrations and adapting generated motions through sampling-time
cost-gradient guidance.

Multi-robot Multi-model planning Diffusion
(MMD) [14] combines single-robot diffusion planners
with constraint-based coordination, resolving conflicts through
guided individual replanning. Simultaneous MRMP Diffusion
(SMD) [9] instead plans trajectories for all robots
simultaneously, using constrained optimization during denoising
to address obstacle and inter-robot collisions. MMD’s local priors capture motion
patterns associated with their training environments, supporting data-adherent planning. During
sampling, obstacle-cost gradients adapt generated trajectories to workspace geometry, while
inter-robot guidance addresses coordination constraints. The current map therefore influences
sampling, but does not explicitly condition the learned denoiser. This distinction matters when
coordination repeatedly requests trajectories: workspace-dependent routing can also be represented
in the learned prior used for each request. Supplying geometry directly to the denoiser offers this
complementary role, while sampling-time guidance continues to address coordination constraints.

Explicit environment conditioning offers a complementary way to incorporate
workspace geometry into trajectory generation. Carvalho et al. [2] encode an occupancy
map and combine its embedding with task features as a single “token” for conditioning a temporal U-Net through
cross-attention. Building on this approach, we examine how trajectory features access the map
during denoising. An aggregated map embedding can encode geometry, while spatially indexed
features presented as separate attention tokens allow different workspace regions to be queried
individually. Spatial map tokens also appear in Roken’s joint multi-robot diffusion
transformer [1]; our focus is their use in a single-robot backbone learned across
workspace layouts and evaluated within inherited multi-robot coordination.

In this paper, we present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a
single-robot trajectory backbone trained across procedurally generated
environments. A convolutional occupancy encoder produces position-aware spatial features that
trajectory features can query separately through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net.
Start and goal states remain fixed through hard endpoint inpainting during denoising.
For multi-robot planning, we integrate SCTD as the low-level trajectory
generator in XECBS [14], retaining inter-agent guidance
to address coordination constraints during sampling and replanning.
This formulation uses one map-conditioned backbone across workspace layouts while
retaining the established coordination machinery.

Our contributions are:

Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion.
We introduce SCTD, a trajectory diffusion model that retains occupancy-derived convolutional
features as position-aware spatial tokens and exposes them to trajectory features through
cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net.

Generalization and map-dependent generation in unseen workspaces.
We show that an SCTD model generates feasible trajectories in
held-out maps without
static-obstacle-cost guidance, including obstacle-dependent and hard-detour tasks. Compared with MPD, SCTD achieves higher single-agent success.

Reusable low-level planning for multi-robot coordination.
We integrate SCTD as the low-level trajectory generator in
XECBS [14], retaining inter-agent guidance and reusing one
map-conditioned model across robots and workspace layouts. On held-out maps,
the resulting system achieves higher team success than MMD at every evaluated
team size from 3 to 15 robots, and than SMD [9] at the shared sizes of 3, 6,
and 9 robots, under a 180-second trial limit.

title: PhysVAM: Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
authors: Yuxiang Yang,Jingbo Zhang,Jiaru Zhong,Junliang Chen,Yirui Zhou,Guangming Wang,Haitao Lin,Huaiyuan Xu,Yi Wang,Lap-Pui Chau
abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot–object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose PhysVAM, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation is increasingly moving beyond static tabletop settings toward dynamic environments, where objects continue to move during robot perception and action execution [1, 2]. Successful manipulation therefore requires actions to remain coordinated with evolving robot–object interactions. Changes in object motion and contact timing can alter whether an intended interaction will succeed before its execution is complete. A central challenge is thus to learn predictive representations that anticipate how future interactions may affect task progress and guide timely action generation.

Recent approaches pursue visual future modeling through future video generation [3, 4] and visual-feature prediction [5, 6]. These methods provide predictive context by modeling how scenes and objects may evolve. However, as illustrated in Fig. 1(A-a), generated futures may exhibit geometric distortions and inconsistent contact predictions, compromising their reliability for physical interaction [7]. More fundamentally, predicting future visual or object states alone does not explicitly characterize how anticipated robot–object interactions will advance or hinder task progress. These limitations motivate a future modeling objective that directly reflects the task consequences of physical interactions.

We approach future modeling from a task-value perspective, representing anticipated robot–object interactions through their effects on future task progress. Rather than reconstructing future visual states, this perspective models how task progress is expected to evolve. Existing value-based approaches have demonstrated the usefulness of task evaluation for policy improvement [8, 9, 10]. However, current-value assessment does not explicitly characterize how task progress may evolve through subsequent interactions. For instance, a favorable current value may still be followed by a missed grasp as the target moves before gripper closure. Predicting task values across multiple future horizons instead provides temporally structured supervision for learning task-directed representations that guide action generation, as illustrated in Fig. 1(A-b).

To instantiate this perspective, we propose PhysVAM, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model for dynamic object manipulation. PhysVAM leverages current observations and historical object and robot motion to model evolving interaction context, while jointly learning action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch predicts task values at multiple future horizons and learns corresponding latent representations from both successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations capture anticipated task progress associated with robot–object interactions and are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that promote task success. As illustrated in Fig. 1(B), the predicted future values can reflect changes in task progress as interactions unfold.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We present a task-value perspective on future modeling for dynamic object manipulation, leveraging multi-horizon future-value prediction to learn task-directed representations for action guidance.

We propose PhysVAM, a physics-oriented framework that integrates historical object and robot motion understanding with multi-horizon future-value guidance for action generation.

Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate improved task success and execution efficiency, with absolute success-rate gains of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines, respectively. Integrating our value branch into other action models yields further improvements, demonstrating the transferability of future-value guidance.

2. We propose PhysVAM, a physics-oriented framework that integrates historical object and robot motion understanding with multi-horizon future-value guidance for action generation.

title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation
authors: Zhengtu Liang,Qiwei Liang,Tao Lin,Shihang Weng,Boyang Cai,Xiangyu Chen,Yikeng Chen,Jiaming Liang,Bohan Tan,Yu Yan,Renjing Xu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X–V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X–V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.

introduction:
Generative robot policies can produce rich, continuous action sequences, but they must do so quickly enough for closed-loop control. Modern vision-language-action (VLA) policies and world-action models (WAMs) commonly use flow matching to transform Gaussian noise into executable action chunks [2, 33, 50, 47]. Each refinement step requires another network evaluation, creating a trade-off between action quality and control latency. While much effort has gone into reducing sampling steps [45, 37, 53], we revisit a more basic question: what should the action network predict?

Most flow-based policies predict the velocity that transports a noisy action toward the data. An alternative is to predict the clean action endpoint directly. Although these two predictions are analytically interchangeable along a linear noise-to-data path [25, 29, 1], they pose different learning problems. Endpoint prediction seeks a structured action, whereas velocity prediction must also account for the injected noise. Moreover, generation itself changes character over time: the model first needs to recover an action from heavy noise, then make increasingly precise corrections as the sample approaches a valid trajectory. There is little reason to expect one prediction target to be equally effective at both stages, from early recovery to final refinement.

We investigate this question by comparing three objectives: velocity prediction (V), direct endpoint prediction (X), and endpoint prediction with a velocity-weighted loss (X–V), as explored in action-manifold learning [48, 46]. Our study covers three policy architectures—StarVLA, FastWAM, and LiLa-WAM [44, 50, 47]—on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 [26, 10, 5]. Within each policy, we keep the architecture, training data, and update budget fixed while varying inference from one to sixteen network evaluations. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X–V performs particularly well with one or two evaluations, while V benefits substantially from additional steps. Direct X, in contrast, improves little as the budget grows. The best prediction objective therefore depends not only on the policy, but also on how many refinement steps it can afford.

Why does this ranking change? We examine the structure of the targets and the behavior of their predictions along the noise-to-action path. Clean action chunks have far more concentrated sample covariance spectra than velocity targets or Gaussian noise. At high noise, endpoint predictions remain substantially more stable across different noise initializations. Near a clean action, velocity-based updates produce lower recovery error: they correct the current estimate rather than predicting the entire action again. These results point to a natural division of labor (Figure 1): endpoint prediction for recovering actions from noise, and velocity prediction for refining them near the end of generation.

Guided by this finding, we introduce UniVEP (Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction). UniVEP trains both prediction modes within a shared action network, using a consistency objective to align the clean actions implied by each mode. A velocity-weighted endpoint loss further strengthens endpoint supervision. During sampling, UniVEP first predicts endpoints at high noise and then switches to velocity prediction for low-noise refinement. Each step evaluates only the selected mode, retaining the inference cost of a single-target policy. Joint training also strengthens the endpoint predictor, allowing the policy to generate effective action chunks with a single network evaluation.

The resulting gains extend across simulated and real-robot manipulation. On RoboTwin Clean, UniVEP with StarVLA achieves 61.36% success in one evaluation, exceeding the strongest single-target baseline at sixteen evaluations (59.96%). On LiLa-WAM, two evaluations achieve 85.96% success, surpassing the best sixteen-step single-target result (82.60%) while cutting action-generation latency by 77.1%. On three real dual-arm tasks, mean success increases from 49.33% to 58.67%.

Our contributions are threefold:

Comprehensive comparison of prediction targets. We systematically study V, X, and X–V across multiple VLA and WAM architectures, manipulation benchmarks, and inference budgets, revealing distinct performance trends as the sampling-step budget changes.

Understanding their complementary strengths. Through action-space statistics and noise-conditioned prediction probes, we find that endpoint prediction is more stable at high noise, whereas velocity prediction is more effective for near-clean refinement.

UniVEP for efficient robot manipulation. We unify endpoint and velocity prediction through joint supervision and noise-dependent switching. Across the policies we evaluate, UniVEP achieves strong manipulation performance with one or two network evaluations. At the same number of sampling steps, it matches the inference FLOPs of a single-target policy.

title: Dynamic Human-Robot Role Allocation through Entropy-Based Monitoring and LLM Reasoning
authors: Elena Merlo,Marta Lagomarsino,Hamidreza Raei,Arash Ajoudani
abstract:
Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user’s ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user’s intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency.
The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions.
The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.
introduction:
Role allocation in human-robot collaboration (HRC) originally relied on fixed, predefined strategies derived from the inherent capabilities of humans and robots. In line with Fitts’ List of “Men Are Better At/Machines Are Better At” [1], humans were typically assigned tasks demanding reasoning, adaptability, or creativity, whereas robots were responsible for operations that were repetitive, precise, or hazardous.
As technology advances and increasingly powerful AI models emerge, the traditional separation between human and robot capacities is becoming less distinct, calling for adaptive and context-sensitive role assignment strategies [2].
By monitoring online the state of the human, the robot, and the surrounding environment, roles can be dynamically adjusted during task execution, optimizing the team performance and fostering fluid collaboration [3, 4].

In industry and healthcare, repetitive tasks and heavy lifting can lead to musculoskeletal injuries and reduced productivity. Embedding physical condition and ergonomic assessments within role allocation strategies facilitates optimized load sharing, promoting both human well-being and system efficiency.
Classical approaches rely on explicit ergonomic thresholds or rule-based criteria. For example, Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA)-based systems [5] reassigned tasks to the robot when human posture becomes unsafe, while other methods combined initial offline allocation with online fatigue estimation from motion tracking [6].
To manage more complex constraints, several works use optimization-based role allocation. Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) formulations [7, 8] balanced makespan, precedence, and ergonomic load from estimated worker’s posture, updating task assignments online as human performance evolves. In [9], authors proposed an AO⋆ search over an AND/OR Graph (AOG) of feasible assembly sequences and agent assignments, with nodes as subassemblies and agent-specific edges as actions. Task costs reflect agent suitability: robots have fixed costs and penalized infeasible tasks, while human costs depend on KWear, derived from Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) scores and posture duration. When KWear exceeds safe limits, tasks shift to the robot until recovery.
Alternatively, data-driven approaches can estimate fatigue through learned biomechanical models [10], assigning demanding tasks to the robot. When tasks cannot be decomposed, allocation shift to the control level, with robots adapting assistance policies based on human fatigue measured via EMG [11] or switching control modes dynamically [12]: a strategy that is effective but often task-specific and difficult to generalize.
However, although these strategies reduce musculoskeletal strain, when tasks have similar ergonomic risk scores, the resulting role assignment may become non-intuitive. While users readily accept not being assigned to clearly high-risk tasks like heavy lifting, being asked to perform a task with comparable risk but against their intentions can also feel frustrating.

Other approaches exploit cognitive load measures or user preferences to improve both performance and user satisfaction. Early approaches relied on rule-based strategies: the robot adjusts its autonomy level or reassigns subtasks when cognitive load, stress, or trust estimates cross predefined thresholds [13, 14].
A second family of methods formulated allocation as an optimization problem, selecting roles that balanced productivity with human well-being, keeping mental or physiological stress within safe limits [15, 16].
More recent work has shifted toward learning-based personalization. Robots learn human capabilities or trustworthiness from task outcomes and allocate roles accordingly [17], or model collaboration as a two-player game in which both partners negotiate roles that satisfy productivity and stress objectives, approaching equilibrium through experience [18].
In this context, estimates of trust or stress are not intentional inputs provided by the user, so the resulting allocations may confuse an operator who still wishes to retain some freedom in choosing what to do. More recently, Large Language Models (LLM)s have been used to process explicit user requests, which represents a step toward more intuitive collaboration thanks to the naturalness of verbal communication.
For instance, [19] allowed users to express states or preferences directly (e.g., “I have a back pain”), which an LLM translated into allocation costs, reducing the likelihood of assigning to the user tasks that strain their back.

While the above-mentioned approaches typically prioritized a single optimization objective, the following combine multiple factors simultaneously.
[20] introduced a capability-based framework scoring agent-task pairs by task complexity, dexterity, and physical effort.
[21] formulated allocation as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem that accounts for makespan, workload, quality, preferences, and spatiotemporal constraints, with dynamic re-allocation during execution, but its computational burden limits online use.
To address this, [22] leveraged Behavior Trees (BT)s to decompose jobs into smaller subproblems, solving a MILP only for currently unlocked tasks. Allocation considered capabilities, ergonomics, and availability.
However, having many factors influencing the allocation decision, it becomes even harder for the user to understand why certain tasks are assigned to them.
In [23], an augmented reality interface was used for negotiation: the user could explicitly accept or reject proposed allocations, updating preference-based costs that influenced future algorithm decisions. In this way, the user became part of the decision-making process, recognizing that their intentions were taken into account.
However, continuously requiring the user to confirm allocations can negatively affect the fluency of the interaction, interrupting task execution and eventually becoming tedious and unnatural [24]. Moreover, the human freedom of action remains limited, as the user can only accept or reject the proposed allocation without actively taking initiative within the collaboration.
Allowing users to choose actions on the fly, rather than following imposed allocations, remains relatively underexplored despite its relevance for tasks admitting multiple valid execution sequences, such as lightweight assembly. To include human decision-making authority in a role allocation framework, [25] used wearable devices to recognize gestures, informing an AOG-based task manager of the human’s ongoing activity and triggering compatible robot actions. However, their approach required task-specific gesture training and did not assess activity completion and correctness.

This work proposes a dynamic role allocation framework that aims to promote both intuitiveness and human agency in HRC tasks.
To foster intuitive interaction, users can communicate with the robot through natural language, as they would with a human teammate. By leveraging the commonsense reasoning capabilities of an LLM, the robot adapts its behavior to the provided instructions, making its actions easier to anticipate and understand.
To support human agency, our framework monitors hand-object interactions through an RGB camera and evaluates their information flow using Shannon entropy measures [26], representing the evolution of human activity through dynamic scene graphs [27] and allowing its identification without any task-specific training phase. Moreover, the structural properties of the generated scene graphs allow the system to assess whether an activity has been completed correctly, providing a basis for detecting execution anomalies and triggering appropriate robot interventions.
The main methodological contributions are the design of:

The remainder of the manuscript is organized as follows. Section II details the design of the BT-based role allocator and the involved cost computation. Section III presents the experimental campaign conducted to validate the framework and evaluate multi-subject experience. Section IV reports the experimental results. Section V concludes the manuscript discussing results and framing limitations and future directions.

title: Reference-Twist-Based Velocity-Domain Spatiotemporal Calibration for mmWave Radar, Event Camera, and IMU
authors: Zhenghao Zou,Yang Lyu,Xiaohu Guo,Chunhui Zhao,Quan Pan
abstract: Multi-sensor navigation requires a common spatial and temporal basis, but geometric calibration relies on targets, features, point clouds, or pose associations that are difficult to establish across mmWave radars, event cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMUs). These sensors nevertheless share rigid-body motion. This paper formulates reference-conditioned velocity-domain spatiotemporal calibration for a rigid suite of two mmWave radars, one event camera, and two IMUs. Given a trusted reference body twist, radar Doppler, event normal flow, and inertial measurements are regressed against the same motion to estimate relative rotations, lever arms, time offsets, and sensor-specific bias and scale without artificial targets, structure from motion, or cross-modal point-cloud registration. The reference is treated as a conditioning input rather than a sensor to be calibrated. We compare joint and reference-conditioned estimation, derive conditional identifiability and CRLB-level covariance and bias bounds, and state the operating conditions under which conditioning is informative. Indoor and forest recordings with axis-separated motion evaluate initialization, temporal alignment, motion degeneracy, reference-input sensitivity, and residual consistency. Because the reference does not add physical observability, the estimates remain conditional on reference accuracy, synchronization, motion excitation, and projection diversity.
introduction:
Robot navigation relies on multi-source state feedback for localization, planning, and control. Multi-sensor fusion is a standard way to obtain such feedback with complementary robustness, but fusion is meaningful only after the measurements have been expressed in a common spatial and temporal basis. Spatial calibration determines relative orientations and lever arms; temporal calibration associates each sample with the same body motion. Without this basis, residuals from different sensors describe different states at different instants, and their apparent complementarity cannot be exploited consistently [1, 2, 3].

Velocity provides a compact state feedback for establishing this basis. Unlike a global pose, velocity is a local quantity: it does not require a map or global position, and high-rate linear and angular velocity constraints remain informative in motion estimation and in directions where geometric observability degenerates. For heterogeneous sensing, velocity-domain observations are also easier to relate than geometric features, because rigid-body kinematics provides a common physical model even when different sensors observe disjoint scene content. The radar, event camera, and IMU considered here are all velocity-sensitive: Doppler measures radial velocity, event normal flow encodes image-plane motion, and inertial measurements provide angular rate and specific force. None alone supplies a complete body twist, but their native observations share motion as a linking variable.

Geometry-based calibration is widely used when targets, features, point clouds, or pose graphs can be associated across sensors [4, 5, 6]. These associations are fragile for the present suite. Radar returns are sparse and susceptible to multipath; event streams report asynchronous brightness changes rather than persistent appearance [7]; and an IMU provides no geometric observation of the scene. Consequently, a radar detection, an event, and an inertial sample have no natural common geometric correspondence, even when each sensor is individually well modeled. Enforcing geometry-based calibration would require additional targets or scene structure and a reliable cross-modal association stage, which the heterogeneous measurements do not by themselves provide.

Motion-based calibration offers an alternative when direct cross-modal correspondence is unavailable [8, 9]. Rigidly mounted sensors share the same body motion, so motion correlation can recover rotation and timing without matching scene features, while continuous-time formulations can represent motion between asynchronous samples. Trajectory alignment is one route, but it requires poses or integrated trajectories and therefore inherits drift, gravity, and initialization errors. Velocity-domain calibration instead compares native velocity observations directly: it avoids pose integration and global attitude propagation while retaining the lever-arm term that couples rotation to translation. The proposed formulation follows this second route.

We further adopt a reference-conditioned setting: given a trusted reference body twist, each sensor is regressed against the same body motion, converting the calibration problem into modality-specific parameter blocks. When the reference is independent, synchronized, and sufficiently excited, this offers an effective engineering route to rapid and accurate spatiotemporal calibration: the reference supplies the common exogenous motion that would otherwise be estimated as a shared latent state, breaks the information isolation between heterogeneous sensor blocks, and avoids propagating the degeneracy and errors of a jointly estimated velocity state into every sensor-specific block. The reference is an input rather than a sensor to be calibrated; it changes the estimation structure but does not add physical observability. Its operating conditions and CRLB-level gain are analyzed in Section III.

The proposed formulation connects each sensor’s native observation to the same reference twist, retains the lever-arm contribution under rotational excitation, and preserves modality-specific measurement models. The resulting estimates remain conditional on reference quality, synchronization, and motion excitation.

The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We analyze the estimation structure, identifiability conditions, and CRLB-level gain boundary of reference-conditioned velocity-domain spatiotemporal calibration, clarifying when a trusted reference removes shared-state uncertainty and when native measurement degeneracy remains.

We propose a reference-twist-based radar–event–IMU spatiotemporal calibration framework that integrates temporal alignment, rotation alignment, lever-arm estimation, and joint refinement through modality-specific residuals.

We develop a body-frame gravity-decoupled inertial constraint that removes explicit world-gravity and attitude integration from the accelerometer residual, reducing sensitivity to global attitude propagation.

We collect and evaluate indoor and forest recordings with axis-separated omnidirectional excitation, and report initialization, timing, motion-degeneracy, reference-input sensitivity, and residual-consistency results on a rigid radar–event–IMU platform.

The scope is deliberately defined by the availability of a trusted reference, not by a claim that one calibration architecture dominates all others. The proposed method is not a replacement for reference-free joint calibration; joint estimators remain the appropriate choice when no reliable reference is available. Rather, it is a practical and theoretically grounded choice for reference-available settings, where it offers an effective engineering route to fast, accurate spatiotemporal calibration without depending on a jointly estimated velocity state. The reference is a conditioning input that simplifies the estimator structure; it does not add physical observability. The analysis and experiments therefore characterize the operating envelope of this choice rather than establish a universal ranking of calibration methods.

1. We analyze the estimation structure, identifiability conditions, and CRLB-level gain boundary of reference-conditioned velocity-domain spatiotemporal calibration, clarifying when a trusted reference removes shared-state uncertainty and when native measurement degeneracy remains.

2. We propose a reference-twist-based radar–event–IMU spatiotemporal calibration framework that integrates temporal alignment, rotation alignment, lever-arm estimation, and joint refinement through modality-specific residuals.

3. We develop a body-frame gravity-decoupled inertial constraint that removes explicit world-gravity and attitude integration from the accelerometer residual, reducing sensitivity to global attitude propagation.

4. We collect and evaluate indoor and forest recordings with axis-separated omnidirectional excitation, and report initialization, timing, motion-degeneracy, reference-input sensitivity, and residual-consistency results on a rigid radar–event–IMU platform.

title: Reference-Free Humanoid Skateboarding via Termination-Shaped Reinforcement Learning
authors: Ganeshvar Soenessardien,Michael Przystupa,Kevin Sebastian Luck
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE-RAS 25th International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids 2026)
abstract:
Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but object-mediated locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult.
One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion.
Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification.
In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning.
The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations.
We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion.
Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot–board locomotion.
Experiments are performed on a simulated K1 humanoid robot in Mujoco.
The results demonstrate the feasibility of reference-free humanoid-object locomotion with modest hardware constraints while identifying limitations in movement style, statistical precision, reproducibility and eventual hardware transfer.
introduction:
Humanoid robots can now walk, balance, recover from pushes and traverse rough terrain using learned controllers trained in massively parallel simulators [1, 2, 3, 4]. Almost all of these skills involve direct contact between the robot’s feet and a static support surface.
However, a large and practically important class of behaviours is more difficult to master: locomotion tasks in which a robot has to interact with a passive object, that is neither actuated nor rigidly attached to the body, to achieve movement.
Pushing a cart, riding a scooter, balancing on a mobility aid, or skateboarding all share this structure.
The object stores momentum, introduces its own contact dynamics and can fail in ways the robot does not always directly control [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

Skateboarding is a particularly demanding instance of object-mediated locomotion and therefore a useful benchmark for embodied artificial intelligence.
To locomote with a skateboard, a humanoid must keep one foot on a small, freely rolling deck, and use the other foot to generate propulsion against the ground while regulating the contacts among three coupled bodies (robot, board and ground).
Misplaced contacts can induce foot slip, unwanted board rotation, incorrect foot-board contact patterns, failed phase transitions, or degeneration into merely pushing the board rather than riding it.
Success therefore requires contact rich whole-body control, robot-object coordination and stable locomotion through an under-actuated external system simultaneously [9, 10, 11, 12].

This paper investigates applying reinforcement learning to humanoid locomotion on a skateboard-like platform without the use of task-specific priors used by recent humanoid skateboarding systems.
HUSKY, for example, achieves agile real-world humanoid skateboarding by combining Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) [13] from human pushing demonstrations with a physics-guided lean-to-steer model and trajectory-guided phase transitions, and validates the resulting controller on real hardware [9].
Such reference data and engineering are powerful when available, but they also make the method depend on human demonstrations, physical modelling and task-specific integration which are often not available or hard to obtain.
Furthermore, such data may be hard to utilize due to the existence of the correspondence problem between robot and human embodiment [14, 15].

This paper focuses on the harder and complementary case of reference-free learning [16]. The controller receives no motion-capture trajectory, no target joint-posture sequence, and no explicit posture-tracking reward that tells it what skating should look like.
The skateboarding behaviour must be selected and emerge by learning from the task reward, the reset geometry and the early termination conditions.
The question is whether recognisable humanoid-board locomotion can emerge from this minimal supervision alone and what behaviour appears when no human motion prior is present to shape its style.

Contribution:  The objective is to design, train, and evaluate a reference free reinforcement-learning controller that enables a Booster K1 humanoid to propel a passive four-wheel roller board forward while remaining upright, keeping one foot on the board and using the other to push on the ground. Three research questions structure the work:

Feasibility and extent. To what extent can a Booster K1 humanoid learn
recognisable skateboard propulsion without any reference motion or explicit
posture-tracking reward, and what is the character of the resulting behaviour?

Feasibility and extent. To what extent can a Booster K1 humanoid learn
recognisable skateboard propulsion without any reference motion or explicit
posture-tracking reward, and what is the character of the resulting behaviour?

Mechanism. Which reward and termination design choices are necessary to
prevent trivial exploit solutions and steer the policy toward skating-like
mechanics?

Consistency and cost. How consistent is the learned behaviour across
independent seeds when trained under a constrained hardware budget, and what does
that budget permit and preclude?

title: AGE-Capture: Autonomous, General, and Efficient UAV Capture for High-Fidelity Scene Reconstruction
authors: Xiaofeng Jin,Ningbo Bu,Matteo Frosi,Yiran Guo,Weilun Ren,Matteo Matteucci
abstract:
High-fidelity scene reconstruction with an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) requires more than identifying valuable viewpoints: the system must autonomously acquire informative observations and determine task completion under different sensing configurations and limited flight resources.
We present AGE-Capture, an autonomous, sensor-adaptive, and efficient active-capture framework for real UAVs.
Building on renderability, the framework uses a lightweight online state to evaluate the utility of candidate views, assess task progress, and guide flight execution.
By decoupling geometric exploration from reconstruction observations and establishing a unified camera-ray interface, the framework allows different range sensors and RGB camera models to share a reconstruction-driven acquisition pipeline.
Reconstruction-frontier viewpoints characterize residual acquisition value for region screening and autonomous termination; dynamics-aware hierarchical planning combined with asynchronous event-driven capture reduces unnecessary inter-region motion, time spent waiting for plans, and repeated observations.
Across ten indoor and outdoor simulation scenes, AGE-Capture achieves a mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) 3.303.30–3.53​dB3.53\,\mathrm{dB} higher than that of the online baselines while using 58.2%58.2\% of the common mission-time budget on average. Its mean peak GPU memory usage is 91.0%91.0\%–93.3%93.3\% lower than that of the same baselines.
Experiments with different sensor configurations validate the adaptability of the shared acquisition pipeline, while flights in nine real-world scenes further demonstrate onboard closed-loop operation under practical computational and motion constraints.
introduction:
Neural rendering and Gaussian Splatting have advanced high-fidelity 3D reconstruction and novel-view synthesis [1, 2]. Yet reconstruction quality remains strongly dependent on the spatial and angular coverage of the acquired observations. Active reconstruction addresses this dependence by selecting observation positions and viewing directions that improve the current scene representation under limited acquisition resources. For large-scale real-world scenes, UAVs provide a practical platform because they can reach viewpoints at different elevations and headings (Fig. ).

Existing active-capture methods primarily address where to observe next. Traditional next-best-view (NBV) methods evaluate candidate viewpoints using geometric uncertainty, information gain, coverage, or visibility [3]. More recent approaches estimate the potential value of candidate observations through neural-field uncertainty, radiance-field feedback, or related reconstruction-aware signals, thereby relating observation utility more directly to the reconstruction objective [4, 5, 6].

Identifying valuable candidate viewpoints, however, is only one part of a deployable UAV active-reconstruction system. The system must also accommodate heterogeneous sensing configurations and coordinate acquisition decisions with execution under limited flight resources. Existing methods commonly evaluate reconstruction under a fixed view count or time budget. These limits constrain capture but do not indicate whether further observations would improve the reconstruction. The system must therefore assess residual reconstruction value online and terminate capture when further acquisition is no longer warranted.

Renderability-based reconstruction gain provides a state representation suitable for this online decision process. R3CON represents the value of candidate observations through a lightweight renderability state that is decoupled from a particular reconstruction backend, avoiding repeated optimization of a complete neural radiance field during planning [7]. Its computation and storage requirements support frequent online queries and updates. We build a closed-loop UAV capture process around this state: heterogeneous RGB observations are converted to a common camera-ray representation and update the state; the state guides region scheduling and local NBV selection; and the UAV acquires the next observation at the selected viewpoint.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A unified active reconstruction architecture for heterogeneous sensing configurations. We decouple geometric sensing from reconstruction observations and construct a common observation interface using camera rays, allowing RGB camera models with calibrated ray mappings to share the same reconstruction-aware active capture pipeline, while the geometric exploration module handles depth-map and LiDAR inputs.

A reconstruction-frontier mechanism for autonomous task completion. We define reconstruction-frontier viewpoints at the position level and use seed-based region screening to assess task progress and residual acquisition value, allowing the system to determine whether to continue capture under the defined reconstruction-value threshold.

An efficient active capture system under limited flight resources. Hierarchical planning coordinates region scheduling with local view selection. Asynchronous perception, state updates, planning, and execution reduce the time spent waiting for plans.

title: Agentic Scaling of Embodied Tasks in Simulation for Synthetic Data Collection and Policy Evaluation
authors: Kang Wang,Xiaolei Zhou,Xiaoyu Wu,Zhendong Wang
comment: . Dataset:this https URLProject website:this https URL
abstract: Scaling embodied interaction data requires a broad collection of usable tasks, yet specifying and validating each task instance remains costly. We present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework that expands existing task collections under human intent. Its central representation links interaction requirements to object and part bindings, scene and robot configurations, initial conditions, and completion criteria. A task-generation agent reuses interaction structure to construct supported variations and revises incompatible configurations using validation feedback. A task-execution agent uses the same bindings and geometric records to select robot-supported skills and check completion against the original task criteria. On RoboCasa, the framework builds the AgenticTask collection, saving 16,45016{,}450 task instances from 20,32320{,}323 construction attempts at a throughput of 166.97166.97 saved instances per elapsed hour, with 62.26%62.26\% of construction attempts passing the configured physical checks. The execution agent completes approximately 38%38\% of evaluated tasks, with successful cases spanning object placement, articulated manipulation, and sequential arrangement. Diagnostic analysis identifies improvement priorities in construction reliability, action selection, task–robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results demonstrate task-collection expansion with measured construction productivity and concrete execution evidence, providing a foundation for subsequent interaction-data collection for embodied AI.
introduction:
Training general-purpose embodied policies requires large-scale and diverse interaction data, yet existing datasets remain insufficient to support robust generalization across tasks and environments. Human-driven data collection alone is unlikely to bridge this gap. Simulation provides a scalable alternative for generating synthetic demonstrations, systematically evaluating learned policies, and enhancing their generalization across diverse tasks and scenarios.

However, scaling embodied task generation in simulation remains hindered by two fundamental challenges: scalable task specification and efficient autonomous execution. Despite advances in automated 3D modeling and simulation engines, defining diverse tasks requires jointly reasoning over task objectives, scene configurations, interactive objects, and simulator capabilities. Automated execution presents further challenges: teleoperation is labor-intensive, scripted approaches lack scalability, and policy-based methods suffer from a circular dependency between policy training and data collection.

Recent work has explored large language models (LLMs) for automating robotic task and data generation. GenSim2 uses multimodal and reasoning models to generate tasks and demonstrations [10], while GENMANIP translates task descriptions into task-oriented scene graphs [4]. SAGE and RoboGene further incorporate tool use and feedback into scene construction and task refinement [27, 30]. These advances demonstrate the potential of language models to translate high-level requests into task proposals. However, constructing usable tasks requires more than generating descriptions or code: candidate tasks must be instantiated, checked against the environment, and revised when incompatibilities arise. These requirements motivate an agent-based approach that connects model reasoning with resource retrieval, simulation tools, and feedback-driven decisions throughout task construction and execution.

Yet equipping an agent with tools does not by itself ensure usable task generation and execution. During generation, object and scene variations require consistent updates to physical targets, initial conditions, and success criteria, together with checks of physical validity and robot compatibility. During execution, the agent must ground task plans in actionable parts, scene geometry, and robot-supported skills. These challenges call for a shared representation that connects task requirements to physical entities, with validation feedback guiding task repair and geometric information supporting action selection.

To address these challenges, we present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework for expanding task collections through two specialized agents. The task-generation agent translates human intent into structured task requirements, retrieves compatible resources, and constructs variations supported by the simulator. Construction and validation feedback guide revisions to permitted configurations while preserving the intended interaction. The task-execution agent grounds the resulting task in robot-supported skills using object bindings, part information, and scene geometry. It updates action choices from execution feedback and checks completion against the task’s original success conditions, providing concrete evidence of task usability.

A hierarchical task representation connects the two agents. Semantic specifications identify the interaction requirements and permitted variations; instantiated task records bind these requirements to objects, parts, initial conditions, and success predicates; geometric scene graphs describe the entities and relations needed for checking and action grounding. This representation gives task construction, validation, and execution a consistent reference as objects and scene configurations change.

Using RoboCasa as a testbed [20], we construct the AgenticTask collection, comprising 16,450 saved task instances. Our experiments characterize construction throughput, physical screening, and the cost of feedback-guided revision. Execution results and four successful trajectories demonstrate usability across several interaction types, while failure analysis identifies obstacles in action selection, task–robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results characterize both the productivity of task expansion and the practical requirements for using the generated collection.

Our contributions are threefold:

An agent-based framework for task-collection expansion. AgenticTask uses human intent to guide task construction across compatible objects and scenes, and couples generation with execution-based usability testing to support embodied interaction-data collection.

A hierarchical task representation connecting generation and execution. Semantic requirements, object and part bindings, and geometric relations provide a shared basis for constrained task variation, feedback-guided revision, and robot skill grounding.

A task collection and an empirical study of its construction and usability. The AgenticTask collection contains 16,450 saved task instances in RoboCasa. Our study characterizes construction productivity, physical screening, execution outcomes, and failure patterns that inform further task and system refinement.

title: Close&Safe: Maximal Task Preservation for Redundant Manipulators via C-Space Boundary Detour
authors: Abhigyan Singh,Manthan Goyal,Fares Abu-Dakka,Ravi Prakash
abstract:
Contact-rich manipulation such as wiping, polishing and surface inspection
specifies the task as a continuous end-effector trajectory rather than a goal
pose. When an obstacle absent from the planning model intersects it,
conventional planners return a collision-free path that may differ from the
nominal throughout, discarding trajectory that was never obstructed. We present Close&Safe (Close to the intended task, Safe from obstacles), which decouples tracking from avoidance: the nominal is followed exactly
wherever it remains feasible, and avoidance acts only on the interval where it
is not, so tracking is hindered as little as the obstacle allows. On that interval we sample the configuration-space obstacle boundary
within a corridor around the nominal, connect the samples into a roadmap, and
search it for the detour that deviates least before rejoining the nominal at
the earliest feasible configuration. We evaluate across diverse simulated obstacle configurations, physical Franka experiments, and ablations of key algorithmic components. The results demonstrate collision-free trajectory repair with localized task modification, while recovering 52.4​–​78%52.4\text{--}78\% in simulation and on hardware.
introduction:
Robotic manipulators are increasingly used for tasks in which the motion of
the end-effector is not a means of reaching a goal but the specification of
the task itself. In wiping, polishing, welding, and surface inspection a
nominal Cartesian trajectory encodes spatial coverage and contact angle, and
departing from it has task-level consequences: a rerouted wiping motion
leaves an uncleaned region, a displaced weld path produces a seam defect, a
perturbed scan yields gaps in coverage. For such a task, producing some
collision-free path between two task-space poses is not a solution. The
nominal trajectory is a specification to be preserved, not an initial guess a
planner may reshape.

The difficulty arises when an obstacle is absent from the model used to
generate that trajectory. In Fig.  a wiping trajectory is
planned across a table and a jug and human(mannequin), unmodeled at planning time, collides in part
of the swept region. The obstacle invalidates a short segment of the motion
and the remainder stays executable. Four requirements follow. The executed
trajectory should track the nominal wherever it remains feasible, depart from
it only over the obstructed segment, minimize the task-space deviation
incurred during that departure, and rejoin the nominal at the earliest
configuration from which it can be resumed. We refer to this objective as
maximal task preservation.

Existing methods trade these requirements against one another rather than
ordering them, and the horizon over which avoidance is decided governs how.
Trajectory optimization [1, 3, 2, 4, 5] and sampling-based planning [6, 7, 8, 9] decide over the whole trajectory and are free to reshape all of it.
Reactive repulsion [10, 11, 15, 12] and
per-instant inverse kinematics [13, 14] decide at one
control instant and cannot look ahead, so a deviation is sized by a gain or a
greedy step rather than by the segment to be covered. Null-space redundancy
resolution [16, 17] is the exception: it tracks the
nominal exactly while a collision-free redundant configuration exists, which
is why we adopt it as the first level of our hierarchy, and offers nothing
once that manifold is blocked. Table I records which
requirements each family meets; Sec. II treats them in
detail.

We propose Close&Safe (Close to the intended task, Safe from obstacles), which orders these requirements instead of weighting them. Interference from an obstacle is classified as reducible, meaning null-space motion can absorb it with no task deviation, or irreducible, meaning no configuration satisfies the task and avoids collision at once. The classification is a feasibility test rather than a comparison against a margin, so it decides when the task may be modified without a quantity to tune. Where interference is irreducible, we take the behavioral principle of Bug algorithms [18, 19]: follow the reference, detour along the obstacle boundary, and rejoin at the first opportunity, but replace greedy tracing with an explicit road-map of the configuration-space obstacle boundary, built in a corridor around the blocked segment and searched. The circumnavigation direction is selected by comparing candidate routes across the blocked segment, rather than by a local gradient, extending the boundary-following principle beyond planar settings. Restricting exploration to a thin boundary shell also avoids sampling unnecessary free-space volume, reducing the computation required for the detour search. Fig.  shows the behavior and the four stages that produce it. Our contributions are:

A minimum-deviation detour confined to the blocked segment, found
by searching a roadmap of the configuration-space obstacle boundary built
in a corridor around it. Concave and multiply-connected geometry needs no
special treatment, and segments never in collision are never discarded.

A minimum-deviation detour confined to the blocked segment, found
by searching a roadmap of the configuration-space obstacle boundary built
in a corridor around it. Concave and multiply-connected geometry needs no
special treatment, and segments never in collision are never discarded.

An evaluation against four baselines on four simulated Franka
scenarios, scored by coverage, the fraction of the nominal path executed
within tolerance. Among methods collision-free throughout, ours
attains the highest preservation in all three cleaning cases, averaging
59.5%59.5\% against 45.6%45.6\%, at a clearance held within a 4.54.5\,mm band.
Absolute values are bounded by the scenarios, in which part of the path is
unreachable for any method.

Hardware validation on two tasks with demonstration-derived
nominal: cleaning with a jug and human(mannequin) in the path and scanning interrupted by a human(mannequin) hand posture.

title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
authors: John Won,Yonghoon Dong,Jinwoo Shin
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world.
Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations.
This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes.
To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations.
Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation.
We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state.
Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes.
On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD.
These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%8.3\%.
introduction:
World models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2025) predict future states conditioned on action sequences without execution in the environment.
Recently, robotics world models (RWMs) (Gao et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026) realize this by building on video diffusion foundation models (Wan et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024), generating photorealistic, temporally coherent videos conditioned on robot actions.
This makes them a promising direction for diverse usage in evaluating policies (Guo et al., 2026; Jeon et al., 2026), planning manipulation trajectories (Assran et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026), or generating training data (Jang et al., 2025).

However, serving these roles requires robotics world models to faithfully reflect how small action changes alter future outcomes. For example, slight changes in reaching motion can determine whether a gripper grasps an object, misses it, or pushes it away (Figure 1).
Yet existing models tend to produce visually plausible videos that ignore such differences (Yang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026). Since such models predict similar outcomes for actions with different real consequences, they are unreliable as policy evaluators and mislead planners into selecting the wrong actions.

Addressing this requires world models to acquire action sensitivity, and by extension, learn the relationship between action variations and resulting dynamics.
We therefore treat action sensitivity as a distributional problem.
Rather than simply reproducing recorded futures with high visual fidelity, we argue that an RWM should capture how the distribution of future observations shifts as actions vary under a given observation context.

To learn such distributions, we introduce action variation directly into the training data. Specifically, we collect robot-environment interactions by running a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation, in which an operator interacts freely with objects without a predefined task. Following Lynch et al. (2020), we refer to such data as play data and to this policy as the play policy.

During data collection, we inject temporally correlated noise into the action chunks produced by the play policy before rollout and log the injected perturbations.
These rollouts expose how visual outcomes vary with action changes without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state or explicit outcome labels.

Building on this data, we introduce AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective that teaches the world model the relationship between action changes and their visual consequences.
AFFECT explicitly uses the noise injected into the training actions to supervise how generated visual outcomes should change with those action perturbations.
In this way, the model is directly encouraged to respond to action variation in the same way as the real environment, rather than merely generating visually plausible futures.
Since AFFECT operates on features from frozen encoders, it can be added to existing RWMs without architectural changes.

We evaluate AFFECT on a simulated UR5e environment and two real-robot settings following the DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and ALOHA-2 (Aldaco et al., 2024) configurations, and apply it to two distinct backbones, DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) and Cosmos3 (Agarwal et al., 2026).
To test whether the world model reflects action differences, we measure how well its predicted policy success rates correlate with real ones.
On this measure, AFFECT improves every one of the six backbone–embodiment combinations, for instance raising the correlation of DreamDojo on DROID from 0.4680.468 to 0.7900.790 and that of Cosmos3 on ALOHA-2 from 0.2980.298 to 0.6940.694.
AFFECT also improves most visual metrics, including FVD reductions of up to 23%23\% on DROID and gains on every metric at both short and long horizons in simulation, suggesting that learning how actions shape outcomes also helps the model predict more realistic futures.
Finally, this improved sensitivity translates into better model-based planning, where AFFECT raises task success rates by around 8%8\% on both UR5e pick-and-place and ALOHA-2 long-horizon tasks.

title: Learning optimal gaits and styles for terrain-adaptive quadruped locomotion
authors: Guillaume Bellegarda,Auke Ijspeert
abstract: Animals use many different gaits to locomote at different speeds across varying terrains. A longstanding question in biology and robotics is: which gait is best? This question is most often addressed from an energy-efficiency perspective on flat terrain, leaving open how the answer depends on terrain and on the criterion optimized. Here we show that gait optimality is determined jointly by terrain, performance metric, and velocity. We use deep reinforcement learning and networks of abstract oscillators, modeling spinal central pattern generators, to learn 11 quadrupedal gaits across diverse challenging terrains, together with the locomotion style (base height, foot ground clearance, foot offsets) that each requires. A second policy then selects among them to optimize a user-specified criterion such as cost of transport, base stability, or joint smoothness. Across these performance metrics and within this repertoire, every gait is optimal under at least one terrain–metric–velocity combination. The framework adapts zero-shot to gait couplings and styles never seen during training, to terrains far beyond the training distribution, and to larger quadrupeds five times the training mass. With a single additional pitch-tracking reward term, the same gait couplings also support bipedal-mode locomotion. Our method provides a general and systematic way to produce expressive locomotion and to select the gait best suited to a given terrain and criterion. title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
authors: Yao Zhang,Bin Yu,Shijie Lian,Haishan Liu,Changti Wu,Yu Wu,Kai Chen
abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success–latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41×2.41\times faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.
introduction:
World models enable visual controllers to compare action
sequences through predicted outcomes in representation
space [16, 24].
However, evaluating many candidate sequences through
predictive search can incur substantial online computation.
This raises a central question: how can world-model planning
advance the success–latency Pareto frontier while retaining
the benefits of predictive search?

A complete planner must decide both which actions are worth considering and how much computation to spend comparing them. A strong initial plan reduces the burden on search, but it does not eliminate the potential value of comparing alternatives. Under a limited online budget, refinement must explore useful candidates while controlling the cost of their evaluation. With recursive scoring, each candidate requires a chain of intermediate state predictions, and this computation is repeated across search rounds.

Action construction and candidate comparison expose different information to the planner. During sequential construction, later actions remain unspecified, so intermediate outcome predictions provide context for subsequent action choices. Once a candidate is complete, all its actions are known. Under a terminal visual-goal objective, comparison requires only its predicted endpoint. This distinction motivates retaining intermediate queries for action construction and using direct terminal queries for candidate evaluation.

We introduce Fast-JEPA, a planning framework that reorganizes predictive computation to support action-sequence search at low planning cost (Figure 2). Fast-JEPA constructs a goal-directed plan through world-model-guided action generation, providing a starting point for predictive search. Complete candidate sequences are then compared through direct terminal predictions under a shared visual-goal objective, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. By concentrating search around an informed plan while reducing repeated candidate-evaluation costs, Fast-JEPA retains the benefits of predictive search within a substantially lower computational budget.

To evaluate world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions and temporal constraints, we introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark comprising three complementary protocols across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom. DynaGoal-Shift evaluates adaptation to changing goals and environment geometry, while DynaGoal-Deadline measures goal completion under joint planning and execution time budgets. DynaGoal-Delay further examines robustness to controlled response delays as environments evolve between observation and action.

Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA
achieves 96.50% average success rate with a mean
complete planning latency of 10.88 ms. This search-based controller plans 2.41×2.41\times faster than INTACT while attaining higher average success (Figure 1). Search-budget sweeps show that its low-latency operating region extends across candidate counts and refinement depths, and the scoring comparison links lower planning cost to cheaper candidate evaluation. Fast-JEPA also achieves 73.83% average success on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline. Together, these results demonstrate that Fast-JEPA maintains competitive success at substantially lower planning latency.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We present Fast-JEPA, a world-model planning
framework that advances the success–latency Pareto
frontier by reorganizing predictive computation for
efficient action-sequence search.

We introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark
evaluating world-model planning under
out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines,
and response delays.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that Fast-JEPA advances the success–latency Pareto frontier of world-model planning across diverse control tasks.

1. We present Fast-JEPA, a world-model planning
framework that advances the success–latency Pareto
frontier by reorganizing predictive computation for
efficient action-sequence search.

2. We introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark
evaluating world-model planning under
out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines,
and response delays.

3. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Fast-JEPA advances the success–latency Pareto frontier of world-model planning across diverse control tasks.
