title: Multiple-Camera Tracking of Rigid Objects
authors: Frédérick Martin,Radu Horaud
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
In this paper we describe a method for tracking rigid objects using
one or several cameras. The tracking process consists of aligning a
3-D model representation of an object with image contours by measuring
and minimizing the image error between predicted model points and
image contours. The tracker behaves like a visual servo loop where the
internal and external camera parameters are updated at each new image
acquisition.
We study in detail the Jacobian matrix associated with this
minimization process in the presence of both point-to-point and
point-to-contour matches. We establish the minimal number of matches
that are needed as well as the singular configurations leading to a
rank-defficient Jacobian matrix. We find a mathematical link
between the point-to-point and point-to-contour cases. Based on this
link we show that the latter has the same kind of singularities than
the former. Moreover, we study multiple camera configurations which
optimize the robustness of the method in the presence of single-camera
singularities, bad, noisy, or missing data.
Extensive experiments done with a complex ship part and with up to
three cameras validate the method. In particular we show that the
tracker may well be used as a camera calibration procedure.
introduction:
The problem of localizing and tracking moving objects using one or
several cameras has been an active research topic. Objects fall into
several categories, from rigid, deformable, articulated and rigid, to
articulated and deformable. A common approach consists of using an
object model and of estimating the position and orientation of this
model such that some image-based error is minimized. The image error
describes the discrepancy between measured object features and
predicted model features. The ability to properly move the model such
that it optimally corresponds to the actual object depends on a number
of factors. Roughly speaking, the 3-D parameters associated with the
object’s behaviour (motion parameters, shape deformation parameters, joint
parameters for an articulated object, etc.) are related to the image
error by a Jacobian matrix.

With only one camera there are inherent ambiguities and
singularities. Indeed, one image configuration may lead to a number of
3-D actions and Jacobian singularities may lead to no action at
all. Therefore, it may be advantageous to use several cameras instead
of one. From a practical point of view this raises the problem of
dealing with multiple camera geometry. It is more tedious to calibrate
a multiple-camera system and to update the calibration data than to
calibrate a single camera. Moreover, the vast majority of previous
approaches consider the multi-camera system as a stereo device
requiring that each object feature is viewed in at least two images
and that image-to-image feature matches are provided.

In this paper we propose a multi-camera based method for tracking
rigid objects. A geometric model of the tracked object is provided in
advance. The method consists of a “visual servoing” approach applied
to the object model, [12]: At each iteration of the tracking process the
image error between model and object features allows to update the
parameters associated with the position and orientation of the model.

First, we investigate the case of one camera. We establish the link
between point-to-point tracking and point-to-contour tracking. We analyse
both the cases of fixed and varying camera internal parameters. We
study the singularities of the Jacobian matrix and we reveal the cases
where single-camera tracking cannot be properly performed.

Second, we investigate the case of several cameras. We show how the
single-camera case can be used to calibrate the multiple-camera
layout. We establish the tracking formulation which allows a rigid
camera layout with possibly varying internal camera parameters. This
formulation consists of running in parallel several single-camera
trackers and does not require any image-to-image correspondences. We
show how most of the single-camera singularities can be avoided by
using two or more cameras.

Third, we describe an implementation using three cameras and a complex
rigid object. Each camera observes a different object part and
therefore the system is very robust with respect to partial occlusions
simultaneously occurring in several images and with respect to total
occlusion of one or two cameras.

The idea of using pose for tracking stems from the work of Lowe
[16] who used line-segment matches and the
Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear minimization method. Tracking with
variable internal camera parameters has been introduced by Kinoshita
and Deguchi [13] who perform visual servoing and
camera calibration simultaneously. Espiau performed an in-depths
analysis of the convergence of visual servoing in the presence of
varying focal length [7].

Harris [9] and Armstrong and
Zisserman [1] proposed to predict a model contour in the
image and to search around this prediction for image points that are
likely to lie on a matching contour. They apply this technique to the
case of straight lines and use a robust method to fit a line to the
image points. Drummond and Cipolla [4, 5, 6] showed
that it is possible to cast the rigid model tracking problem into a
linear problem using the Lie algebra of the rigid motion - the
kinematic screw. They suggest a series of papers dealing with a
complex 3-D object (a ship part) and with articulated objects. The
approach of Drummond and Cipolla is interesting because it relies only
weakly on point or line matches. Instead their technique relies on
contour-to-points matching. They show that their approach can be used
for calibrating a camera. Other similar approaches to tracking using
an image prediction and searching in a window around this prediction
can be found in [21] and [24].

All these approaches to tracking consider only one camera and put
emphasis on
the data association problem. Multi-view
tracking has been barely investigated. There are several ways of using
several cameras. One way is to consider the multi-camera setup as a
3-D sensor, capture 3-D measurements, and perform the tracking
directly in 3-D space, [23],
[2]. Another way is to use the epipolar
constraint into the tracking loop itself and Lamiroy et
al. [15] combine the tracking equations
with the epipolar geometry constraint. Finally, when the cameras are
far apart, there are very few image-to-image correspondences and
single camera trackers may be performed in parallel. Thompson et
al. [22] extended the work of Harris and
of Armstrong and Zisserman to
multiple cameras and parallel trackers. They studied the improvements
in performance using several cameras rather that using one
camera. They describe an interesting and orignial teleoperation
application where synthetic views are produced on-line thus
maintaining, at a distance, visual information about the spatial
distribution and location of polyhedral objects.

In this paper we derive an explicit algebraic expression for the
Jacobian matrix associated with point-to-contour
correspondences. Although in the past robust results were obtained
with this type of data association, none thoroughly studied the
algebraic structure of the Jacobian, the minimal data sets necessary
to run a tracker, and the possibly singular configurations which lead
to tracking failures. Based on this analysis we are able to show that
a multiple-camera approach based on point-to-contour correspondences
lead to a robust rigid-object tracker that can deal with large occlusions.

Previous work on object tracking has mainly dealt with off-line
calibrated cameras (with the notable exception of [6]). This means
that on-line changes (focus setting, zooming, etc.) cannot be taken
into account and they are likely to affect the accuracy of
inter-camera calibration and of the pose parameters. The possibility
to adjust these parameters during tracking is thoroughly investigated
and evaluated in this paper.

The remaining of this paper is organized as
follows. Section 2 reviews the problem of
tracking a rigid object using a perspective camera model. The
relantionship between the pose parameters (to be estimated by the
tracker) and errors associated with the internal camera parameters is
thoroughly investigated. Rigid object tracking is treated as a
minimization problem and explicit formulae are derived for two types
of image-to-model matches: point-to-point and point-to-contour
assignments. Section 3
analyses the singularities associated with point-to-point assignments
while section 4 provides a
similar analysis for point-to-contour assignments. In particular,
singular cases are revealed especially when the internal camera
parameters are allowed to vary. Multiple-camera tracking is studied in
section 5 where it is shown that the
singularities associated with one camera disappear when two or more
cameras are being used. Finally section 6
describes extensive experiments that illustrate all the variations of
the tracking method.

title: From Sequence to Space: Explicit Spatial Belief with Vision-Language Distillation for Active Geo-Localization
authors: Ziyang Xu,Peng Han,Hai Zhou
abstract: Active geo-localization (AGL) asks an agent to navigate a small aerial search grid and reach a target specified by an aerial image, a ground-level photograph, or text. Existing methods align the goal modalities well, but they keep the navigation state inside a large sequential Transformer and train with a dense distance reward that uses the hidden goal location. This paper proposes EAGLE, an Explicit spatial-belief Agent for Geo-Localization and Exploration. Offline training jointly optimizes a teacher-conditioned Swin branch and a context-free Swin student from the same randomly masked partial mosaics. The teacher branch attends to frozen full-scene context extracted by Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both branches receive masked-cell aerial-feature reconstruction and uncertainty supervision, while the student additionally distills stop-gradient feature predictions from the teacher. After distillation, Qwen, its cached context, and the teacher-attention branch are discarded. The retained student predicts cell-level aerial-feature embeddings and predictive uncertainty from partial observations alone. These predictions are combined with the modality-aligned goal embedding and a trajectory-derived visitation mask to construct the spatial belief tensor. The student is then frozen while a compact CNN actor–critic is optimized with PPO. EAGLE achieves state-of-the-art average success rates of 78.1%, 76.4%, and 76.8% on MASA, xBD zero-shot transfer, and the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split, respectively, without using a VLM or cached visual tokens at inference. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Learning-Based System Identification for DVL-Constrained AUV Localization
authors: Mingxi Zhou,Emir Cem Gezer,Lin Zhao,William McConnell,Chengzhi Yuan
abstract: Nowadays, most AUVs utilize Doppler velocity logs (DVLs) and inertial measurement units (IMUs) to achieve satisfactory dead-reckoning results. However, the DVL bottom lock may not be available in some scenarios, such as moving over a soft bottom or traveling further away from the seafloor beyond the DVL’s range. As a result, the localization system solely reliant on the IMU data will experience significant drift. The relatively high cost of DVLs also inhibits multirobot or swarm operations. In this article, we present the results of using fully connected feedforward neural networks to predict vehicle velocity (surge, sway, and heave) for AUV localization. Approximation functions for the vehicle velocities are derived based on the generalized six degree-of-freedom dynamic equation and kinematics, proving that they are suitable for feedforward neural networks with measurable inputs. The neural networks are trained using field data collected using an AUV. An ablation study was conducted to investigate the impacts of hyperparameters, and the most effective models were selected using the Akaike information criterion. The selected neural network models are tested on three new sets of mission data collected on two different days. The quantitative results show that localization using vehicle velocities predicted by neural networks yields lower averaged root-mean-square distance errors and standard deviation compared to the DVL-aided dead-reckoning method. However, the extent of this improvement was found to depend on ocean current conditions. The promising results show that lightweight fully connected feedforward neural networks offer an attractive approach for inertial-based underwater localization when DVLs or their measurements are not available.
introduction:
AUTONOMOUS underwater vehicles (AUVs) have been widely used for ocean observation and monitoring. Georeferencing the observations collected by an AUV is critical to produce meaningful measurements (such as seabed images, current profiles, and dissolved oxygen observations) for quantifying the spatial extents of ocean processes. However, positioning AUVs underwater is challenging due to the lack of GPS signals underwater. Over the years, AUV localization has been studied extensively [1], with methods that can be typically divided into two types: external-aided methods and self-contained methods.

External-aided approaches usually leverage acoustic devices, such as long baseline (LBL), short baseline (SBL), and ultra-SBL (USBL). More recently, two-way-travel-time and one-way-travel-time localization methods have been extensively studied [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. These methods use the time-of-flight of acoustic messages to estimate the relative range between an underwater vehicle and another device at a known location. The range measurement is then fused using an extended Kalman filter (EKF) to update the vehicle pose. Acoustic-based methods work well in a bounded area, typically within several kilometers, where an AUV is within the reception range of the acoustic instrument. In contrast, long-range acoustic-aided localization methods are rarely studied [8] as the sound speed variations in the water columns increase the measurement uncertainty. Furthermore, the update rate when using acoustic communication devices is relatively slow, typically several seconds or even longer at further distances. Therefore, a self-contained localization method is still needed to estimate the vehicle position between acoustic receptions. The acoustic-aided localization also complicates the logistical operations, as acoustic instruments have to be deployed and recovered before and after the missions.

Given these limitations, self-contained localization approaches emerge as favorable alternatives because they utilize sensors onboard the vehicle to estimate vehicle positions. Compared to external-aided approaches, it is appealing due to its simplicity of setup and ease of use. Dead-reckoning, also referred to as inertial-based navigation, is the most common self-contained method. The simplest dead-reckoning can be implemented using a kinematic model where the vehicle body frame velocity is estimated based on actuator commands (e.g., the duty cycle, r/min, current, or voltage of the thrusters) [9]. The velocity is then transformed into the Earth frame based on the orientation estimated from an inertial measurement unit (IMU) and integrated from a known location (e.g., the last GPS fix before being submerged) to estimate the underwater locations. However, due to the noise in the IMU measurements, uncertainty in thruster-velocity mapping, and ocean currents, the error in dead-reckoning will accumulate with a drift up to several kilometer per hour [10]. To help reduce such errors, a Doppler velocity log (DVL) is typically installed on a modern AUV to measure the vehicle’s velocity over the ground. The DVL-aided dead-reckoning algorithm normally uses a filter (e.g., EKF) to merge DVL and IMU measurements, and the drift rate can be reduced to about 5% or lower [11]. Over the years, DVL costs have decreased, but a decent DVL still costs at least several thousand US dollars. Besides the cost, DVL-aided dead-reckoning requires the AUV to maintain consistent DVL bottom locks, meaning it must operate within the DVL’s range off the seabed. This limitation restricts the AUV operation near the seabed, making the AUV less applicable for mid-water surveys to address some important scientific questions [12].

Terrain-aided navigation (TAN) is another method that has gained attention in recent years (see [9], [13], and [14]) because it is self-contained and provides bounded error. Using TAN requires the AUV to stay within the sonar range off the seabed and mandates access to a prior map of the seafloor. For achieving a satisfactory TAN result, variations in seafloor elevation are desired for bounding the uncertainty growth [15]. Perception-aided simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) has recently gained significant traction because it eliminates the requirement for prior environmental knowledge, i.e., the terrain map [16]. At its core, the method leverages features detected by onboard perception sensors (e.g., cameras and sonars) at different moments to constrain the drift in dead reckoning [17]. Underwater SLAM has experienced slower progress compared to land-based SLAM, primarily due to challenges, such as sensor noise and reduced features. Nevertheless, seminal works have been done in underwater SLAM using multibeam sonar point clouds (see [18] and [19]), fusing visual and sonar measurements (see [17],[20], and [21]), with multi-AUVs [22], and imaging sonars (see [23] and [24]). The main disadvantage of SLAM is its computational intensity since nonlinear optimization is needed to estimate the feature locations. As a consequence, the overall vehicle endurance may be reduced due to the need for a powerful computer. Furthermore, the robustness of front-end feature tracking is not universally applicable, as different scenes may require different imaging enhancement, feature detection and tracking algorithms to prevent failures in finding corresponding features observed at different times.

In this article, our research is focused on the self-contained localization methods when there is no DVL measurement available or the AUV is not near the seabed. Under the above conditions, model-aided approaches have been explored where a vehicle dynamics model is built based on prior data to provide velocity estimations for vehicle localization using IMU measurements. Even though the model-aided approach will suffer from drift, it has shown promising improvement (accuracy and consistency) when compared to DVL-aided approaches. For example, the model-aided approach presented in [25] could fuse the estimation from a hydrodynamic model and inertial measurements for localization. The method also accepts additional information about the relative velocity between the vehicle and the water measured by an acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) to further improve the performance. Overall, the drift is about 75 m/h with a relatively expensive IMU (over $10 k). In a recent work [10], a simplified hydrodynamic model was proposed to estimate velocity in the Earth frame. The model coefficients were estimated using the prediction error method from prior field trial data where the vehicle velocities were estimated by differentiating the vehicle position measured by an LBL system. In [10], the model uses the IMU-based forward speed from the front seat computer and angular acceleration by differentiating the gyro. However, this approach is less applicable to other vehicles, as the IMU-based forward speed may vary across different AUVs, and the angular acceleration is rate dependent. When an IMU is operated at a high sampling rate, such as 100 Hz, significant noise and erroneous acceleration and angular velocity measurements can be observed. Nevertheless, promising results were obtained from field tests, showing that the maximum drift is about 100 m/h when predicting the velocity using an affordable IMU (less than $1 k). As discussed in this article, the localization performance is also environment dependent, as the impact of the water current is not included in the model. Due to the fact that the AUV model is highly nonlinear, the multivariable regression used in many model identification studies [10] may not provide a good model approximation and have uncertainties when predicting the vehicle states for localization. To this end, some advanced approaches, such as unsupervised online system identification, were explored (see [26] and [27]).

Recently, machine learning techniques, such as neural networks (NN) and deep learning, have been explored for underwater localization. Zhang et al. [28] introduced NavNet, a deep sequential learning-based navigation framework. It uses a recurrent neural network (RNN) and an attention mechanism to approximate the system model and measurement model for underwater localization. Improvements were shown when compared to conventional EKF and unscented Kalman filter sensor fusion methods. However, the proposed framework still needs DVL measurements as an input during operation. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the research in DVL-free localization strategies using deep learning is still limited. A recent study [29] has investigated five different deep learning methods for predicting AUV’s surge speed based on the navigation data collected with AutoSub500 and AutoSubLR. In [30], an RNN was trained to predict vehicle surge and sway velocity. The paper demonstrated the approach on the Tethys AUV using field trial data and on a simulated underwater glider. A good agreement between the vehicle track estimated from the RNN outputs and DVL outputs was found.

This article takes a similar approach presented in [30] where NN models are trained to predict body-frame velocities. When training the NN models, a DVL is needed to provide reference velocity measurements. Once the models are trained, the NN models will predict the vehicle’s linear velocity components for localization, allowing the AUV to localize itself without the DVL or if it is away from the seabed beyond the DVL range. In the scenario that the DVL has been removed after the training for the purpose of reducing the overall AUV cost, a “dummy” DVL should be placed at the same location as the DVL. The dummy DVL should have a similar in-water weight and shape such that the vehicle’s kinematics and dynamic characteristics remain unchanged. The dummy DVL could be 3-D printed to have the same shape as the actual DVL and have small voids for adding small metal inserts (e.g., washers and nuts) for fine-tuning its in-water weight to match the real DVL used when collecting the training data.

Compared to the existing works (particularly, [30]), the work presented in this article has three major differences. First, we provide a detailed explanation of deriving the approximation function of the vehicle velocity based on the six degree-of-freedom marine vehicle dynamic equation, justifying our NN design (inputs and feasibility). Second, the feedforward neural network (FFN) is used, which is relatively small (less than 1500 parameters for the most complicated model) and fast to train (an hour per training session) compared to the ones used in the existing works. Third, we have added system voltage and current draw as model inputs, which will affect the forces generated from the thrusters that will ultimately impact vehicle velocity components. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, research on the integration of FFN for underwater inertial-based localization is still rare, and this article seeks to advance this topic with the following contributions.

This article has derived the approximation function of the vehicle linear velocities (see Section II) based on the general 6-DOF marine vehicle dynamic equation of motion. We show that the linear velocities in the vehicle body frame are nonlinear functions of measurable vehicle states, including linear acceleration, angular velocity, orientation, thruster commands, system voltage and current, and vehicle depth. Three FFN are trained separately for predicting individual vehicle velocities along three body frame axes. The separation allows us to avoid the influence due to the skewness in the data. For example, for an AUV performing survey missions, its sway and heave motion are relatively small compared to the surge velocities.

An ablation study (see Section IV) is conducted to investigate the effects of hyperparameters (including batch size, neuron numbers, and layer numbers). We found that two layers with eight neurons are effective for these tasks, indicated by the minimum Akaike information criterion (AIC) values. The network is significantly smaller (less than 500 parameters) compared to relevant works (see [29] and [30]) where complicated NNs with a large amount of parameters (over 1000) are used. This finding makes the method presented in this article applicable to computing resource-limited AUVs.

We have validated the performance of localization using the velocity predicted from the trained NN models. We found that the new method has improved performance when compared to DVL-aided methods, especially when there is a relatively strong ocean current. The method also produces a similar performance compared to the model-aided DVL-free approaches (see [10] and [25]) with a less expensive instrument setup.

title: Design and Validation of a Telescopic Chassis-Assisted Stair-Climbing Mechanism for Powered Wheelchairs
authors: Yasuhiro Fukuoka,Haruya Shirado,Yuto Nakamura,Haruto Okabe,Ahmad Najmuddin Ibrahim,Takahiro Fukui
abstract:
We propose a simple stair traversal mechanism that augments a
four-wheel wheelchair with an auxiliary telescopic chassis actuator. The proposed mechanism provides the following key contributions during stair
ascent: (A) enhanced safety by ensuring that either the front or rear
wheels remain stationary at all times; (B) primary reliance of the required force and mechanical work on the telescopic chassis rather than the wheels; (C)
insensitivity of the required force and mechanical work to stair inclination; and
(D) reduced risk of wheel slip on steeper stairs.
In addition, the telescopic chassis is expected to improve level-ground mobility
by enabling tight turning with the shortest wheelbase and enhancing stability
with the longest wheelbase.
introduction:
Although stairs can act as barriers that restrict
wheelchair users’ access to certain destinations, situations in which
stair climbing is unavoidable are relatively infrequent because
elevators and ramps are often available. Therefore, climbing speed is of secondary importance, whereas safety should be prioritized because falls on stairs can result in severe injuries. The ability to traverse stairs safely, even at a slow speed, can substantially expand users’ range of activities.

Many powered wheelchairs capable of ascending stairs without assistance from
caregivers have been developed over the past several decades.
However, no such wheelchair has yet achieved widespread adoption in general use.
One of the contributing factors is believed to be the excessive mechanical complexity of these systems.

Accordingly, our study aims to develop a simple mechanism that enables stair traversal while minimizing any degradation in level-ground mobility performance.
As illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b), we
propose a mobility mechanism for powered wheelchairs that enables safe
stair ascent and descent by assisting a four-wheel configuration with a single additional chassis extension-retraction actuator. The
proposed mechanism is characterized by its simplicity in mechanical structure, control strategy, and user operation.
As in commercially available stair-climbing wheelchairs [1, 2, 3, 4], the proposed system’s stair ascent is performed in a backward-facing direction, whereas descent is carried out facing forward.
Each pair of front and rear wheels is driven by a single motor through self-locking worm gears, while chassis extension and retraction is achieved using a geared-motor via a ball-screw mechanism.
Specifically, stair ascent is performed as follows. In the configuration
shown in Fig. 1(a), the lower (front) wheels are held stationary on the stair tread by the self-locking mechanism. When the chassis is extended, the upper (rear) wheels are rolled upward about the stair edge.
After the upper wheels have landed on the next stair tread, in the
configuration shown in Fig. 1(b), the
upper wheels are held stationary, and when the chassis is retracted, the lower wheels are rolled upward about the stair
edge. By repeatedly performing the motions illustrated in Fig.
1(a) and (b), the wheelchair ascends the stairs
step by step.
The entire motion sequence can be observed in https://youtu.be/2KtJypNziDs.
Stair descent is achieved by performing the same sequence with the roles of the front and rear wheels exchanged.

The main contributions of the proposed mechanism are summarized as follows.

High safety is ensured by maintaining either the front or rear wheels in a stationary state during stair traversal.

Required force and mechanical work for stair ascent rely primarily
on the telescopic chassis rather than the wheels.

Required chassis force and total mechanical work are largely
insensitive to stair inclination.

Increased stair steepness improves traction of the stationary wheels, enhancing stability.

A changeable wheelbase enabled by the telescopic chassis improves level-ground mobility.

Contributions (B)-(D) constitute the novel contributions of this study.
Contribution (B) arises from the fact that the wheels can be rolled
about the stair edge by the chassis extension-retraction force as described above.
Experimental results of climbing stairs with gentle, moderate, and steep inclination angles demonstrate that the wheel motors are
required to output only a very small torque, which is sufficient to roll the
self-locking wheels in coordination with the chassis extension and retraction
motion.
Moreover, experiments conducted on the three stairs demonstrate that,
because the mechanical power required for the telescopic chassis is much
larger than that required for the wheels, the contribution of the
telescopic chassis to the total mechanical work exceeds 94%.

Reducing reliance on wheel-driven actuation for stair ascent offers significant advantages.
As illustrated in Figs. 1(a) and (b), in the proposed wheelchair, the wheel radius is designed to be larger than the
riser height of typical outdoor and public stairs, while remaining smaller than
the tread depth so that the wheels can remain stationary on the treads.
Although wheels larger than the riser height can theoretically climb stairs using wheel torque alone, doing so with a heavy occupant requires excessively high wheel torque.
This approach has several drawbacks. First, the required torque may
exceed the rated torque of motors commonly used in powered wheelchairs,
increasing energy consumption and the risk of motor overload. Second,
steep stairs require a very high coefficient of static friction between the wheels and stair edges to avoid slipping. Third, the large tangential forces applied to the stair edges damage the stairs. Finally, the large wheel torque generates a reaction torque on the wheelchair body, increasing the risk of tip-over, particularly on steeper stairs.
However, the proposed wheelchair effectively avoids the
concerns because of contribution (B).

In many conventional powered wheelchairs that climb stairs by lifting
the wheels using some form of assistive mechanism
[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], the wheel radius is significantly smaller than the stair riser height.
However, the small wheels tend to prevent progress of the vehicle over bumpy terrain.
In addition, small wheels are prone to becoming trapped in recessed gaps in the ground
as well as in the space beneath stair risers, particularly on stairs without a vertical riser or with a
protruding stair nosing.
Thus, when priority is given to usual level-ground mobility, larger wheel radii are desirable.

Regarding the second novel contribution (C), it is generally expected that
steeper stairs require larger actuation forces and mechanical work; however, this is not the case for the proposed mechanism.
During stair ascent, the largest chassis extension-retraction force is required when the rear (upper) and front (lower) wheels lift off the stair tread, as shown in Figs. 1(a) and (b), respectively.
Because the steeper configuration shown in Figs.
1 results in a larger gravitational
component acting along the body axis, a correspondingly larger
extension-retraction force is required to counteract gravity. However, the chassis extension-retraction
force required to rotate the wheels about the stair edge against gravity
is, in fact, smaller than in less steep configurations.
Specifically, for the same rolling force FF in
Fig.1(a) acting on the upper wheels about
the stair edge, the required chassis extension force F1F_{1} is smaller than F2F_{2} required in gentle inclination.
Our experiments demonstrate that the overall maximum chassis actuation force
required does not vary significantly with changes in the inclination of the
three tested stairs. Moreover, the maximum force was only approximately 10 % of
the rated actuation force.
The experimental results further indicate that the total
mechanical work normalized by vertical displacement decreases as the stair
steepness increases.

For the third novel contribution (D), chassis extension and retraction
generate backward forces on the stationary lower and upper wheels,
denoted as fLf_{\rm{L}} and fUf_{\rm{U}}, respectively (Fig.
1(a), (b)). With increasing body
inclination, the actuation force shifts toward the vertical direction,
reducing the horizontal forces fLf_{\rm{L}} and fUf_{\rm{U}} while
increasing the normal forces NLN_{\rm{L}} and NUN_{\rm{U}}. As a result,
analysis and experiments show that wheel slip is less likely on steeper stairs.

Contribution (E) represents an additional benefit for usual level-ground operation.
Although turning is outside the scope of this paper, since chassis retraction
enables a substantially reduced wheelbase,
a smaller minimum turning radius can be achieved than that of conventional powered wheelchairs.
In addition, extending the chassis on bumpy terrain or slopes increases the wheelbase, reducing the probability of forward and backward tipping.
Thus, the telescopic chassis may further enhance the performance of
conventional wheelchairs.

1. High safety is ensured by maintaining either the front or rear wheels in a stationary state during stair traversal.

2. Required force and mechanical work for stair ascent rely primarily
on the telescopic chassis rather than the wheels.

3. Required chassis force and total mechanical work are largely
insensitive to stair inclination.

4. Increased stair steepness improves traction of the stationary wheels, enhancing stability.

5. A changeable wheelbase enabled by the telescopic chassis improves level-ground mobility.

title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
authors: Wai Ka Sun,Waiyiu Pong,Bowen Wang
abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10∘10^{\circ} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
introduction:
Wheeled-legged robots can take over outdoor work that is dangerous for people, such as
shipyard and industrial inspection, mountain patrol, and search and rescue. Their routes chain stairs and ledges with loose ground and slopes, and the robot has to cross the same transitions on every run. We met the difficulty while preparing such a route for a competition. An earlier version of our system simply followed the taught path and treated ledges as ordinary waypoints, and it stalled at the first ledge in both full-speed runs: the robot’s ledge gait mounts a ledge only when the robot arrives within about ten centimetres and ten degrees of a workable entry, and nothing in the path enforced this. Avoiding collisions is not enough either. After a detour, the robot may have too little room to slow down, may need a
gait change before the controller is ready, or may reach the next step at an angle. Every successful crossing, however, shows an entry that works, and this experience is worth keeping.

Keeping it is hard: replaying the taught track cannot handle local changes, and editing its geometry can throw away what made the next passage work. This leads to our question:
how can a robot adapt to local changes and still keep the entry conditions that
a successful passage showed?

Locomotion on legged robots often comes as a fixed library of skills: gaits that ship with the robot, as on our platform, or learned policies that a higher-level module chooses among (Hoeller et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Each skill succeeds only from a limited set of entry states, its initiation set in
the language of options (Sutton et al., 1999), and a detour can leave the robot outside
that set where skills switch at a stair or ledge. Existing methods obtain this set in one of two ways: planners derive entry constraints from a robot model, and skill-chaining methods learn initiation sets from many further trials (Section 2). For a frozen library on a new site, neither way is available: the skills are black boxes, and controllers that come with the platform or were trained once cannot be retrained for each site. We find that one teaching session already supplies what these methods derive or learn: for every transition, one crossing that the skill has completed. We therefore treat the library as a black box and retrain nothing. On the robot the skills are the factory gaits; in simulation they are policies that we trained with PPO and then froze. One teaching session in the
real environment (three passes of about six minutes and five short re-drives, 27 minutes of
driving in all) crosses every transition. Building the stored route needs no training, and
autonomous runs began the same day.

We store each terrain transition on the route as an event, placed by its distance along
the route, so that it persists across runs and still applies after a local replan. Each stairs
or ledge event carries a gait interval and a speed cap. A ledge event also carries the
position and direction of the taught crossing (its crossing frame) and an
approach window, inside which the robot slows down and steers toward a point close
ahead. At a fixed distance before the ledge, an entry gate checks the robot’s sideways
offset and heading in the crossing frame; if the check fails, the robot turns in place or
backs up and approaches again (Figure 3). Teaching supplies each event’s
position, direction, and gait interval; the limits of the check (0.10 m, 10∘10^{\circ}) and the
other settings are shared by the whole environment. In the language of options, the gate
tests at run time whether the robot is inside a conservative part of the next skill’s
initiation set, centred on the taught crossing. The method is simple and cheap, and it adapts
during the run: the robot detours around obstacles that are not on the map, corrects its
pose before each ledge, and returns to the route within 2 s of a stall.

(i) A route representation that keeps what teaching
showed (position, direction, gait interval) apart from the rules we configure, and ties each
stored item to the run-time decision it changes (Table 1).
(ii) A controlled test of what the stored events add, with path, gait schedule, and sensing
fixed. Conventional tracking brings 22.4% of disturbed ledge crossings within the entry
limits, the approach window raises this to 47.6%, and the entry gate to 100% (24.1%,
46.0%, and 88.6% under localization noise). Of 1,470 approaches made with the window but without the gate, all
350 that pass the gate’s check end within the limits. With our learned policies in contact
simulation, a robot pushed off course before stairs does not fall once in 180 climbs, against
9 falls when the stored direction is ignored, and ledge entries outside the gate’s limits fall more than twice as often as entries
inside (Section 5.2).
(iii) Because the stored route persists, a robot pushed 1.2 m off it returns and completes
75.7% of segments, the level of runs without a push (77.4%), in contact simulation over 23
seeds (Section 5.3). On the robot, with factory gaits, the system completed all
six competition-day runs in a complete multi-obstacle environment and won third place (Section 5.5).

title: ECHO: In-Context Behavior foundation model for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
authors: Xingyi Wang,Bin Li,Jiyuan Shi,Chenyun Zhang,Weiji Xie,Xiangyu Miao,Junsong Wu,Wei Song,Shiqiang Zhu,Chenjia Bai
abstract:
Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) acquire diverse skills
through large-scale motion imitation and massively parallel
reinforcement learning, yet broad behavioral capability does not
ensure precise execution across physical conditions.
Without distinguishing the underlying dynamics, policies may
favor conservative compromises over environment-specific precision.
We introduce ECHO, an in-context BFM that turns interaction
experience into environment-specific control, separating general
behavioral capability from dynamics-specific execution.
Mixed and Annealed Sampling first establishes a behavior
prior in a single pretraining stage by balancing targeted practice
with broad motion coverage.
Building on this prior, Context Representation and Residual
Adaptation learns structured dynamics representations from
interaction histories to guide residual corrections to the frozen
prior, enabling adaptation without test-time parameter updates.
Extensive experiments show that ECHO outperforms all
baseline methods across diverse motions and physical conditions.
Moreover, deployment on the Unitree G1 demonstrates whole-body teleoperation
spanning extreme acrobatics and terrain interaction, alongside
payload adaptation in manipulation and whole-body control. Page is
available at https://mwondering.github.io/echo-bfm/.
introduction:
For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them.

Humanoid robots are expected to execute diverse whole-body behaviors accurately, responsively, and robustly in human-centric environments. Large-scale motion imitation and massively parallel reinforcement
learning (RL) have advanced this goal through behavior foundation
models (BFMs) (Luo et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; RoboParty Lab Team, 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Cheng et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026b).
Yet a broad behavior repertoire alone does not ensure precise
execution across physical conditions: the same reference motion
may require different control responses as payload, friction,
or actuator dynamics vary. Without adequately distinguishing these dynamics, a policy trained
across environments may learn conservative compromises that favor
broad reliability over environment-specific tracking
precision (Mehta et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2026b).
The key challenge is therefore to enable a BFM to understand the underlying dynamics across environments
and adapt to different physical conditions.

Recent work in robotic manipulation has demonstrated in-context
adaptation through human demonstrations (Shah et al., 2025)
or retrieved interaction experience (Chen et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025a),
without updating the model weights at test time.
These advances motivate equipping humanoid BFMs with the ability
to learn environmental dynamics from interaction context and
tailor whole-body actions accordingly.
As a BFM executes diverse behaviors, its actions and the resulting
state transitions provide evidence about how the underlying dynamics
shape its response.
By encoding this evidence into structured dynamics representations,
the model can learn control-relevant properties of the current
environment and use them to guide subsequent actions.
Interaction histories thus serve not merely as records of past
execution, but as context for environment-specific action corrections.
This allows a shared behavior prior to pursue the same
objective with control responses tailored to different physical
conditions, adapting its execution without test-time parameter updates.

To this end, we introduce ECHO, an in-context behavior
foundation model for humanoid whole-body control that separates
general behavioral capability from dynamics-specific execution. Specifically,
we first train a motion-tracking prior, ECHO-PRE, using
Mixed and Annealed Sampling (MIAS).
By balancing targeted practice with broad motion coverage,
MIAS enables a single policy to jointly learn everyday motions,
highly dynamic skills (Wang et al., 2026c), contact-rich floor behaviors, and terrain
motions within one pretraining stage

A context-conditioned residual policy then uses these representations

title: Hindsight Self-Distillation: Teaching Robots to Act from the Present
authors: Haisen He,Yechi Liu,Tianle Shi,Haoyun Liu,Chuanzhang Meng,Tiancai Jiao,Yifan Bai,Xinyuan Chang,SongLin Dong,Zhiheng Ma
abstract: A robot must choose an action before it can see the outcome. In a recorded demonstration, later camera frames show what happened after the robot moved. Hindsight Self-Distillation (HSD) uses these later frames to teach a policy what to extract from current images. During training, a teacher sees both the current and later frames, while a student sees the current frames. They share a visual encoder and an action predictor. Each branch summarizes its images with a small set of feature vectors. These visual summaries supply all visual input to the action predictor. The teacher learns from demonstrated actions. For each noisy action sequence, the student learns from either the demonstration or the teacher’s denoising prediction. It also learns to match the teacher’s visual summaries. We analyze which aspects of the teacher’s predictions the student can recover from its inputs. At deployment, the student encodes the current images once and reuses its summaries at every denoising step. HSD achieves average success rates of 98.50% on LIBERO and 92.31% on RoboTwin 2.0.
introduction:
A robot must choose an action before seeing its consequences. A demonstration, by contrast, records both the action and what followed. Subsequent observations reveal how an interaction unfolded, providing hindsight that is unavailable at the moment of action selection. This asymmetry creates a learning opportunity: future outcomes can teach a policy what to extract from the present. Figure 1 shows how a teacher uses these later frames to guide a student that acts from the current observation.

Generalist policies draw on vision-language and robot pretraining [49, 16, 10]. Video-based policies use video for planning, for learning predictive features, or for modeling video and actions jointly [7, 12, 48]. Fast-WAM trains on video and actions and encodes the current observation once at deployment [44]. FLARE trains tokens inside the action denoiser to predict future visual features [47]. Being-H0.7 aligns a branch that sees the current context with one that also sees later frames [27]. We ask how later frames can supervise both the features a policy extracts from current images and the actions it predicts from those features.

In Hindsight Self-Distillation (HSD), the teacher and student share a video encoder and an action predictor but use separate sets of learned queries. The teacher’s queries attend to current and future frames from the demonstration, while the student’s queries attend only to current frames. In each branch, the resulting visual summaries supply all visual input to the action predictor, which also receives the robot state and task instruction.

The teacher learns from demonstrated actions and provides two targets for the student within the same policy. For each noisy action sequence, the student learns either from the demonstration or from the teacher’s prediction at the same noise level. It also learns to match the teacher’s final visual summaries. When a teacher output serves as a target, gradients from that comparison flow through the student branch. When the robot acts, only the student runs. It encodes the current images once per action chunk and reuses the resulting features as it denoises the actions.

With the model weights held fixed, we compare the action distributions of the teacher and student. Their difference has three components: information available only in later frames, information lost when the student summarizes the current observation, and error in the student’s approximation. A separate analysis of squared error identifies the part of a teacher target that the student can predict from its inputs.

Our contributions are threefold. (i) We train two sets of visual summaries on demonstrated actions. Each set supplies all visual input for action prediction in its branch. (ii) Within this shared policy, the teacher supervises both the student’s denoising predictions and its final visual summaries. (iii) We characterize how later frames, compression of the current images, and student approximation each contribute to the difference between the two action distributions. We evaluate HSD on LIBERO, on task variants in LIBERO-Plus, on RoboTwin 2.0, and on six manipulation tasks with a physical robot. We also vary the two transfer losses and the number of summary tokens, and measure inference latency.

title: On the Hamel Coefficients and the Boltzmann-Hamel Equations for the Rigid Body
authors: Andreas Müller
abstract:
The Boltzmann-Hamel (BH) equations are central in the dynamics and control
of nonholonomic systems described in terms of quasi-velocities. The rigid
body is a classical example of such systems, and it is well-known that the
BH-equations are the Newton-Euler (NE) equations when described in terms of
rigid body twists as quasi-velocities. It is further known that the
NE-equations are the Euler-Poincaré respectively the reduced
Euler-Lagrange equations on S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right) when using body-fixed or
spatial representation of rigid body twists. The connection between these
equations are the Hamel coefficients, which are immediately identified as
the structure constants of S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right). However, an explicit
coordinate-free derivation has not been presented in the literature. In this
paper the Hamel coefficients for the rigid body are derived in a
coordinate-free way without resorting to local coordinates describing the
rigid body motion. The three most relevant choices of quasi-velocities
(body-fixed, spatial, and hybrid representation of rigid body twists) are
considered. The corresponding BH-equations are derived explicitly for the
rotating and free floating body. Further, the Hamel equations for
nonholonomically constrained rigid bodies are discussed, and demonstrated
for the inhomogenous ball rolling on a plane.
introduction:
The Boltzmann-Hamel (BH) equations are a milestone result of the research on
the dynamics of nonholonomic systems, which was initiated by Hertz [22]. Hamel continued previous works of Volterra [48]
(who continued the work of Beltrami), Tzénoff [46, 47] (who built upon the work of Chaplygin [11, 13, 12]), Poincaré [39], Voronets [49, 51], and Boltzmann
[4] in particular, into a general concept. Key elements in
these equations are the three-index symbols that are referred to as ’Hamel
coefficients’, which reveal the nonholonomic nature of the quasi-coordinates
respectively of the constraints a system is subjected to.

If the Lagrangian is invariant under the action of a Lie group, then the
Hamel coefficients are identical to the structure constants of this group.
The BH-equations are then the Euler-Lagrange equations corresponding to a
reduced variational principle on this symmetry group, respectively the
Euler-Poincaré equations [3, 31, 30]. For this reason
the BH-equations are often used as synonym for the reduced Euler-Lagrange
equations [1, 3]. The configuration
space of a rigid body is the Lie group S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right) (the special
Euclidean group [30, 31, 35, 40]), and
the BH-equations are the Euler-Poincaré equations (when formulated in
terms of body-fixed twists), or the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations (when
using spatial twists). The rigid body is often used as the typical example
to study fundamental aspects of nonholonomic systems in a coordinate-free
geometric setting. However, a systematic treatment of the original
BH-equations [18, 19, 21] in local
coordinates along with the original derivation of the Hamel coefficients for
the rigid body, in a way that links them to the Euler-Lagrange equations on S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right), has not yet been reported in the literature. Key to
this is evaluating the Hamel coefficients taking into account the geometry
of rigid body motions (possibly without resorting to local coordinates),
which not only demonstrates technicalities of the actual determination of
these coefficients, but also offers insight into the geometric nature of the
problem. Moreover, the Hamel coefficients are specific to the particular
representation of rigid body velocities (i.e. the definition of
quasi-velocities) and the corresponding invariance of the rigid body
Lagrangian under action of the symmetry group. The three most relevant
representations of rigid body velocities, are the body-fixed, spatial, and
hybrid representation [33, 35]. The first two correspond to
a left-invariant and right-invariant Lagrangian on S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right),
respectively. The hybrid representation assumes the direct product group S​O​(3)×ℝ3SO\left(3\right)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{3} as symmetry group and
corresponding right-invariant Lagrangian, which clearly implies a different
geometric model of rigid body motions [34, 45]. The
derivations of the Hamel coefficients for the rigid body reported in the
literature almost exclusively use particular local coordinates to describe
rigid body motions (see e.g. [18, pp. 18-20] or [37, p. 369] for the rotating body, and [50, pp. 43 & 217] or [26, p. 76] for the free body), which
leads to rather involved expressions. Some of the few exception are Hamel’s
derivation for the rotating body described in terms of the body-fixed
angular velocity (see [21, p. 489]), and the derivation for the
rotating nn-dimensional body by Hurtado & Sinclair [25].

In this paper, a systematic derivation of the Hamel coefficients for the
rigid body and the corresponding BH-equations are presented for the three
representations of rigid body velocities mentioned above. The Hamel
coefficients are derived without resorting to local coordinates (no
parameterization of rigid body motions). Hamel’s Euler-Lagrange equations
equally apply to systems subjected to Pfaffian constraints, where the
nonholonomic geometry is encoded in the Hamel coefficients. This is recalled
and several formulations of the Hamel equations are presented. The Hamel
equations for the rolling ball with inhomogenous mass density are presented,
which is a typical example for a nonholonomically constrained rigid body
[24].

Despite the long history of analytical rigid body dynamics, this paper seems
to be the first publication reporting an explicit geometric construction of
the Hamel coefficients, which are indeed determined by the structure
constant of the Lie group underlying the respective definition of rigid body
twist. The paper summarizes material that is scattered in the literature
along with references to the original sources, and presents novel
derivations of Hamel coefficients. The paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 briefly summarizes the BH-equations in their original
form and the definition of the Hamel coefficients. First the BH-equations
for general unconstrained systems described in quasi-coordinates are
reviewed. Then the Hamel equations for constrained systems described in
quasi-coordinates as well as in ’holonomic’ coordinates are recalled. In
order to make a connection to the modern approach in geometric mechanics,
the BH-equations for the rigid body are finally identified as the
Euler-Poincaré respectively the reduced Euler-Lagrange equations when
using S​E​(3)SE\left(3\right) as rigid body configuration space. The Hamel
coefficients are derived in section 3 for the rotating
rigid body when the angular velocity in body-fixed and spatial
representation is used as quasi-velocity. The corresponding BH-equations are
derived in section 4. The Hamel coefficients for the free
rigid body are derived in section 5 where the
body-fixed, spatial, and hybrid representations of twists are used as
quasi-velocities. The corresponding BH-equations are derived explicitly in
section 6. In addition, the Hamel equations for an
inhomogenous ball rolling on a horizontal plane are derived as an example
for a nonholonomically constrained rigid body. A list of symbols and
abbreviations is given in appendix B and C,
respectively. Throughout the paper, the Lagrangian will be the kinetic
energy.

Notation: With reference to the original development by Hamel and Boltzmann,
the classical notation in terms of local coordinates is used. Tensor
notation and the Ricci summation convention is applied throughout the paper.
Cartesian vectors are resolved in orthogonal frames, and their covariant
coordinates (lower indices) are used. εi​j​k\varepsilon_{ijk} denotes the
Levi-Civita symbol, and δi​j\delta_{ij} the Kronecker symbol.

title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning When to Refine Actions with Touch for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Xudi Ge,Yepeng Liu,Haifeng Liu,Enze Shi,Liangqi Zhang,Yongchao Xu
abstract:
Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision–tactile–language–action (VTLA)
policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and
how touch refines actions under changing visual
conditions remains challenging.
We introduce TipDex-VTLA, a VTLA policy that combines estimated
visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification
to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically,
Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual
reliability from a frozen reference policy’s action sensitivity
to illumination perturbations.
Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE)
compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and
combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability
to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average
full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.
introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies generate manipulation actions
from visual observations and language instructions [17, 9, 2, 1].
In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, however, the hand often
occludes the interaction region, making the onset and evolution
of local contact difficult to observe. Besides,
visual guidance is also sensitive to illumination: lighting changes
can alter policy predictions even when the physical scene remains
unchanged [5, 10, 7, 36].
Their impact depends on action-relevant cues: a dim image may
preserve grasp geometry, whereas a localized reflection may
obscure the intended contact region.

Vision–Tactile–Language–Action (VTLA) policies complement visual
observations with tactile feedback during action generation and
execution [19, 28, 45].
For example, fingertip pressure is expected to increase when
grasping an egg. An increase beyond the expected level
may indicate excessive compression.
Interpreting such changes requires a reference for how contact
is expected to evolve under the planned actions.
Tactile forecasting provides this reference, allowing incoming
measurements to be compared with earlier predictions during
execution [26].
Such verification assesses whether contact follows the current
plan, but leaves open whether that plan remains reliable under
the current visual conditions.

This motivates jointly considering visual reliability
and tactile forecast agreement (Fig. ).
A plan perturbed by illumination may still produce the tactile
responses predicted for it, while unexpected contact can arise
even under reliable vision.
These complementary signals define four refinement
regimes.
When touch agrees with the forecast, low visual reliability
motivates visual compensation, whereas high reliability
favors nominal preservation.
When touch deviates from the forecast, low visual reliability
motivates stronger joint correction, while high reliability
can still favor contact correction.
Together, these regimes motivate us using visual reliability for refinement, with tactile forecast
discrepancies further increasing correction strength as contact
deviates from expectation. The question is how to learn visual reliability and jointly refine actions.

In this paper, we present TipDex-VTLA, a predictive and reactive
VTLA framework that uses estimated visual reliability and tactile forecast
verification to gate tactile feature corrections.
Specifically, we introduce
Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE),
which learns a proxy for visual reliability from the action
discrepancies of a frozen VTLA policy across paired real normal and synthesized perturbed observations
that differ only in illumination.
For tactile-guided refinement, we develop
Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE),
which compares incoming tactile measurements with temporally
aligned forecasts consistent with the intervening executed actions.
The estimated visual reliability and verified tactile discrepancies jointly control
the strength of bounded feature corrections computed from current
tactile feedback and execution context.
By reusing cached flow states, the fast branch refines
replaceable, unexecuted actions while preserving their original
execution times.

We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation
tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark [4].
Across the four real-world tasks, our TipDex-VTLA achieves average
full-task success rates of 87.5% under standard lighting and
73.8% under challenging unseen lighting.
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of reliability-aware
tactile refinement under illumination changes. The main contributions are as follows:

We develop TipDex-VTLA, a predictive
and reactive VTLA framework that effectively refines actions under practical yet challenging unseen illumination variations.

We introduce the concept of action-grounded
visual reliability via VASE and jointly regulate tactile refinement using verified tactile forecast discrepancies via TACE.

Experiments on UniVTAC benchmark [4] and four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks demonstrate TipDex-VTLA’s effectiveness and significantly improved performance
under unseen illumination.

1. We develop TipDex-VTLA, a predictive
and reactive VTLA framework that effectively refines actions under practical yet challenging unseen illumination variations.

2. We introduce the concept of action-grounded
visual reliability via VASE and jointly regulate tactile refinement using verified tactile forecast discrepancies via TACE.

3. Experiments on UniVTAC benchmark [4] and four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks demonstrate TipDex-VTLA’s effectiveness and significantly improved performance
under unseen illumination.

title: LeCompass: Task-Level Execution through State-Indexed Interfaces
authors: Kai Shi,Shiqi Zhao,Zimo Li,Hairong Qu,Hongyu Ma,Yongsong Yang,Jiahao Ai,Ziran Yin,Peng Yin
abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context–goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
introduction:
A central promise of world models is to support deliberation: an agent can predict the consequences of candidate actions and choose among them, rather than relying solely on a direct mapping from observations to actions (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019). Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn predictive latent spaces without reconstructing pixels (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). LeWorldModel (LeWM) uses an action-conditioned JEPA to rank CEM-sampled action sequences by the distance between their predicted outcome latents and the target latent (Maes et al., 2026b), enabling local planning over roughly 25 frames.

Local reachability alone does not provide task-level execution. A short-horizon predictor can evaluate whether candidate actions approach a specified latent target, but it does not determine how to select intermediate targets without oracle waypoints, generate useful action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets, or verify that predicted progress has been realized during execution. In multi-stage manipulation, execution must also account for contact-dependent transitions and recovery from deviations. We study how explicit predictive planning with a frozen short-horizon world model can be organized into task-level closed-loop execution.

We introduce LeCompass, a task-level execution framework that pairs state-indexed outer execution with time-indexed local imagination. The outer loop re-indexes task progress from observations, while the frozen LeWM predicts over a short temporal horizon. This separates task progress from prediction time, trajectory generation from predictive evaluation, and predicted reachability from realized execution state.

A proposer amortizes demonstration transitions into latent references conditioned on observed history and the final goal, recomputed after each executed segment. CompassFlow pairs a target-independent trajectory prior with frozen-LeWM scoring, so the reference guides candidate selection through predictive evaluation rather than directly conditioning the prior. Patch-token readouts and observation-based memory supply execution geometry, phase transitions, and bounded recovery.

State-indexed proposal raises cross-episode composition success from 2.9% to 63.7% on PushT and from 39.1% to 60.5% on TwoRoom. At 192 predictive evaluations per plan (approximately 47× fewer than the original action-space CEM budget of 9,000), CompassFlow Source-CEM reaches 52.5±2.552.5\pm 2.5% on PushT, compared with 16.2% for action-space CEM at the same budget and 44.9±1.144.9\pm 1.1% for ranked IID sampling from the same trajectory prior. On TwoRoom, Source-CEM achieves 77.3±1.077.3\pm 1.0%, compared with 37.2% for action-space CEM. On the 1,000-episode official Cube panel, the complete system achieves 86.9% native reach; bounded recovery raises semantic completion under induced contact loss from 5.8% to 80.4%.

We contribute:

state-indexed latent references for cross-episode goal composition and reorientation from observed progress;

CompassFlow, a target-independent trajectory prior for low-budget predictive search, with frozen-LeWM scoring and source-coordinate refinement; and

an observation-grounded Cube execution interface with patch-token readouts, temporal state, and bounded recovery.

1. state-indexed latent references for cross-episode goal composition and reorientation from observed progress;

2. CompassFlow, a target-independent trajectory prior for low-budget predictive search, with frozen-LeWM scoring and source-coordinate refinement; and

3. an observation-grounded Cube execution interface with patch-token readouts, temporal state, and bounded recovery.

title: CauSyncVLA: Causal Latent World Modeling for Asynchronous Robot Control
authors: Xu Pan,Chubin Zhang,Xingrui Yu,Runmin Lan,Zihao Wang,Wenkai Guo,Bofang Jia,Bo An,Ziwei Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies transfer pretrained multimodal knowledge to robotic manipulation [44, 17, 9].
They pair foundation backbones with generative action heads to synthesize continuous motion [6, 3, 2].
During physical deployment, however, the environment does not pause for model inference.
Approaching, grasping, and placing continuously alter the robot–scene configuration and demand timely closed-loop decisions grounded in the evolving physical state.

Meeting this requirement is difficult because heavy visual encoding cannot match the rate of fast physical execution, stalling synchronous closed-loop feedback.
Action chunking [42, 6] and asynchronous execution [4, 33] amortize this latency by overlapping inference with ongoing motion, yet leave perception and action temporally misaligned because replaying open-loop tails or stitching boundaries keeps intermediate queries conditioned on delayed perceptual memory when contacts shift mid-chunk.
Existing methods address stitching or latent extrapolation [4, 25, 40], motivating a common execution reference for perceptual conditioning and action refinement.
As illustrated in Figure 1, asynchronous control must reconcile reactivity, perceptual freshness, and trajectory continuity across mismatched sensing and control timescales.

To resolve this misalignment, we observe that actual robot execution supplies a shared temporal reference to align perception and action.
Observed state transitions and applied commands record physical evolution since the latest visual frame, while the unexecuted tail of the preceding plan provides a structured motion prior.
Rather than predicting pixels or physical states independently of control, we formulate asynchronous control as coupled perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction under one physical clock, updating prefix key–value (KV) memory from execution history before refining remaining actions.

We instantiate this principle in CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller [15].
A slow visual stream periodically publishes KV memory anchors from observed images, while a fast control stream predicts current perceptual memory and refines subsequent actions.
Specifically, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current KV memory from the latest delayed anchor and executed state–action history under action-sensitive distillation.
Conditioned on this predicted memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon to the current step and refines it in one flow step.
Training only the lightweight predictor keeps the backbone and action expert frozen, retaining pretrained competence while supporting rapid closed-loop replanning between visual updates.

On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA raises task success from 91.2% to 93.8% over the ten-step synchronous policy while delivering 5.04×\times higher model replanning capacity on a shared GPU.
Ablations, perturbation tests, and physical trials isolate the complementary roles of causal perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction.
Our principal technical contributions are organized around three axes.

Execution-grounded asynchronous control. We formulate asynchronous control as coupled perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction, evaluating execution-aligned replanning across simulation and physical trials, reducing feedback latency with frozen VLAs.

Execution-grounded asynchronous control. We formulate asynchronous control as coupled perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction, evaluating execution-aligned replanning across simulation and physical trials, reducing feedback latency with frozen VLAs.

Causal, action-relevant latent world modeling. We propagate delayed KV anchors along realized state–action history in latent prefix space, supervising residual updates via action-sensitive distillation, which recovers control-relevant perceptual conditioning.

Training-free predictive trajectory correction. We propose PFWS to reuse unexecuted action horizons as intermediate flow priors, refining trajectories in one frozen-expert Euler step, which suppresses boundary mode switching across perturbed trials.

1. Execution-grounded asynchronous control. We formulate asynchronous control as coupled perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction, evaluating execution-aligned replanning across simulation and physical trials, reducing feedback latency with frozen VLAs.

2. Causal, action-relevant latent world modeling. We propagate delayed KV anchors along realized state–action history in latent prefix space, supervising residual updates via action-sensitive distillation, which recovers control-relevant perceptual conditioning.

3. Training-free predictive trajectory correction. We propose PFWS to reuse unexecuted action horizons as intermediate flow priors, refining trajectories in one frozen-expert Euler step, which suppresses boundary mode switching across perturbed trials.
