title: GNetSS: Towards Learning GNSS Corrections without Ground Truth
authors: JiaXu Chee,Simon Denman,Fahira Afzal Maken,Qingqing Cheng,Amir Khodabandeh,Milad Ramezani
comment: Submitted to NAVIGATION, Journal of the Institute of Navigation. Seethis http URL
abstract:
We present GNetSS, a self-supervised GNSS position correction framework that improves the robustness of single point positioning (SPP) without requiring ground-truth locations for training. GNetSS combines a transformer-based network with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver. The network predicts satellite-wise pseudorange corrections by modelling inter-satellite geometry and temporal context, while the solver converts these corrected measurements into receiver position corrections under GNSS geometry and optional motion constraints. Unlike supervised GNSS correction methods that rely on ground-truth, GNetSS derives its training signal directly from GNSS measurement consistency.
Experimental results show that GNetSS improves robustness across open-sky, urban, and forested environments. The method is particularly effective at suppressing large-error outliers, reducing the maximum 3D positioning error by over 50%\% compared with SPP. These results demonstrate the potential of self-supervised pseudorange correction for scalable and robust GNSS positioning in real-world autonomy applications. Code and the in-house dataset will be released upon acceptance.
introduction:
Accurate global positioning is a fundamental requirement for autonomous robotic systems, particularly in applications such as autonomous driving (Bresson et al., 2017), field robotics (Aguiar et al., 2020), and large-scale navigation (Yin et al., 2024). Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) provide a widely available solution for global localisation. However, their accuracy is often degraded in real-world environments due to factors such as multipath interference, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) reception, atmospheric disturbances, receiver noise, and poor satellite geometry. These challenges are especially pronounced in urban canyons, forested areas, and other cluttered environments, where reflected or blocked signals introduce biased pseudorange measurements that cannot be fully compensated for by conventional stand-alone GNSS positioning solutions (Kaplan and Hegarty, 2017).

Classical GNSS positioning methods (e.g., SPP (Odijk, 2017)) rely on
physics-based correction models to account for satellite clock bias, atmospheric delays, the Earth’s rotation, and other systematic effects (Kaplan and Hegarty, 2017). While such model-based approaches are interpretable and effective under favourable assumptions, they remain vulnerable to environment-dependent errors such as multipath and NLOS reception.

Learning-based GNSS correction methods have recently shown promise in modelling complex pseudorange errors that are difficult to describe analytically. Existing approaches have been used to classify line-of-sight (LOS)/NLOS signals, estimate pseudorange errors, predict measurement weights, or directly regress position corrections. However, most of these methods are supervised and require ground-truth labels obtained from real-time kinematic (RTK), simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) or 3D city models. This dependency limits scalability, since collecting accurate reference trajectories across diverse environments, receivers, and satellite conditions is expensive and often impractical.

In this article, we propose GNetSS, a GNSS Network for Self-Supervised position correction. GNetSS learns satellite-wise pseudorange corrections directly from GNSS-derived measurements without requiring ground-truth receiver positions. The proposed framework combines a transformer-based correction network with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver. The network models inter-satellite relationships at each epoch and temporal context across sequential observations, while the solver enforces the geometric structure of GNSS positioning by converting learned measurement corrections into receiver position corrections. Training is performed using a self-supervised objective, allowing the model to learn from GNSS measurement geometry and temporal consistency rather than external position labels.

The design of GNetSS follows a hybrid learning-and-model-based formulation that retains the strengths of GNSS geometric positioning while improving adaptability to environment-dependent errors. Rather than replacing the positioning solver with a direct position regressor, GNetSS learns corrections at the measurement level and passes them through the solver. This keeps the correction process tied to the underlying GNSS measurement geometry and makes the learned outputs physically interpretable. In addition, the self-supervised formulation allows the model to exploit raw GNSS sequences collected across diverse environments, while the dynamic solver encourages temporally consistent trajectory estimates.

Experimental results show that the proposed method is particularly effective at suppressing large-error outliers, as illustrated in Figure 1, achieving the lowest or near-lowest maximum 2D and 3D positioning errors in most cases.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We introduce GNetSS, a self-supervised GNSS position correction framework that learns pseudorange corrections without ground-truth receiver positions.

We propose a transformer-based correction network coupled with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver, preserving GNSS measurement geometry while enabling end-to-end learning.

We formulate a self-supervised training objective that enables learning from raw GNSS sequences using measurement and trajectory consistency.

We validate the proposed method on public and in-house datasets, and demonstrate improved robustness to large positioning outliers in challenging environments.

1. We introduce GNetSS, a self-supervised GNSS position correction framework that learns pseudorange corrections without ground-truth receiver positions.

2. We propose a transformer-based correction network coupled with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver, preserving GNSS measurement geometry while enabling end-to-end learning.

3. We formulate a self-supervised training objective that enables learning from raw GNSS sequences using measurement and trajectory consistency.

4. We validate the proposed method on public and in-house datasets, and demonstrate improved robustness to large positioning outliers in challenging environments.

title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
authors: Chenyuan Zhou,Chaoyi Huang,Zibo Wang,Zhiyuan Li,Yong-Lu Li
abstract:
Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills
across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting
the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances
that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new
tools in performing similar work. We present A2-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines
an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct,
test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent
reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance
features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops
affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous
experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable
skill library for unseen tools. Finally,
A2-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone during
training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and
real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success
in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances.
On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A2-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage
points over π0.5\pi_{0.5}.
introduction:
People can often reuse a familiar manipulation skill with an unfamiliar tool after inspecting it
and attempting to interact with the environment using it. A differently shaped implement may still provide
functional regions similar to those of a familiar tool, such as an edge for cutting or a tip for
hooking, even though its appearance and required wrist motion differ substantially from those of
the original tool. What transfers is therefore neither the tool’s identity nor a fixed
end-effector trajectory, but an understanding of the properties that make the intended interaction
possible. Enabling robots to acquire and reuse this understanding from limited tool experience
would reduce the need to collect demonstrations for every new tool–grasp combination.

Toward this goal, we study how to enable a robot system to adapt to new tools that can perform
the same task, starting from teleoperated demonstrations using a small set of source tools.
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies already possess some tool-manipulation
capabilities [6, 3, 14], but adapting them to entirely new tools still requires
repeated rollout collection and fine-tuning to maintain performance. Predefined functional
representations of tools have shown useful structure for transfer: MimicFunc establishes
functional correspondences through keypoints and
function frames [18], and FuncBridge learns functional trajectories separately from
their grounding into actions [23]. Meanwhile, improvements in the embodied
manipulation capabilities of general-purpose large vision-language models (VLMs) make autonomous
analysis of tool function possible. Our focus is how an agent system can autonomously identify
task-relevant functional regions and determine their key geometric features, capturing functional
commonality across tools to guide a VLA policy in adapting to new tools.

We treat task-relevant affordance features as experimentally testable hypotheses. Although
hierarchical robot systems already connect reasoning by general-purpose VLMs to low-level policy
execution through language or spatial guidance [16, 7, 4], language or
keypoints alone cannot fully represent the geometric details of tools. Cross-tool adaptation
additionally requires deciding which tool properties should be represented for a specific task
and testing whether these properties can guide the policy to complete it correctly. We introduce
A2-VLA, in which the agent starts from a few real-robot teleoperated demonstrations, reconstructs
the demonstrated scenes and tools in simulation, and conducts experiments within them.
The agent analyzes how different source tools accomplish the task, determines task-relevant
affordance features, develops affordance-extraction skills, and applies them to other tools to
attempt task execution. Based on experimental feedback, it analyzes unsuccessful interactions
and refines the selected functional regions, geometric features, or extraction skills.
Successful skills and their applicability conditions accumulate during this process in a
reusable skill library. When faced with an unseen tool, the agent can therefore reuse previously
validated skills to identify corresponding functional regions and extract the same features.

We condition the low-level VLA execution policy on agent-encoded functional-region
features through a low-dimensional affordance interface. While analyzing the source
tools, the agent determines task-relevant affordance features, which are encoded under a
unified protocol as conditioning inputs for VLA training. Unseen tools’
affordances are described through the same protocol: their specific affordance parameters are
extracted while the coordinate representation and feature semantics remain unchanged. This gives
the agent freedom to select functional regions and geometric features while maintaining
a consistent policy input format. Encoded features serve as conditioning inputs
when training a π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy with an auxiliary affordance prediction head. During
deployment, the agent reconstructs the unseen tool in simulation, extracts and tests candidate
affordances, and refines their parameters from simulation feedback before encoding them
under the same protocol for the VLA policy.
At execution time, the VLA conditions each action chunk on the updated
affordance features and current observations.

Our evaluation examines the reliability and reusability of autonomously discovered
affordances and their effectiveness in cross-tool transfer.
Simulation tests compare our affordance discovery and validation process with
other tool-adaptation methods, including task success when using affordances to retarget
trajectories in reconstructed scenes. Three
real-robot tool-use tasks test the robustness of cross-tool transfer. Human Oracle uses human-provided
affordances for both VLA policy training and inference to distinguish failures caused by poor
affordance features from those caused by the VLA’s execution capability.

Our main contributions are:

An agentic tool-adaptation framework that starts from teleoperated demonstrations using
a small set of source tools and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features.
The agent reconstructs the demonstrated scenes in simulation, tests and refines these features
through autonomous experiments, and retains refined affordance-extraction
procedures as reusable skills across tools.

An affordance-guided VLA model that integrates the resulting low-dimensional
feature vectors into action generation. Affordance conditioning and auxiliary
affordance-trajectory supervision train the policy to faithfully follow the supplied affordance
information while using current observations
and robot state to complete tool-use tasks.

1. An agentic tool-adaptation framework that starts from teleoperated demonstrations using
a small set of source tools and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features.
The agent reconstructs the demonstrated scenes in simulation, tests and refines these features
through autonomous experiments, and retains refined affordance-extraction
procedures as reusable skills across tools.

2. An affordance-guided VLA model that integrates the resulting low-dimensional
feature vectors into action generation. Affordance conditioning and auxiliary
affordance-trajectory supervision train the policy to faithfully follow the supplied affordance
information while using current observations
and robot state to complete tool-use tasks.

title: Beyond Easy Clients: Difficulty- and Improvement-Aware Aggregation for Federated Reinforcement Learning in Robot Navigation
authors: Ye Lin Tun,Chu Myaet Thwal,Eui-Nam Huh,Choong Seon Hong
abstract:
Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared
navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots
rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a
cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules
ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still
learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high
returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the plateau
problem: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new
information even though its reported return remains high. We propose FedDIA,
which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it
received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred
from the model’s own performance, without requiring any description of the
environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are
comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous
clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of 75.5%75.5\% across training and
held-out environments, against 68.7%68.7\% for the strongest federated baseline. Its
advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and
living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.
introduction:
Robots increasingly operate autonomously, from warehouses and hospitals to homes
and city streets. Reinforcement learning (RL) [1, 2, 3, 4] provides a way to learn the control
policies they need through interaction rather than programming them in advance. Navigation
is a common requirement in robotics: reaching a goal while avoiding obstacles. Learning
it from onboard sensors [5, 6] avoids
the hand-built maps and motion planners [7] that are hard to
construct for unknown or changing environments. In practice, robots rarely operate under
identical conditions: an open aisle, a cluttered room, and a narrow corridor each demand
different behavior. A fleet deployed across such conditions spans environments of
varying difficulty [8], and can improve faster by pooling
experience than by learning alone [9]. With federated
reinforcement learning (FRL) [10, 11], each robot or client trains
locally and sends only its policy parameters to a server, which combines these updates
into a shared policy. Since only parameters are shared, no client reveals the layout of
its workplace.

However, not every client’s update is equally valuable to the shared policy.
A naive aggregation rule such as FedAvg [12] cannot
distinguish whether a client is actively improving, and assigns equal weight to every
update. A natural alternative is to weight each client by how well its policy
performs [13, 14], treating a higher return
as a sign of a better model. Yet this can make the problem worse. Clients in easy
environments may master the task early in training, after which their local updates
provide little new information even though their returns remain high. Weighting by return
then favors these saturated clients over clients in harder environments that are still
improving. This creates a mismatch between a client’s absolute return and its actual
contribution to the shared policy. An effective aggregation rule must therefore weight
clients by how much their local training improves the shared policy, not by absolute
return. Among clients that are still improving, it should also give greater weight to
those in more difficult environments.

To meet both requirements, we propose FedDIA, for Difficulty- and Improvement-aware
Aggregation. It measures each client against the same baseline. Before training
locally, a client evaluates how well the shared policy (global model) performs in its
environment, and evaluates its own updated policy after training. The difference between
the two evaluations measures how much the client improves the shared policy. The initial
evaluation also reveals how hard that environment is, without requiring environment
metadata. A low initial return indicates that the shared policy struggles there. Since
every client measures against the same policy, these signals are comparable across
clients. FedDIA combines the two signals into a single aggregation weight that grows
with client improvement and is amplified for harder environments. This amplification
applies only when the client is improving, and a saturated client therefore receives
no additional weight from environment difficulty.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

We formalize the plateau problem in heterogeneous FRL, where clients in
easy environments saturate early and subsequent local training yields little
improvement despite persistently high returns. Uniform averaging treats these saturated
clients equally with those still learning, and return-based weighting assigns them even
higher weights. This mismatch between absolute return and actual contribution motivates
the two requirements our method targets.

We propose FedDIA, which scores each client using two signals: the
improvement its local training brings to the shared policy and the difficulty of its
environment. The two signals are combined so that difficulty amplifies a client’s
weight only when that client is still improving. Among those still improving, the ones
in harder environments receive greater weight. Saturated clients are discounted
regardless of their absolute return.

On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a
mean success rate of 75.5%75.5\% across training and held-out environments, against
68.7%68.7\% for the strongest federated baseline.
Its advantage carries over to two hand-authored layouts built from industrial equipment
and household furniture, evaluated without further training. FedDIA also maintains
its performance when the client population includes a defective one.

title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving
authors: Chengkai Xu,Yicheng Guo,Jiaqi Liu,Yiming Cui,Shiyu Fang,Peng Hang,Hao Zhang,Jian Sun
abstract:
End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains.
However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another.
Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility.
To address this, we introduce Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD), a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy.
PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy.
A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families.
On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by 3.53.5 points on NavTest and 5.05.0 points on NavHard.
Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions.
These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving has advanced rapidly through increasingly capable policy architectures (Zheng et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024), yet attainable performance remains constrained by the quality and composition of their training data (Feng et al. 2026).
The success of large-scale vision and language models has consequently motivated the continued expansion of real and synthetic driving corpora (Jiang et al. 2025).
Data volume, however, does not translate predictably into policy improvement.
Additional demonstrations may be redundant, inconsistent with the learning objective, or harmful because of distribution and supervision errors (Shumailov et al. 2024; Jiao et al. 2026; Atakishiyev et al. 2025).
Such data can produce diminishing returns and scenario-specific regressions even when aggregate performance improves.
The central data problem is therefore not simply how much to collect, but which demonstrations improve a given driving policy (Dimlioglu et al. 2026; Xu et al. 2026a).

Addressing this problem requires a policy-dependent definition of data value.
Research on data attribution and model-aware filtering increasingly evaluates training samples through their effects on learned models (Yu et al. 2024; Guo et al. 2026).
This perspective reveals that a demonstration has no policy-independent utility.
The same sample may reinforce useful behavior in one policy while exerting negligible or adverse influence in another (Choe et al. 2026; Hammoudeh and Lowd 2024).
We accordingly define policy-aware data valuation as estimating the downstream utility of an individual demonstration with respect to the target policy that learns from it.

Existing driving-data construction and curation methods capture only part of this policy dependence.
Dataset-generation methods expand scale and coverage, usually treating complex or challenging scenarios as inherently valuable (Rowe et al. 2025; Xiao et al. 2025).
Data-intrinsic heuristics similarly prioritize rarity, diversity, or difficulty without measuring downstream learning effects (Jiao et al. 2026).
However, scenario complexity is not equivalent to training utility and cannot reflect whether a demonstration induces a beneficial update for a particular policy.
Training-dependent signals such as loss, uncertainty, and gradient salience reflect the current policy but need not correspond to downstream driving performance (Luo et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2024a).
Dataset- or cluster-level filtering can further conceal substantial variation among demonstrations within the same group (Calian et al. 2026; Chhabra et al. 2025).
The unresolved challenge is a scalable, per-demonstration estimator that connects a candidate’s effect on policy optimization to its downstream utility.

To address this challenge, Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD) is introduced.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, PAD evaluates a target policy on an independent calibration set and uses the resulting scene-level outcomes to weight gradients of its native training objective.
Projected gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry then yield a policy-specific value for each candidate demonstration, which supports budgeted selection for retraining.
Controlled removal experiments show that these values predict realized training effects, while cross-policy analysis reveals distinct valuations of the same candidate pool.
On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by 3.53.5 points on NavTest and 5.05.0 points on NavHard, with consistent gains across multiple policy families and fewer scene-level regressions.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Policy-aware data valuation. We formulate the value of each driving demonstration relative to the target policy and its downstream utility, rather than as an intrinsic property of the sample.

Scalable per-demonstration estimation. We develop an influence-based estimator that integrates scene-level policy outcomes, projected training gradients, and regularized local geometry within a unified interface across policy families.

Comprehensive empirical validation. We show that PAD predicts realized training effects, produces distinct valuations across policies, improves downstream driving performance, and reduces scene-level regression exposure.

1. Policy-aware data valuation. We formulate the value of each driving demonstration relative to the target policy and its downstream utility, rather than as an intrinsic property of the sample.

2. Scalable per-demonstration estimation. We develop an influence-based estimator that integrates scene-level policy outcomes, projected training gradients, and regularized local geometry within a unified interface across policy families.

3. Comprehensive empirical validation. We show that PAD predicts realized training effects, produces distinct valuations across policies, improves downstream driving performance, and reduces scene-level regression exposure.

title: GraF-VTA: Neuro-Symbolic Trajectory Generation from Vision and Temporal Logic via Graph-Based Fusion
authors: Zezhi Liu,Zhiwei Zheng,Hanqian Luo,Deyun Qin,Shizhen Wu,Yongchun Fang
abstract: Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Across five simulation environments, the single-graph configuration achieves higher open-loop Success@KK than TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at the reported budgets K≥16K\geq 16. On Panda, matched-update ablations increase Success@256 from 53.91% without observation history to 62.50% with pyramid memory. In closed-loop Dubins evaluation, it reaches 64.06% Success@1024, compared with 12.50% for adapted S-MSP and 27.34% for adapted Logic-VLA. These results support combining structured visual conditioning with observation history and replanning to improve coverage of STL-satisfying trajectories.
introduction:
Robotic tasks often combine goal achievement with deadlines, ordering, and obstacle avoidance. Signal temporal logic (STL) expresses these requirements precisely through spatial predicates and bounded temporal operators [32, 2, 26]. Trajectory generation and execution from visual observations, STL specifications, and robot state are therefore important for fulfilling these requirements.

Visual input provides a practical interface between STL planning and robot sensing, with grounding mechanisms relating symbolic references to image regions [18, 24, 30].
Pretrained vision-language models have also been used to propose visual predicates and evaluate them from images, enabling the learning of symbolic world models for long-horizon planning [1].
For STL-conditioned trajectory generation, TeLoGraF [35] conditions trajectory generation on syntax graphs containing exact object geometry, which must be supplied externally. End-to-end visuomotor learning [23, 6, 53, 25] demonstrates that perception can instead be trained jointly with action prediction. Vision-TL-Action (VTA) [31] brings visual grounding to STL-conditioned generation by connecting logic nodes to image tokens. This supports a learned observation-to-trajectory mapping without exact object geometry in the STL specifications.

Executing trajectories planned by generative models is challenging because model mismatch, disturbances, and tracking errors can separate intended and realized motion. Receding-horizon STL control [39, 38, 33] and Diffusion Policy [7] motivate repeated planning from execution feedback. We therefore execute short action prefixes and refresh visual observations and robot state before generating subsequent actions, allowing plans to respond to observed deviations.

Refreshed observations alone may not reveal the robot’s recent interactions with the environment or the current task stage. MemoryVLA [40] demonstrates the value of historical perceptual and semantic information for temporally dependent manipulation. This motivates conditioning STL planning on causal observation history. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations while compressing older frames, providing recent execution context within a finite memory window.

A complementary challenge is exposing task semantics to the generator. An STL syntax graph preserves composition, time bounds, and object references. Yet, as Xie et al. [46] observe for finite-trace LTL, equivalent formulas can have different syntax trees, complicating semantic learning. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) makes the accepted event sequences explicit through transitions and accepting states. This motivates combining timed, visually groundable syntax with a semantic view.

We introduce GraF-VTA, a unified visual temporal-logic planning framework supporting STL syntax graph and DFA graph conditioning (Fig. 1). It also combines bidirectional logic–vision fusion, causal observation memory, and action-prefix replanning within a conditional flow-matching generator. The optional dual-graph configuration adds a frozen RADE embedding [47] after pooling and base-condition encoding. Our main empirical analysis concerns the single-graph configuration; dual-graph conditioning is a complementary representation extension.

Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We present a unified framework for end-to-end trajectory generation from visual observations, STL specifications, and robot state. Building on TeLoGraF’s graph-conditioned flow matching and VTA’s visual grounding, bidirectional logic–vision fusion connects object references to scene evidence while retaining temporal constraints. Conditioning uses the STL syntax tree alone or adds a DFA embedding for complementary task-transition structure.
(2) To address execution errors, we interleave action-prefix execution with replanning from updated visual observations and robot state. A causal temporal pyramid retains detailed current observations while compressing older frames, providing recent execution context for multi-stage tasks. This feedback-driven design responds to observed deviations, aiming to improve robustness to execution errors.
(3) We evaluate open-loop trajectory generation and dynamics-executed rollouts across five simulation environments, complemented by comparisons with related planners and observation-memory ablations. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking: Memory-Guided Adaptive Reasoning for Embodied Navigation
authors: Weile Gong,Zijian Lu,Jiahao Zheng,Bo Xu,Yiping Zuo,Jiajia Guo,Xin He,Weijun Wang,Weibei Fan
abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy’s stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.
introduction:
Recent advances in multimodal foundation models are expanding embodied intelligence. Robot-control evaluations of general-purpose multimodal models [4] and advances in manipulation with Gemini Robotics 2.5 [21] illustrate the promise of connecting visual understanding and language instructions with embodied action. For navigation, vision-language models (VLMs) interpret scenes, ground goals and instructions, and generate movement through unfamiliar environments [32, 28, 12, 35]. Sustained navigation requires coordinating this inference with physical execution.

Repeatedly invoking large vision-language policies incurs computational cost over many physical actions. Action chunking amortizes this cost by predicting several future actions per invocation [33, 8]. Its benefit depends on execution: frequent refreshes limit reuse, while extended execution can carry a prediction beyond its supporting observations and motion conditions. Efficient navigation requires deciding how long to act on a prediction and when new evidence warrants another policy invocation.

Existing approaches adjust inference timing or execution horizons using consistency or uncertainty signals [23, 13, 19, 10, 1]. Navigation must also account for movement-induced changes: a turn reveals a new action direction, a completion cue warrants fresh inference, or the controller cannot realize the requested motion. Refreshing changes subsequent actions, observations, and execution before termination. Its computational effect therefore extends beyond the immediate cost of a new call, motivating decisions based on current evidence and retained context.

Our key insight is that retained visual context and visitation history can guide both inference timing and terminal execution. Visual references and observation coverage preserve the context available when each prediction was generated. Completion cues and motion feedback complement this context when deciding whether to reuse or refresh a prediction. Executed actions also leave a position history that remains available after prediction replacement. Our offline trajectory analysis reveals episodes in which the robot enters a suitable stopping region but later stops outside it (Section 5.5). Nearby visited positions can therefore provide a geometric reference for a bounded terminal correction.

We introduce Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy (Fig. 1). CHAC determines when to reuse a cached prediction and when to invoke the policy again. Its cognitive horizon counts the ordered waypoints executed before refresh. A visual boundary compares appearance along newly observed action directions with retained visual context. A commitment boundary checks completion cues and controller-supported progress. Together with inherited motion feedback, they determine inference timing. At native STOP, local visitation history guides a bounded correction, adding at most one movement and no model calls.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce CHAC, a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning combining an online cognitive horizon for policy invocation with history-guided terminal correction.

We identify how refresh decisions interact with subsequent execution to determine inference demand, including a reversal of visual refresh’s computational effect under commitment checks.

We evaluate navigation quality and inference cost across two benchmarks and physical tasks, with matched terminal interventions testing visitation history’s directional information.

1. We introduce CHAC, a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning combining an online cognitive horizon for policy invocation with history-guided terminal correction.

2. We identify how refresh decisions interact with subsequent execution to determine inference demand, including a reversal of visual refresh’s computational effect under commitment checks.

3. We evaluate navigation quality and inference cost across two benchmarks and physical tasks, with matched terminal interventions testing visitation history’s directional information.

title: Trajectory-Calibrated Merging of Embodied Policies
authors: Wenshuo Chen,Honglei Jin,Le Yang,Jianfei Song,Shaofeng Liang,Lei Wang,Junze Zhu,Kailong Wang,Zhengxi Jin,Haozhe Jia,Honglin Chu,Songning Lai,Xiucheng Wang,Yutao Yue
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities.
Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution:
parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy.
Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation.
To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block’s input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert’s computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts’ linear outputs.
A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers.
The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four π0.5\pi_{0.5} specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.
We also find that continued training from a merged checkpoint improves peak success: TCR reaches 97.75% versus 94.00% when training from the common base.
These results show that calibrating model merging around execution dynamics and evolving internal representations provides an effective path toward preserving diverse embodied skills in a unified policy.
introduction:
General-purpose robots need policies that can perform diverse physical tasks.
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising foundation (Black et al., 2025a; Kim et al., 2025a), but demonstration data cover limited tasks and environments, making it difficult to acquire a broad skill set through a single training run.
Training task specialists from a shared foundation model expands coverage, but leaves their capabilities in separate checkpoints.
We seek to consolidate them into one policy.

Model merging can do this without joint training or selecting an expert at inference.
We focus on post-hoc consolidation of independently trained VLA specialists into one static policy, without redesigning the experts or adding a task router.
Parameter-space methods combine weights or align task updates to reduce interference (Wortsman et al., 2022; Yadav et al., 2023; Stoica et al., 2025).
But the mapping from weights to actions is nonlinear: reducing conflicts between weights does not ensure that the merged policy preserves expert actions or closed-loop success.
Regression-based methods instead fit merged weights to expert outputs on calibration inputs (Jin et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2026).
Such a fit is only as useful as the inputs it covers.
An action error can change not only the current output but also what the policy sees next; matching a fixed set of expert observations may leave later inputs unconstrained and allow errors to accumulate.

A slightly misplaced grasp, for example, can change both the camera observation and the robot state at the next decision. Even when the observation is held fixed, the input to an iterative action generator changes across calls as each intermediate prediction updates the action state passed to the next call. Calibration using only the final call can therefore miss states encountered earlier in generation. During merging, a further change occurs within the network. Updating an upstream block can alter the features passed to a downstream block, so a block fitted on the original expert’s features may receive different inputs in the merged policy. The regression fit thus depends on which states are sampled during execution and action generation, and on how the features used to fit each block are computed (see Figure 1).

We introduce Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), a gradient-free framework for merging compatible robot experts.
TCR uses frozen experts as teachers and collects two kinds of inputs: observations, robot states, and instructions across expert rollouts, and intermediate call states from each expert’s native action generator.
The first covers stages reached after earlier expert actions; the second covers generator inputs, such as noisy actions and flow times, that an observation alone does not specify.
TCR fits adapted perception, conditioning, and action modules to expert outputs on these inputs.
Following blockwise feature replay (Nguyen et al., 2026), it recomputes each block’s inputs through the blocks already merged before fitting that block.
Downstream regressions therefore use features produced by the merged prefix rather than relying only on the original expert features.
TCR makes two passes over separate rollout caches: the first updates the parameter average, and the second uses that checkpoint as its prior while still matching the frozen experts.
The second cache adds expert calls not used in the first fit, and the updated prior carries the first pass into the second.
The result is one policy with the original inference graph, no expert router, and no gradient training.

We evaluate TCR on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) using four π0.5\pi_{0.5} specialists trained for 10,000 steps each.
Across 1,200 episodes, TCR achieves 77.83% success, the highest among the static post-hoc mergers evaluated in this π0.5\pi_{0.5}-LIBERO setting.
This is 9.50 points above FeatCal (68.33%), 24.17 above RegMean (53.67%), and 33.00 above direct weight averaging (44.83%).
The gains are strongest on Goal and Long, although FeatCal remains ahead on Spatial.
All methods share the same experts and evaluation protocol, while retaining their own calibration budgets.
Ablations test the calibration choices; real-robot and cross-benchmark evaluations test TCR beyond LIBERO.
We also find that merged checkpoints are useful starts for joint training: all four attain higher peak success than common-base training, with TCR highest at 97.75% versus 94.00% for the base.

title: Communication-Aware UAV Spatio-Temporal Relay Cooperation and Planning in Complex Urban Environments
authors: Haoyu Zhang,Yingjie He,Zehao Zhuo,Xiqun Chen,Zhenyu Gao
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed in low-altitude urban airspace for delivery, emergency response, and other applications. However, UAV mobility across spatially heterogeneous urban communication environments can lead to time-varying communication outages, disrupting mission execution and compromising flight safety. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a Spatio-Temporal Relay Cooperation and Planning (ST-RCP) framework that leverages delivery UAVs as opportunistic communication relays for disconnected UAVs without requiring additional communication infrastructure. The framework predicts communication blind-spot events over a finite planning horizon, constructs a helper–event compatibility graph, and jointly optimizes relay selection, obstacle-aware trajectory replanning, and communication-aware scheduling. Multiple planners are evaluated to investigate the trade-offs among communication coverage, computational cost, and energy consumption. Experiments based on real-world traffic scenarios compare the performance of ST-RCP against baseline methods. In the peak scenario, ST-RCP improves descent-phase communication coverage by 29.93% compared with the base-station baseline and by 27.38%, 22.02%, and 15.20% compared with configurations using one, two, and three dedicated relay UAVs, respectively. Process flexibility analysis demonstrates that predictive task-aware relaying expands the pool of feasible relay resources and improves communication continuity while maintaining the feasibility of delivery missions. These findings demonstrate the potential of trajectory-enabled UAV coordination to enhance the safety and resilience of urban aerial operations.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are playing an increasingly important role in low-altitude urban air mobility, with growing applications in logistics delivery, emergency response, and search and rescue [1, 2]. Reliable communication is essential for these operations, as command and control signals, traffic management information, and mission-related data must be exchanged between UAVs and ground infrastructure to ensure safe and efficient operations [3, 4]. Communication disruptions can pose significant risks to flight safety, as the loss of command and control connectivity may compromise UAV operations and increase the risk of accidents.

Maintaining reliable connectivity, however, is particularly challenging in dense urban environments. High-rise buildings can obstruct line-of-sight (LoS) communication links and cause signal reflection, diffraction, and scattering, leading to substantial spatial variations in received signal strength and localized communication coverage gaps, particularly in urban canyons and areas obstructed by buildings [5, 6], as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Simply increasing base station density may not fully resolve these challenges. UAVs may establish strong propagation links with multiple neighboring base stations simultaneously, potentially exacerbating co-channel interference and limiting the coverage and throughput gains of network densification [7]. Furthermore, additional base stations may not eliminate coverage gaps caused by signal blockage from urban structures [6]. UAV connectivity is also inherently trajectory dependent, particularly when mission locations are uncertain. As a UAV moves through a spatially heterogeneous radio environment, its received signal quality varies over time, causing it to repeatedly enter and leave communication coverage regions [8]. Therefore, reliable urban UAV communication depends not only on the spatial distribution of radio coverage but also on the spatiotemporal interaction between UAV trajectories and communication conditions.

Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate intermittent UAV connectivity. One representative approach is to establish flying ad hoc networks (FANETs), in which neighboring UAVs exchange data through multi-hop communication links. However, the high mobility of UAVs leads to rapidly changing network topologies, making it difficult for conventional routing protocols to maintain reliable end-to-end communication paths [9]. Moreover, network-wide flooding of routing messages can generate substantial redundant transmissions, increasing channel contention and routing overhead [10]. An alternative approach is to deploy UAV-mounted base stations or dedicated relay UAVs to restore or extend communication coverage. Although such aerial relays can effectively improve connectivity, they require additional aerial resources and incur substantial deployment and operational costs [11, 12]. More recently, studies have explored the use of delivery UAVs as communication relays by adjusting their flight routes and introducing communication waypoints to support multi-hop connectivity [13]. Such studies demonstrate the potential of leveraging the mobility of task-performing UAVs to support communication without relying exclusively on dedicated relay platforms. However, existing approaches largely plan communication topologies and delivery routes in advance, rather than dynamically adapting to time-varying communication outages arising from task uncertainty. This limitation motivates a more dynamic planning framework that treats future communication blind spots as time-dependent service events and predictively reserves and reroutes available task-performing UAVs to provide relay assistance while satisfying communication, flight safety, obstacle avoidance, energy, and delivery constraints.

To address this research gap, this paper proposes a spatio-temporal relay cooperation and planning (ST-RCP) framework to enable self-organizing UAV communication in complex urban environments. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on dedicated relay platforms, ST-RCP leverages the mobility of UAVs already performing delivery missions, allowing available UAVs to temporarily serve as opportunistic communication relays while maintaining the feasibility of their original tasks. Furthermore, rather than optimizing communication locations along predetermined routes, ST-RCP models communication outages as time-varying service demands and coordinates relay resources based on both spatial reachability and temporal availability. Specifically, future communication blind-spot events and their associated attributes are predicted over a finite planning horizon. For each event, ST-RCP identifies candidate delivery UAVs capable of providing relay assistance while satisfying their original mission constraints. A helper–event compatibility graph is then constructed to capture spatial, temporal, and communication feasibility. This formulation transforms relay selection from a static waypoint placement problem into a constrained spatio-temporal resource allocation problem. Based on the selected helpers, smooth, obstacle-aware relay trajectories are subsequently generated using Bézier curves.

The proposed framework is evaluated in terms of communication performance, operational efficiency, and computational cost. Beyond conventional coverage metrics, this study introduces a process flexibility perspective to characterize the structural adaptability of the task-performing UAV relay system. This analysis complements conventional performance evaluations by examining not only the effectiveness of relay strategies under given scenarios but also the system’s ability to accommodate varying communication demands, resource contention, and fleet sizes. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A spatio-temporal relay cooperation and planning (ST-RCP) framework is proposed to enable task-performing UAVs to opportunistically provide communication relay assistance without requiring additional infrastructure.

Communication blind-spot recovery is formulated as a predictive helper–event assignment and constrained trajectory planning problem, enabling time-dependent, event-driven relay resource allocation.

A process flexibility analysis framework is introduced to quantify the scalability and adaptability of UAV relay systems, characterizing their ability to maintain feasible relay options under increasing traffic demand and resource contention.

title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
authors: Jiachen Tao,Gengyu Zhang,Haoxuan Wang,Bing Liu,Yan Yan
abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy’s own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy’s atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6×4.6\times over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
introduction:
Humans become skilled in the physical world not by being shown every motion, but by practice: they act, observe the outcome, and adjust. Repeated over many attempts, this loop turns a clumsy first try into a reliable skill, and it continues long after instruction ends. Generalist robot policies now perform a wide range of manipulation tasks [9, 8, 42, 41, 24, 6, 5, 40], yet they rarely improve this way: when a policy fails, making it better typically means collecting new human demonstrations. Enabling a robot to improve from its own experience is the goal of self-improvement in physical AI [35, 7], and it would scale robot learning beyond what human teleoperation can supply.

The most direct form of self-improvement changes the policy itself: the robot acts, keeps its successful rollouts, and is fine-tuned on them. This recipe has two limitations. First, a policy acting alone stays within its own distribution, so its successes show it only what it can already do. Second, on the long-horizon tasks where improvement matters most, the policy fails often and has few successes to collect. Experience improves a policy when it contains successes the policy cannot yet produce, and self-collected experience contains few of them.

Existing methods obtain such successes with supervision from outside the policy. Interactive imitation learning brings in a human operator who takes over when the robot errs and supplies corrective actions [23, 2]. Every correction costs operator time, so the supervision scales with human effort, the cost that self-improvement is meant to remove. Reinforcement learning replaces the operator with reward and value models that score the robot’s own attempts [45, 10]. These models must themselves be trained before they can supervise the policy. Hierarchical systems place a vision-language model above the policy to decompose the task into steps [1, 47]. The policy itself is left unchanged, and the system depends on the high-level model at every deployment.

To understand what keeps a policy from producing these successes on its own, we analyze rollouts of generalist policies on long-horizon tasks. We find that the missing successes are closer than they appear. The policies execute atomic skills reliably, yet fail when the same skills are composed into a long-horizon task [37, 29, 16, 48], and the failures take a specific form: partway through the task the policy stalls, and a stalled policy almost never recovers on its own. In a recurring case, the robot is already at the right object and holds the required skill, yet does not act. What the policy lacks in that moment is not a skill but the next step. What it needs is therefore far less than corrective actions or rewards: a single instruction.

We introduce CoachSI (Fig. 1), a self-improvement method guided by language alone. Its central component is a language coach: a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) that watches the robot and replaces the task instruction with the next step, phrased in the format of the policy’s atomic instructions. The coach never outputs an action; every motion is produced by the policy’s own skills. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction [3] and used to fine-tune the policy, which is then deployed on its own. On a World Action Model, fine-tuning updates only the video backbone and keeps the action backbone frozen. CoachSI needs no human operator, no reward model, and no VLM at test time.

We evaluate CoachSI on RoboCasa365 [39] with a World Action Model (WAM) [49] and a Vision-Language-Action model (VLA) [55]. On states where the two policies have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6×4.6\times over the unchanged task instruction, and a VLM coach that sees only the policy’s camera images delivers 91% of the gain of an oracle that always names the correct step. With the coach, the policy completes more than a quarter of the episodes it fails on its own. After fine-tuning the WAM on coached experience, unassisted success on 18 long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The action backbone is frozen throughout, so the entire gain comes from what the policy predicts will happen next: the skills were already there.

Our contributions are:

We identify a class of stalls in long-horizon manipulation in which the policy has the skill but lacks the next step, and show that a single next-step instruction resolves them, for both a WAM and a VLA.

We propose CoachSI, a self-improvement method of language coaching, hindsight relabeling, and fine-tuning, guided only by a frozen VLM’s next-step instruction.

We show that CoachSI turns coached experience into unassisted capability and outperforms both human demonstrations and self-collected experience at an equal data budget.

1. We identify a class of stalls in long-horizon manipulation in which the policy has the skill but lacks the next step, and show that a single next-step instruction resolves them, for both a WAM and a VLA.

2. We propose CoachSI, a self-improvement method of language coaching, hindsight relabeling, and fine-tuning, guided only by a frozen VLM’s next-step instruction.

3. We show that CoachSI turns coached experience into unassisted capability and outperforms both human demonstrations and self-collected experience at an equal data budget.

title: Learning Ankle Exoskeleton Control for Reactive Standing Balance Through Neuromusculoskeletal Simulation
authors: Maria T. Tagliaferri,Inseung Kang
abstract: Deficits in reactive balance can increase fall risk among older adults and individuals with neuromuscular impairments, motivating the need for interventions that improve balance recovery. Wearable robotic exoskeletons offer a promising approach to addressing this need by augmenting balance control. However, developing controllers that deliver appropriately timed and scaled assistance remains challenging, as evaluating each candidate strategy requires repeated exposure to destabilizing perturbations. We propose a simulation-to-real framework that combines motion imitation and reinforcement learning to develop balance-assistive ankle exoskeleton control. A muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal model was trained using a small set of motion-capture data from a single subject to reproduce kinematic and kinetic responses to backward-translation perturbations. This model served as a virtual human for training a reinforcement-learning exoskeleton controller. The resulting controller generated bilateral ankle assistance using only inertial sensor measurements, without explicit perturbation detection. We implemented the controller on-board a bilateral ankle exoskeleton and evaluated it in five healthy subjects whose data were not used for training. Assistance increased the perturbation magnitude that subjects could withstand without stepping by 11.8% and reduced peak center-of-mass displacement and velocity by 13.5% and 28.2%, respectively. Individual benefits varied with baseline recovery strategy and body mass. These results indicate that a single virtual human can yield transferable balance assistance, and that more diverse virtual humans could further improve its effectiveness.
introduction:
Maintaining upright standing balance requires continuous neuromuscular control to regulate the body’s center of mass (CoM), which is positioned above a relatively small base of support (BoS). This control relies on coordinated muscle activity across the ankle, knee, and hip joints to regulate CoM motion and maintain postural stability. Impairments in these mechanisms can compromise balance and increase susceptibility to falls, which are a major source of injury among older adults and individuals with neuromuscular impairments [1, 2]. Wearable robotic exoskeletons offer a potential approach to augment these balance responses by supplementing the joint moments involved in CoM regulation. Several studies have shown that assistive exoskeleton torque can improve measures of postural stability following a balance perturbation [3, 4, 5].

Existing balance-assistive controllers generally apply a predefined torque profile during perturbation. For example, studies have evaluated brief plantarflexion torque pulses at the ankle during standing perturbations [3, 6] or spline-based hip torque profiles during walking perturbations [7]. Although these approaches demonstrated the benefits of assistive torque, the assistance was not adaptive to the user’s real-time balance response. An alternative approach is to leverage the underlying mechanisms of human balance control to inform exoskeleton assistance. Jakubowski et al. demonstrated that physiologically inspired CoM feedback models can predict coordinated, multi-joint balance-correcting torques across different perturbation conditions and users [8]. These findings suggest that biological balance-control strategies could provide a basis for developing adaptive, physiologically grounded assistance. However, whether reproducing these torque patterns through an exoskeleton improves balance recovery remains unclear. Furthermore, implementing CoM-based feedback on wearable devices requires accurate, real-time estimation of whole-body CoM motion.

Therefore, determining the appropriate timing and magnitude of assistance to improve postural stability during perturbation recovery remains a central challenge [9, 6]. Beck et al. demonstrated that ankle assistance improved standing balance only when delivered before the onset of physiological reactive joint moments [3]. Regarding assistance magnitude, moderate ankle torque consistently improved CoM displacement during standing perturbations, whereas higher torque magnitudes produced greater inter-subject variability without additional group-level benefits [6]. These findings indicate that multiple assistance profiles must be evaluated to identify effective balance assistance across users. Systematic parameter exploration and human-in-the-loop optimization have identified effective assistance profiles for reducing the metabolic cost of locomotion [10, 11, 12], but both require repeated human-subject testing across conditions. For reactive balance, each evaluation also requires exposure to destabilizing perturbations, which increases experimental burden and concerns regarding subject fatigue and habituation [9, 13].

Physics-based neuromusculoskeletal simulation offers an alternative for developing and evaluating balance-assistive controllers before human-subject testing. Simulation-to-real transfer of exoskeleton controllers has already been demonstrated for locomotor tasks, such as walking, with an emphasis on improving energetic outcomes [14, 15, 16]. Separately, neuromusculoskeletal simulations have been used to investigate human neuromuscular control and postural stability during perturbed standing [17, 18]. However, these two areas have not yet been combined to develop and deploy exoskeleton controllers specifically for reactive balance. By reproducing human responses to perturbations, neuromusculoskeletal simulation provides a controlled environment for learning exoskeleton assistance policies using stability-focused objectives. This approach reduces the number of human-subject perturbation trials needed during controller development, which reduces experimental burden and habituation. Human-subject experiments are then reserved for validating the transferred controller.

In this work, we present a simulation-to-real framework for learning ankle exoskeleton assistance for reactive standing balance. Using approximately 2 minutes of motion-capture data from a single participant, we first train a muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal model to reproduce human responses to backward-translation perturbations. We then use this model as a virtual human to train a separate reinforcement-learning controller that learns stability-oriented ankle assistance using only device-available sensor inputs, without explicit perturbation detection. Finally, we deploy the learned controller on a bilateral ankle exoskeleton to evaluate its real-time performance and balance benefits in five participants whose data were not used for training.

title: Demonstration-Free Skill Composition for Navigation and Manipulation
authors: Madeleine Nouri,Gelareh Mohammadi,Francisco Cruz
comment: . Accepted at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026). Project page:this https URL
abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill. Code and videos are available at https://madeleinenouri.github.io/acra-skill-composition/.
introduction:
Tasks requiring an extended sequence of decisions can be decomposed into a sequence of primitive behaviours. Examples include transitions between rooms in navigation and sequences of reaching, grasping, lifting, transporting and placing in manipulation. Flat reinforcement learning treats the full sequence as a single control
problem, which can lead to poor sample efficiency when exploration must discover a long chain of behaviours from a sparse terminal reward [10].

Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) offers a structured alternative in which the task is decomposed into reusable skills, each operating over a shorter horizon with a localised reward signal, and a high-level controller that sequences the skills at execution time [18, 1]. Some skill-chaining methods improve composition reliability by
aligning upstream termination distributions with downstream initiation
distributions using expert demonstrations as a reference
[14, 5]. Another approach uses engineered rewards instead of demonstrations [11, 13]. Trained skills can also be reused as components of new
tasks [10]. This paper evaluates demonstration-free skill pipelines in navigation
and manipulation, examining training requirements, task performance
and reuse of the trained policies.

The contributions of this paper are:

An empirical evaluation of demonstration-free hierarchical
pipelines for discrete navigation and continuous manipulation,
in which each downstream skill is trained on reset states
covering its predecessor’s success states.

title: Stereo Visual Odometry with In-the-Loop Geometric Feed-Forward Models Towards Dense Metric Mapping
authors: Fahira Afzal Maken,Sagun Man Singh Shrestha,Edward Vanderfeen,Lucas Carvalho de Lima,Rongxin Li,Changming Sun,Milad Ramezani
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
We present a stereo visual odometry (SVO) framework that integrates geometric feed-forward models (GFMs) for dense depth prediction with factor-graph-based visual odometry to achieve accurate localisation and dense metric mapping. Our key idea is to exploit sparse but reliable metric geometry estimated from stereo and temporal multi-view observations to calibrate dense GFM predictions, while retaining the robustness and efficiency of model-based SVO. Rather than directly conditioning the GFM on potentially noisy stereo depth, optimised 33D landmarks are used to jointly estimate a scale–shift transformation over all keyframes within each local submap, yielding metrically consistent dense depth predictions. To balance accuracy and computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical factor-graph architecture. At the local level, sliding-window optimisation estimates high-frequency camera poses and multi-view-refined 33D landmarks. Dense predictions are generated only for selected keyframes and registered within each submap using SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) Generalised ICP. Consecutive submaps are further aligned in Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3) using their shared geometry, allowing residual scale inconsistencies to be corrected. These intra- and inter-submap constraints are incorporated into a global factor graph to produce a consistent trajectory and dense metric reconstruction.
Extensive experiments on public and in-house datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive odometry accuracy against geometric and learning-based baselines while providing accurate dense metric reconstruction and improved robustness to failures in learned depth prediction.
introduction:
Recent advances in deep learning have transformed visual simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM), with geometric feed-forward models (GFMs) showing strong capability in recovering dense 33D scene structure directly from images. Building on these advances, systems such as MASt3R-SLAM [1] and VGGT-SLAM [2] have demonstrated impressive localisation and reconstruction performance. However, dense inference remains computationally demanding, inconsistencies across local reconstructions must be reconciled over long trajectories, and predicted depth may still exhibit residual scale inconsistencies with metric geometry.

While recent feed-forward SLAM systems can recover dense scene geometry, maintaining globally consistent and metrically scaled reconstructions over long trajectories remains challenging. Approaches such as VGGT-SLAM address reconstruction ambiguity through global alignment and optimisation of local submaps [3], although over the SL⁡(4)\mathrm{SL}(4) manifold with 15 degrees of freedom (DoF). On the other hand, feature-based stereo visual odometry (SVO) [4, 5, 6] provides accurate metric geometry through joint optimisation of camera poses and visual landmarks, leveraging both stereo and temporal multi-view observations. However, conventional SVO typically produces only sparse scene structure. This motivates combining the metric consistency of stereo geometry with the dense reconstruction capability of GFMs.

In this work, we present an SVO framework that integrates geometric feed-forward depth prediction with factor-graph optimisation through a hierarchical architecture. At the local level, sliding-window factor graphs estimate high-frequency camera poses and multi-view-refined 33D landmarks. For each local submap, the optimised landmarks from all selected keyframes are jointly used to estimate a scale–shift transformation that metrically calibrates the dense GFM predictions. The resulting dense reconstructions are registered between keyframes, while consecutive local submaps are aligned through Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3) transformations to correct residual scale discrepancies. These geometric constraints are incorporated into a global factor graph to provide accurate localisation and globally consistent dense metric mapping (Figure 1). By restricting dense inference and registration to selected keyframes, the proposed hierarchy balances reconstruction accuracy with computational efficiency.

The main contributions of this work are:

We propose a hierarchical factor-graph stereo visual odometry framework that combines sparse metric geometry with dense geometric feed-forward predictions, using SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) constraints within local submaps and Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3) alignment across submaps for globally consistent dense metric mapping.

We introduce a metric-guided depth calibration strategy that uses multi-view-optimised 33D landmarks to estimate a shared scale–shift transformation for all keyframes within each submap, providing metrically consistent dense depth predictions without directly conditioning the GFM on uncertain stereo depth.

We extensively evaluate the proposed framework on KITTI, Newer College, and in-house datasets against representative geometric and learning-based baselines, considering both trajectory accuracy and dense reconstruction quality.

1. We propose a hierarchical factor-graph stereo visual odometry framework that combines sparse metric geometry with dense geometric feed-forward predictions, using SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) constraints within local submaps and Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3) alignment across submaps for globally consistent dense metric mapping.

2. We introduce a metric-guided depth calibration strategy that uses multi-view-optimised 33D landmarks to estimate a shared scale–shift transformation for all keyframes within each submap, providing metrically consistent dense depth predictions without directly conditioning the GFM on uncertain stereo depth.

3. We extensively evaluate the proposed framework on KITTI, Newer College, and in-house datasets against representative geometric and learning-based baselines, considering both trajectory accuracy and dense reconstruction quality.
