title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners
authors: Junhyeok Lee,Dongheon Lee,Kyu Sung Choi
abstract:
Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle.
Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself.
We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks.
In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress.
The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles.
We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode’s prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan.
With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts.
A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break.
Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
introduction:
A world model that predicts the consequences of actions lets an agent plan toward new goals from reward-free offline data [23].
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs), which forecast the embedding of a future frame rather than its pixels, have become a standard route to planning from pixels toward goal images [48, 35, 3, 43].
With model predictive control (MPC) [12], the planner optimizes a short action sequence toward the goal embedding at every step, by gradient descent (GD) through the model [38, 5] or by the cross-entropy method (CEM) [33, 14], executes the first chunk, and replans.

When such a planner fails on a task its model should handle, test-time adaptation attributes the failure to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode’s transitions [37, 41, 25].
For JEPA world models, AdaJEPA [42] does so after every executed chunk and reports large gains.
Analyses of latent planners likewise score plans or candidate actions [40, 46, 24].
Both views locate the failure in the model’s predictions, and so expect that better predictions, if necessary from updated weights, make a better planner.
Neither view checks this attribution against the planning loop.

This expectation leaves out the loop, in which MPC replans from the states its own actions produce, so an error that leaves the state unchanged can recur at every replan, however well each plan is scored.
On pushing tasks, where an agent pushes a block to a goal pose, the executed loop of the base planner, the pretrained model with standard MPC (GD unless stated otherwise), fails mostly through stalls, in which the block stays in place while the model predicts progress (Fig. 1).
In most settings, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, including those on the training shapes and clean frames, so shift alone does not explain them.
Test-time adaptation also adds a backward pass to every replan and risks forgetting and collapse [26, 27].
We therefore trace what keeps the loop in place and test whether a planner with fixed weights can break it.

Two ingredients keep the loop in place.
At the stalled states we analyze, the model, not the search, is mostly at fault: it never prefers a one-chunk plan that would succeed to staying, whereas the objective on simulated frames often does.
The executed chunk moves the agent out and back. The deterministic GD planner, warm-started from its previous plan as in real-time MPC [9], then returns nearly the same plan from the unchanged state, so the loop reaches a fixed point in which the agent mostly idles.
With CEM, which samples new plans, the agent moves, yet the block stays in place.

These two ingredients hold the planning loop at the fixed point, which neither more accurate predictions alone nor test-time weight updates target directly.
We therefore propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning (FT) with a fixed-weight loop breaker (Fig. 1).
Fine-tuning corrects the model, before deployment, on the base planner’s own executions of separate episodes, because the planner visits states that offline data miss [1, 31], but alone leaves the agent idle in most remaining failures.
In Unstick-Mem, a residual memory (Mem) adds the model’s one-step errors on executed chunks back to predictions near them, so a re-proposed stay-in-place chunk is predicted to stay in place.
In Unstick-ReInit, random re-initialization (ReInit) starts every replan from a random plan instead of the warm start, so the same state no longer yields the same plan.
With GD and after on-policy fine-tuning, the memory recovers most of the gain of test-time adaptation on pushing tasks, and re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts.
A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, not an error that only test-time weight updates can fix.
JEPA planners should therefore be evaluated in closed loop, by checking whether the state moves and whether the plan repeats, before their failures are attributed to distribution shift, and test-time adaptation should be compared with remedies that keep the weights fixed.

Our contributions are:

Closed-loop diagnostics show that JEPA planners on pushing tasks fail mainly by stalling, which a deterministic GD planner turns into a fixed point.

We break the stall without test-time weight updates, with an episodic memory of model residuals or random re-initialization, which after on-policy fine-tuning recover most of the adaptation gain.

We trace failure cases that neither remedy fixes to an encoder that discards a task variable or to local minima of the planning objective, rather than to the planner.

1. Closed-loop diagnostics show that JEPA planners on pushing tasks fail mainly by stalling, which a deterministic GD planner turns into a fixed point.

2. We break the stall without test-time weight updates, with an episodic memory of model residuals or random re-initialization, which after on-policy fine-tuning recover most of the adaptation gain.

3. We trace failure cases that neither remedy fixes to an encoder that discards a task variable or to local minima of the planning objective, rather than to the planner.

title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics
authors: Zexun Lin,Yuan Feng,Xike Xie
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86×\times–4.28×\times end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) offer a new paradigm for embodied policy learning by integrating visual dynamics modeling with action generation, providing predictive representations for robotic control [43, 47, 21, 50, 49, 52, 18, 3, 56].
However, most existing WAMs generate actions via flow matching [26, 31], which uses predicted velocities to update noisy actions over multiple Euler steps, incurring substantial inference cost and limiting task efficiency.
Speculative inference [19] provides a promising solution for accelerating flow-matching-based WAMs. It achieves this by generating draft denoising trajectories and leveraging parallel verification to advance multiple denoising steps in a single round, reducing inference latency while maintaining outputs close to those of the target model.

Existing speculative inference methods for embodied policies [42, 54, 55, 41, 37] rely on lightweight draft models trained for specific tasks, which must be retrained whenever the robot or task changes, introducing additional training overhead.
In parallel, recent work on image and video generation exploits velocity smoothness in flow matching by reusing a previously computed velocity as an anchor to approximate subsequent ones [1, 40].
This allows us to construct readily available drafts for speculative inference without additional training.
However, as shown in Fig. 2, we revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and uncover a previously overlooked dual nonuniformity that breaks the smoothness assumption underlying prior velocity reuse.
First, velocity smoothness is nonuniform along WAM denoising trajectories, with pronounced changes between adjacent velocities at the beginning and end of denoising.
Second, nonuniform integration time steps translate comparable velocity residuals into different local state errors, which accumulate and propagate to the final action distribution.
These observations make it necessary for us to fundamentally rethink and naturally reshape two key questions in WAM’s speculative inference:

1.

When to Draft: Which velocities in WAMs can serve as reliable anchors for reuse?

2.

How to Verify: What factors affect the final action distribution error induced by velocity reuse in WAMs?

To answer these questions, we formulate speculative inference as a trajectory error tolerance problem. Concretely, we bound the discrepancy between speculative outputs and reference Euler outputs using a weighted sum of anchor velocity reuse residuals. Our analysis shows that unreliable anchors introduce larger velocity residuals, increasing the error bound as these residuals propagate through subsequent nonuniform integration steps and affect the final action distribution. Based on this analysis, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to this dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It is built on two mechanisms: First, we perform Reliable Anchor Velocity Selection by deferring drafting until after the first Euler update. Second, we design a Time-Step-Aware Verification rule based on the quadratic relationship between squared velocity residuals and integration time step size, tightening verification for larger steps and relaxing it for smaller ones while providing a trajectory error tolerance guarantee.

We seamlessly integrate WAMotor into three representative WAMs, Joint-WAM [49] (a controlled implementation representing Joint-WAMs [52, 48, 45]), Fast-WAM [49] and Faster-WAM [52], replacing their standard flow matching denoising pipelines. Comprehensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate that our method achieves greater speedups with near-lossless task performance relative to vanilla models, outperforming cache-based and other speculative inference baselines. Our experiments show that WAMotor accelerates flow matching inference by 3.24×\times–6.62×\times, yielding overall speedups of 2.86×\times–4.28×\times over vanilla models. Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

In this paper, we revisit WAM denoising dynamics and uncover a previously overlooked dual nonuniformity in velocity smoothness and integration time steps.

In this paper, we revisit WAM denoising dynamics and uncover a previously overlooked dual nonuniformity in velocity smoothness and integration time steps.

We propose WAMotor, a training-free speculative inference method combining reliable anchor selection with time-step-aware verification. It achieves 2.86×\times–4.28×\times end-to-end speedups across three WAMs while maintaining comparable task success rates.

We further derive trajectory error bounds linking velocity-reuse residuals and integration time steps to final action distribution error. This analysis provides a principled foundation for future WAM acceleration, paving the way for more efficient and reliable embodied control.

2. We propose WAMotor, a training-free speculative inference method combining reliable anchor selection with time-step-aware verification. It achieves 2.86×\times–4.28×\times end-to-end speedups across three WAMs while maintaining comparable task success rates.

title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
authors: Chengyang Dong,Ze Chen,Kai Ye,Chutian Wang,Heng Xu,Wei Mo,Maomao Li,Jiayan Xu,Jiayuan Wu,Yihao Xiao,Linhua Ye,Zhonghua Peng,Ruize Han,Jialong Sun
abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
introduction:
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into effective actions across a wide range of robotic manipulation and embodied control tasks [17, 3, 5, 4, 21, 7]. In dynamic environments, agents must reason over long spatiotemporal horizons and adapt their actions as conditions change. Most VLA models rely on large-scale offline pretraining [13, 23, 29, 16, 22]. They perform well on in-distribution tasks but struggle in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, where they encounter tasks and environmental variations that pretraining data rarely cover [3, 13, 36].

Test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a way for VLA models to respond to distribution shifts during deployment [33, 1, 30, 24]. As a robot acts, incoming visual observations and the resulting environmental feedback provide supervision without expert action labels [14]. These signals can help the model adapt its perceptual representations and action decisions while retaining knowledge acquired during pretraining. On-device fine-tuning with first-order (FO) optimization remains difficult because the memory and compute demands of backpropagation (BP) can exceed the resources available on robotic platforms, particularly those that use low-bit quantized weights for inference [9, 27].

Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization reduces the memory cost of TTA by estimating gradients from forward evaluations under perturbations [2, 38, 41, 42]. MeZO uses this approach to fine-tune large language models with near-inference memory usage and achieves performance comparable to first-order fine-tuning on several downstream tasks [27]. Dust, a state-of-the-art ZO optimizer, uses activation-space perturbations and parallel evaluations to match or exceed the performance of backpropagation at large perturbation population sizes [8]. In our preliminary VLA-TTA experiment (Figure 1), Dust quickly approaches AdamW’s task success rate [19, 26]. After 6,000 steps, Dust’s success rate plateaus and then drops substantially, eventually reaching a level comparable to that of SignSGD. We refer to this pattern of stagnation followed by decline during long-horizon ZO adaptation as the performance plateau problem.

The performance plateau problem motivates Dune (Dust Using Nodewise Error-feedback), a memory-efficient ZO optimizer that uses regression over historical statistics to recover reliable update directions when perturbation noise overwhelms the dominant error signal. At each step, Dune constructs regression features from model output residuals and time buckets that encode the stage of adaptation. It uses historical statistics with decaying weights to predict layerwise error signals from these features. Dune then forms a weighted combination of these predictions and the current ZO perturbation observations to preserve the dominant direction of the error signal and suppress high-frequency perturbation noise. Finally, it updates the historical statistics with the raw perturbation observations from the current batch, allowing the regression to track changes as adaptation proceeds. This mechanism stabilizes long-horizon VLA-TTA while retaining the memory efficiency of ZO optimization. Our paper mainly makes the following contributions:

Dune Paradigm. To overcome performance plateaus in VLA-TTA, Dune predicts layer-wise error signals via online ridge regression over output residuals and flow-matching time buckets, fusing them with current perturbation observations for stable updates without backpropagation or extra forward passes.

Performance Plateau Theory. Under Gaussian perturbation and convex quadratic objectives, we establish a loss recursion showing how estimation variance limits convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, theoretically motivating historical error regression.

Extensive Experiments. Across LIBERO benchmarks and real-world robots, Dune substantially boosts long-horizon task success rates with a significantly reduced memory footprint, while ablations confirm improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

1. Dune Paradigm. To overcome performance plateaus in VLA-TTA, Dune predicts layer-wise error signals via online ridge regression over output residuals and flow-matching time buckets, fusing them with current perturbation observations for stable updates without backpropagation or extra forward passes.

title: RefreshGrad: An Online Adaptive Data-sampling Method for Diffusion-based Visuomotor Learning
authors: Dijia Zhan,Jinyi Li,Xuemiao Xu,Yan Zhou,Yu Liu,Shaoshan Liu,Jie Tang
abstract: Training vision–language–action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window’s value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.
introduction:
Adapting visuomotor and vision–language–action (VLA) policies to downstream manipulation tasks relies heavily on demonstration supervision [2, 14, 3]. However, a fundamental yet under-appreciated property of demonstration datasets is the severe disparity in data value across temporal windows. Across episodes, demonstrations inevitably mix clean executions with visual corruptions—such as dim lighting, sensor blur, and background texture shifts—as well as demonstrator inconsistency. Even within a single successful episode, temporal segments vary sharply in supervision utility: repetitive free-space reaching motions offer diminishing returns once mastered, fine contact and articulation transitions demand concentrated optimization, and hesitant or occluded intervals can induce conflicting parameter updates. Treating all segments equally under uniform sampling wastes optimization budget on redundant motions while allowing corrupted or inconsistent windows to degrade policy learning.

Our analysis shows that training value is both window-dependent and policy-dependent: windows within the same episode contribute unequally (Fig. 1(a)), and per-window signals that are stable between adjacent refreshes decorrelate steadily as training proceeds, under both RefreshGrad and uniform sampling (Sec. B.2). A fixed assessment of data quality therefore cannot fully capture a window’s current learning value. A clean but already-mastered window may offer limited additional supervision, whereas an imperfect window may still contain learnable transitions. This observation motivates adapting exposure to the evolving learner, beyond static offline selection [23, 5]. Since high loss can also reflect corruption or inconsistent actions, this adaptation requires feedback about both learning progress and prediction consistency.

Motivated by this insight, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that repeatedly estimates window utility from the current policy and reallocates training exposure accordingly (Fig. 1(b)). Following a uniform warmup, RefreshGrad scores windows using learning progress, cross-episode gradient agreement, temporal prediction consistency, residual disagreement, and photometric sensitivity under deterministic diffusion probes. These complementary signals distinguish actively learnable windows from redundant or unreliable supervision. Robust normalization and temporal smoothing yield comparable, stable utilities, which a rank-based sampler combines with a uniform coverage floor to update anchor sampling probabilities. Alternating scoring with policy updates allows exposure to track changing window value while preserving nonzero support for every valid segment. The procedure requires no external scorer or rollouts and leaves the policy architecture, per-sample loss, and inference pipeline unchanged.

We instantiate RefreshGrad on an action-chunking Diffusion Policy backbone [3] and evaluate it across ten LIBERO-Plus tasks. As summarized in Fig. 1(c), RefreshGrad improves perturbed success over Uniform on all ten tasks, raising the average from 60.7% to 76.1%. It also exceeds the 68.2% achieved by FAKTUAL [23] and improves clean success from 57.4% to 81.3%, supporting the effectiveness of online adaptive window allocation.

Our contributions are threefold:

Characterization of demonstration data value. We reveal that temporal-window value is non-uniform and evolves with the learner, and identify its principal sources as learning progress, cross-episode gradient agreement, temporal prediction consistency, residual disagreement, and photometric sensitivity. This provides a policy-native account of why different windows contribute unequally.

Data-value-driven online window allocation. We introduce RefreshGrad to periodically estimate these value cues from the current policy and adapt training exposure through rank-based sampling with a uniform coverage floor, without environment rollouts or inference overhead.

Empirical and mechanistic validation. We evaluate RefreshGrad across ten LIBERO-Plus tasks and show gains in both perturbed and clean success. Training-trace diagnostics, sampler controls, and signal ablations support multi-cue valuation and periodic online adaptation.

1. Characterization of demonstration data value. We reveal that temporal-window value is non-uniform and evolves with the learner, and identify its principal sources as learning progress, cross-episode gradient agreement, temporal prediction consistency, residual disagreement, and photometric sensitivity. This provides a policy-native account of why different windows contribute unequally.

2. Data-value-driven online window allocation. We introduce RefreshGrad to periodically estimate these value cues from the current policy and adapt training exposure through rank-based sampling with a uniform coverage floor, without environment rollouts or inference overhead.

3. Empirical and mechanistic validation. We evaluate RefreshGrad across ten LIBERO-Plus tasks and show gains in both perturbed and clean success. Training-trace diagnostics, sampler controls, and signal ablations support multi-cue valuation and periodic online adaptation.

title: Differentiable Hydrodynamics for Whole-Body MPC of Underwater Robots
authors: Hefan Wang,Yvan Petillot,Carlos Mastalli
abstract: Underwater vehicle–manipulator systems distribute actuation across thrusters and joint motors. Whole-body model predictive control (MPC), rather than separate vehicle and arm controllers, can coordinate both to extend the workspace and exploit the system’s full kinematic capability. Doing so, however, requires a hydrodynamic model and derivatives throughout the prediction horizon. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) captures geometry-dependent forces and moments for such a model, but is too expensive to evaluate online. We present a differentiable analytical hydrodynamic model combining smooth spherical-harmonic force and moment fields with a coupled added-inertia matrix identified from CFD. It compactly represents velocity and acceleration-dependent loads and provides their derivatives in closed form. These derivatives are propagated through free-floating vehicle–manipulator dynamics for whole-body trajectory optimization and receding-horizon control, jointly optimizing thruster forces and joint torques for reaching and continuous tracking. Held-out CFD tests validate the principal translational-force and rotational-moment fields and the added-inertia response. The analytical Jacobians evaluate faster and avoid the step-size sensitivity of central finite differences. Closed-loop Stonefish experiments demonstrate whole-body MPC in an independent marine simulator. By making geometry-dependent hydrodynamics directly available to gradient-based control, the model incorporates water forces and their sensitivities into motion allocation between the vehicle and arm, rather than treating them only as disturbances.
introduction:
Underwater vehicle–manipulator systems (UVMS) combine vehicle thrusters and manipulator actuators within a strongly coupled floating-base system. Manipulator motion induces vehicle reactions, while vehicle motion reshapes the reachable workspace and end-effector dynamics, with these interactions becoming particularly pronounced in lightweight platforms with comparable vehicle and manipulator inertial scales [1, 2]. Conventional decoupled control architectures regulate the vehicle and manipulator separately [3, 4]. This is effective when base motion must be suppressed but limits their coordinated use to extend reach, redistribute control effort, or anticipate subsequent maneuvers.

Whole-body model predictive control (MPC) addresses this limitation by optimizing thruster forces and joint torques over the same horizon, following the joint treatment of floating-base and joint dynamics demonstrated in legged robots [5, 6]. The vehicle can move to enlarge the reachable workspace, while the arm can be positioned consistently with vehicle momentum and actuator limits. Marine MPC has been applied to trajectory tracking and predictive rejection of wave disturbances [7, 8]. For gradient-based whole-body MPC, every prediction node requires the dynamics and their derivatives, including the water forces and moments that govern acceleration, braking, and turning.

Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) can resolve the geometry-dependent hydrodynamic forces and moments of open-frame vehicles across different directions of translational and rotational motion [9]. Its computational cost, however, precludes direct evaluation within an MPC loop. Conventional linear or diagonal quadratic damping models provide an efficient alternative [10]. Diagonal models distinguish resistance along the principal axes but restrict angular variation and omit cross-component coupling. A richer directional representation lets the whole-body optimizer predict how changes in vehicle motion alter the hydrodynamic wrench during planning.

We bridge this gap with a compact model identified from steady and oscillatory CFD. Spherical harmonics represent velocity-dependent forces and moments, while a symmetric added-inertia matrix describes the acceleration of the surrounding water. The model provides closed-form derivatives through the free-floating vehicle–manipulator dynamics. The resulting action model allows the optimizer to decide how vehicle motion, arm motion, directional resistance, and fluid inertia should be combined in a whole-body maneuver.

This work introduces a differentiable hydrodynamics approach for whole-body MPC of underwater robots (see Fig. 1). It relies on three contributions: (i) a compact model of CFD forces and moments with positive directional resistance and positive-definite coupled added inertia; (ii) closed-form hydrodynamic derivatives propagated through free-floating multibody dynamics; and (iii) whole-body trajectory-optimization and MPC experiments in which thrusters and manipulator motors are optimized together, including evaluation in an independently implemented Stonefish plant.

title: Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies: Spatializing Latent Action Representations for Goal-Pose-Free Mobile Manipulation
authors: Siyuan Zheng,Zhong Cao,Henry X. Liu
abstract: The success of manipulation policies is closely tied to the spatial relationship between the robot and the target object, as well as the task being performed, making the ability to adjust the robot’s pose critical for successful execution. When the robot starts away from the task, such adjustments require coordinating navigation with local manipulation. Jointly training these capabilities incurs substantial computational and data costs, while navigating toward a predefined goal pose limits the flexibility needed to adapt to task-specific manipulation requirements. To address these challenges, we propose Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies (M4M), a framework that learns manipulation-aware mobility directly from pretrained manipulation policies. By leveraging the hidden representations of the policy’s action-generating network as dense supervision, together with a limited number of manipulation execution outcomes, we learn a spatially conditioned embedding that captures task-dependent manipulation success across candidate robot poses. From the robot’s current stereo observations, this representation estimates manipulation success at unvisited poses without rolling out the manipulation policy at each location. It is further integrated into navigation policy training, while a learned handoff policy decides when to transition from navigation to manipulation, enabling the robot to move and manipulate in a unified, task-aware manner. Across eight articulated-object tasks in unseen RoboCasa kitchens, M4M achieves 47.0% mean task success, compared with 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation execution, and refrigerator-closing experiments show consistent improvements across four frozen manipulation policies.
introduction:
A robot that can close a refrigerator from a favorable pose may still fail when it starts farther away. It must approach the appliance, avoid obstacles, and establish a distance and viewpoint from which its manipulation policy can complete the interaction. The handle may otherwise appear in an unfamiliar part of the image, or the base may leave insufficient space for the door’s motion. Extending learned manipulation skills to mobile robots therefore requires coordinating the approach with the conditions under which those skills succeed [42, 6].

Learning navigation and manipulation together from demonstrations requires data covering both behaviors and their coordination [42]. Reusing an existing manipulation policy reduces what must be relearned, but leaves a central question: how should the robot move, and when should it hand off, before it has visited the candidate stances? Geometric reachability and target proximity do not fully capture a learned policy’s preferences [6]. Figure 3 illustrates this dependence: four manipulation policies evaluated at the same refrigerator poses exhibit different success landscapes.

We introduce M4M, which learns both decisions from policy-derived success supervision. The policy’s latent action representations at candidate stances are spatialized into a success field that a student predicts from the current view, so the robot can score stances before reaching them. A compact controller reads this field, together with the target and traversability maps, and decides at every step whether to keep moving or hand off, without committing to a target base pose. Goal-pose-free refers to this execution interface: candidate stances are scored, but no fixed navigation endpoint is selected.

Executing the manipulation policy at every training candidate is expensive. Instead, candidate-view action representations supply dense supervision, linked to success by limited execution outcomes. Cross-view distillation transfers this information to the current observation; privileged value iteration supervises movement and handoff. Deployment requires neither candidate-view rendering nor action-expert queries at candidate stances. Figure 1 shows local approach and handoff in unseen kitchens, evaluated at 0.5–2.5 m starts.

Our contributions are: (i) spatializing a frozen policy’s latent action representations into a success field over unvisited stances; (ii) distilling policy-derived movement and handoff values into a controller that uses this field without explicit goal-pose selection; and (iii) evaluation on eight tasks in unseen kitchens, four-policy refrigerator experiments, ablations, representation comparisons, and a shared-budget study.

title: MoRE: Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Physics Robotic World Models
authors: Ziyu Zhu,Shaowei Liu,Albert J. Zhai,Henry Che,Wei-Chiu Ma,Shenlong Wang
abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at MoRE-WM-site.
introduction:
Robots that operate intelligently in the physical world should be able to predict how the environment evolves under their actions. Such an ability is fundamental for planning, control, and long-horizon decision making [71, 74, 25, 20, 46, 19, 62], and is especially crucial in contact-rich real-world manipulation [54, 60, 37, 67, 66]. For instance, a house-cleaning robot must anticipate how cloth moves when wiping a surface, while a cooking robot must predict how ingredients deform under tool interactions.

Building such a dynamics model is challenging because real-world manipulation involves heterogeneous physical behaviors, complex contacts, and diverse interaction mechanisms. To capture these effects, a robotic world model must be accurate, physically plausible, 3D-aware, and grounded in robot-object interactions. It should generalize across physical regimes, from rigid objects to deformable materials, and across manipulation modes, including prehensile grasping and non-prehensile interactions with rigid or soft tools. In short, we need models that are geometry-grounded, multi-physics, multi-tool, and contact-rich.

Unfortunately, existing approaches address only parts of this problem. Physics-based methods [28, 63, 15] leverage differentiable simulators and can support long-horizon rollouts, but they often require heavy system identification and expensive optimization. In contrast, learning-based dynamics models [69, 10, 34, 36, 42, 64, 5, 52, 55, 67] avoid explicit system identification by learning dynamics directly from data, yet most are designed for a specific material type, tool, or task, limiting their ability to generalize across heterogeneous manipulation regimes. More recent generative world models [19, 22, 74, 39] offer greater scalability and broader scene coverage, but they are primarily optimized for visual prediction and often lack the accurate 3D structure and action grounding needed for real robotic execution. This leaves a gap between scalable prediction models and the physically grounded, controllable dynamics required for robot manipulation.

We aim to close this gap with MoRE, a scalable robotic world model that predicts future 3D point trajectories from a short history of object-tool interaction and the current robot action. Our key insight is that scaling alone is insufficient: to generalize across diverse robotic dynamics, scaling must be paired with a physics-informed mixture of motion experts. On the data side, we scale across simulation and real-world settings, covering diverse object geometries, materials, contact patterns, tasks, and tools. On the model side, we avoid forcing all dynamics into a single monolithic predictor. Instead, inspired by interaction-centric dynamics modeling [5, 34, 66, 67, 51] and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures [53, 16], MoRE decomposes robotic dynamics into specialized motion experts aligned with physical regimes and interaction types, such as rigid/non-rigid and prehensile/non-prehensile. These experts share a common encoder for scalable representation learning, while each expert incorporates regime-specific inductive biases and constraints, such as rigidity preservation. A learned gating module routes each interaction to the appropriate expert based on short motion history, allowing the model to infer material properties and interaction modes directly from observation.

We evaluate MoRE in both simulation and real-world manipulation, covering pushing and grasping with rigid and deformable objects. Trained on a large-scale interaction dataset, our model runs at 20 FPS for model inference and integrates naturally with tuning-free MPC for closed-loop control. Across dynamics benchmarks and real robot tasks, MoRE consistently outperforms prior methods.

In summary, we make three contributions. First, we introduce MoRE, a 3D robotic world model for contact-rich dynamics prediction. Second, we design MoRE around a Mixture-of-Motion Experts architecture that explicitly captures heterogeneous physical regimes and interaction types. Third, we demonstrate that MoRE enables accurate real-time prediction and effective closed-loop control across both simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.

title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
authors: Gustavo Rezende Silva,Tobias John,Francisco Martín,EinarR Broch Johnsen
abstract: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.
introduction:
Autonomous robots are required to operate reliably in increasingly complex environments and to perform a larger number of tasks with distinct functional and quality requirements, potentially requiring different architectural configurations to satisfy them. A key challenge in designing such systems is ensuring that the robot continues to meet its requirements throughout mission execution, particularly under uncertainty, such as sensor failures or environmental disturbances (Correll et al., 2017; Krotkov et al., 2018). For example, an underwater robot might require different sensor configurations depending on the water visibility, or it might need to navigate through different paths depending on water currents. Addressing these challenges requires coordinating task execution and architectural adaptation while accounting for their interdependencies.

Task and architecture co-adaptation (TACA) (Cámara et al., 2020) addresses the interdependencies between task execution and architectural adaptation. Reactive TACA approaches such as ROSA (Rezende Silva et al., 2025) select a configuration for each action only when that action begins executing, without accounting for how the choice constrains the rest of the mission. However, selecting a suitable configuration for the current action alone does not establish whether subsequent actions can be performed under the conditions anticipated along the mission. Considering these dependencies during mission planning allows configuration requirements to influence the task plan before execution begins, so that each configuration choice is made with its downstream task consequences in view. To the best of our knowledge, the approach by Cámara et al. (Cámara et al., 2020) is the only approach that jointly plans task actions and reconfiguration actions and produces a complete plan ahead of execution. Their approach, however, requires substantial planning time and memory and relies on domain models expressed across multiple specification languages with manually developed integration code, increasing modeling effort and the potential for errors. Furthermore, their approach requires modeling probabilities to enable optimal planning, although these probabilities can be difficult to estimate accurately.

To address these limitations, this paper proposes PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach that formulates task and architecture co-adaptation as a single planning problem by automatically integrating task and architectural knowledge. PLANTA uses a Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontology (Aguado et al., 2024) to represent the functional requirements of robot actions, the architectural alternatives that realize those requirements, and the quality attributes and requirements used to assess the applicability and utility of each alternative. The Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) (Karpas and Magazzeni, 2020) describes task actions, the current system state, and mission goals. Architectural knowledge is automatically translated into PDDL and integrated with the task model, allowing task actions and architectural reconfiguration actions to be considered within the same search space. This integration preserves a separation between task modeling and architectural knowledge modeling. The resulting problem can be solved by standard PDDL planners. To support timely runtime adaptation, PLANTA favors satisficing planning over guaranteed mission-level optimality. Rather than explicitly modeling uncertainty and its probabilities, it plans from the currently observed state and handles changes during execution through replanning when monitored conditions invalidate the current plan. By relying on two established modeling languages and automating their integration, PLANTA aims to reduce modeling effort.

Figure 1 depicts the PLANTA framework across design time, deployment time, and runtime. At design time, the system architecture is modeled using the PDDL-TOMASys ontology, and the task problem is modeled in PDDL. At deployment time, Owl2PDDL translates the ontology into PDDL, combines it with the planning problem, and incorporates their mutual dependencies, i.e., TACA concerns. At runtime, the planning system, based on PlanSys2, jointly plans and executes task and reconfiguration actions. PDDL-TOMASys builds upon the Teleological and Ontological Metamodel for Autonomous Systems (TOMASys) (Aguado et al., 2021; Corbato, 2013) and draws inspiration from the ROSA model (Rezende Silva et al., 2025).

PLANTA is evaluated with respect to feasibility, performance efficiency, and scalability on two use cases: an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) scenario from the SUAVE exemplar (Rezende Silva et al., 2023), and an autonomous ground vehicle (AGV) scenario adapted from (Cámara et al., 2020). These dimensions are formulated as research questions RQ1–RQ3 in Section 8.
Feasibility (RQ1) is addressed by implementing PLANTA and integrating it with PlanSys2, an existing planning system for robotics. This required extending PlanSys2 with derived predicates and existential preconditions (Edelkamp and Hoffmann, 2004), PDDL constructs that the models generated by Owl2PDDL rely on.
The results of running PLANTA on the ROS 2-based SUAVE exemplar support the feasibility of applying it to robotic systems.
Performance efficiency (RQ2) is assessed on the AGV use case, where PLANTA is, at the median, 3.003.00 times faster than the approach by Cámara et al. (Cámara et al., 2020) and its peak memory usage is 6.846.84 times smaller, while both approaches produce plans with near-identical path length and estimated remaining battery at the end of the mission.
In the AGV use case, scalability (RQ3) is assessed by varying the map size, the number of architectural configurations, the number of quality requirements, and the number of mission-level PDDL action schemas, independently and in combination. The results show that satisficing planning remains tractable in scenarios where optimal planning becomes impractical, supporting the use of PLANTA in robotic applications that require online task-level replanning.

The main contributions of this paper are:

an ontology-mediated planning approach for mission-wide task and architecture co-adaptation that combines task and reconfiguration actions in a single PDDL formulation and supports satisficing planning with runtime replanning.

an open-source implementation of the proposed approach, designed for integration with ROS 2-based robotic systems, including an extension of the PlanSys2 framework to support derived predicates and existential preconditions in PDDL.

a systematic evaluation of the proposed approach, including a comparison with the state-of-the-art approach by Cámara et al. (Cámara et al., 2020) and a scalability analysis that demonstrates the feasibility of satisficing planning in regimes where optimal planning becomes impractical.

title: WEVO: World Model-Enabled VLA Optimization for Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
authors: Qianzhong Chen,Muyuan Lin,Yuyin Sun,Mac Schwager,Cheng-Hao Kuo,Roberto Martín-Martín
abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 2020 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3%23.3\% to 75.0%75.0\%, compared with 48.3%48.3\% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement.
Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] couple pretrained vision-language backbones with action heads learned from demonstrations, whose scale and quality strongly determine performance. Collecting such demonstrations through teleoperation is particularly difficult for high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) humanoids. Whole-body controllers (WBCs) [6, 7] coordinate balance, locomotion, and bimanual control but do not remove this data bottleneck. Real-to-sim-to-real (R2S2R) systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [8, 9, 10] instead reconstruct deployment scenes and generate whole-body trajectories without teleoperation. Policies trained on these synthetic demonstrations can transfer to hardware, but residual appearance and dynamics gaps still require learning from deployment experience.

Reinforcement learning can improve a behavior-cloned (BC) policy under compounding errors and residual sim-to-real mismatch, but VLA post-training requires long-horizon rewards and optimization through diffusion or flow action heads. Offline-to-online methods often update simple MLP policies [11, 12, 13], limiting expressiveness through their tractable action densities. Advantage-weighted methods support richer policies [14, 15, 16, 17], but often require human DAgger interventions. RL-100 [18] differentiates the PPO objective [19] through the full denoising process at high computational cost. Steering [20], residual methods [21, 22], and DICE-RL [23] adapt pretrained policy outputs more directly. Nevertheless, these approaches rely on continued real robot interaction or fixed offline data, neither of which supports exploratory whole-body humanoid learning.

Learned world models (WMs) shift policy optimization away from hardware by predicting future observations under candidate actions. Existing systems use either compact dynamics representations or generative video models. Latent dynamics models and explicit 3D digital twins [24, 25, 26, 27] enable sample-efficient learning, but are usually scene-specific and do not provide the open-world visual inputs required by VLAs. Generative video WMs instead adapt large pretrained models to robot actions. VLAW [28] treats successful WM rollouts as behavior-cloning targets, while WMPO [29] and related methods optimize policies on generated trajectories [30, 31, 32, 33]. WoVR [34], WorldSample [35], and PlayWorld [36] improve rollout initialization, transition selection, and autonomous data collection, respectively. However, these methods remain limited to fixed-base tabletop manipulation and use human teleoperation data during training.

These limitations raise a central question: how should scalable synthetic data and limited autonomous policy rollouts be combined for whole-body humanoid VLA post-training without teleoperation? WEVO uses simulation to train the initial VLA and broaden the WM’s dynamics coverage. Autonomous real robot rollouts then close the remaining visual sim-to-real gap in its predictions, after which the video WM serves as the policy-improvement environment. This forms the flywheel shown in Fig. 2. Our contributions are:

We build WEVO, to our knowledge the first WM-RL system for whole-body humanoid VLAs beyond fixed-base tabletop manipulation, coupling egocentric video generation with whole-body dynamics and dense progress rewards.

We develop autonomous whole-body play data for WM mid-training: manipulation play improves contact-dynamics prediction, while locomotion play improves consistency under large egocentric viewpoint changes.

We study how photorealistic simulation and a video WM can form a teleoperation-free policy-improvement flywheel. Experiments on three loco-manipulation tasks show that simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM provides a more useful environment for policy improvement.

title: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems
authors: Ivan A. Fernandez,Jingdao Chen
abstract:
Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation
to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or
manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an
autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work
presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed
developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of
perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making.
A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located
virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative
IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter,
occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including
sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and
false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn
Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering
trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and
uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost.
The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how
sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and
resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
introduction:
Agentic systems increasingly combine perception, state estimation,
reasoning, and autonomous action to interact with dynamic
environments (Pati, 2025; Sapkota et al., 2025). In
cyber-physical applications, degraded or manipulated sensor
observations can therefore influence downstream autonomous decisions.
This concern is particularly relevant to Counter-Unmanned Aircraft
System (C-UAS) architectures, where detection, tracking,
classification, and sensor fusion may support subsequent decision and
response functions. Recent U.S. defense requirements similarly
emphasize robust C-UAS sensing, tracking, multi-target handling, and
operation under challenging conditions
(U.S. Department of the Army, 2026; U.S. Department of the Air Force, 2026). The operational relevance
of drone and counter-drone technologies has also increased
substantially in recent conflicts (Mittal and Goetz, 2025).

Real-world datasets remain essential for evaluating C-UAS sensing and
tracking; however, they provide limited control over the occurrence,
severity, and repeatability of individual stress conditions.
Standardized C-UAS evaluation efforts have likewise emphasized
scenario-based testing, repeatability, and quantitative performance
metrics (De Cubber et al., 2025). Multi-modal datasets such as
MMAUD provide synchronized camera, LiDAR, radar, and other sensing
data for anti-UAV research (Yuan et al., 2024), while synthetic
datasets such as SynDroneVision demonstrate the value of simulation
for increasing scenario diversity and supplementing real-world data
(Lenhard et al., 2025).

This work develops a lightweight synthetic C-UAS testbed for security
stress testing of perception and tracking components that may feed
agentic decision pipelines. The objective is not to reproduce
high-fidelity aerodynamics or fully calibrated sensor physics.
Instead, the testbed emphasizes repeatable target motion, known ground
truth, configurable scene conditions, and controlled sensing
degradation so that downstream algorithm behavior can be observed
under systematically varied conditions.

title: Verify2Act: Critic-Guided Latent World Models for Verifying Language-Conditioned Manipulation Plans
authors: Chrisantus Eze,Christopher Crick
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3% task success, compared with 61.7% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3% for the VLM alone, and 46.7% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30×\times fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
introduction:
Solving multi-stage manipulation requires both semantic planning and physical verification. Vision-language models (VLMs) are strong at semantic planning  [1, 2, 3], but lack a grounded model of how actions change the scene. Pixel-space or generative world models can provide this foresight  [4, 5, 6, 7], but are computationally expensive and prone to visual drift over long horizons  [8].

Latent visual world models offer a more efficient alternative. DINO-WM [9] and RLA-WM [8] model dynamics in DINOv2 [10] feature space, but neither is designed for language-driven plan verification: DINO-WM searches with CEM, while RLA-WM uses a Markovian architecture without temporal memory, limiting language-conditioned planning, robustness to occlusion, and accumulating background drift over multi-step rollouts.

We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that decouples semantic action proposal from latent physical verification (Fig. 1). The VLM serves only as a semantic heuristic that proposes a small set of candidate plans. These candidates are then imagined by V2A-WM, which builds on the flow-matching cores of DINO-WM and RLA-WM with two changes: (1) cross-attention action grounding between DINOv2 patch features and CLIP [11] tokens, which ties language commands to visual object patches; and (2) a causal temporal history window with validity masks, which preserves visual memory across gripper occlusions. A dual-head critic then scores the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before any action is committed.

We evaluate Verify2Act on a robot arm and in simulation. For the robot, the world model and the critic are trained only on data generated in a digital twin of the workspace, and an optional real2sim input-alignment step carries them over to the real camera. Our contributions are:

Verify2Act, a low-level-policy-agnostic verification layer that decouples semantic action proposal from latent physical simulation.

V2A-WM, a visual feature-based flow-matching world model with cross-attention action grounding and causal temporal history.

A dual-head critic that scores temporal consistency and goal satisfaction for beam-search plan selection.

An evaluation of four verification strategies on a robot arm over six language-conditioned tasks, with models trained only on digital-twin data and with planning errors separated from execution errors, together with simulation results on CALVIN [12] and Robosuite [13].

title: Ferrofluid Shape Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Anthony Czubarow,Antonio Terpin,Raffaello D'Andrea
abstract:
Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control
through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports
their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and
manipulate objects.
Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging.
Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields
from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid
configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the
fluid’s dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes
that may not be sustainable at equilibrium.
Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning to control these transient
shapes. Learning directly through physical interaction, our policies select
current commands for a single fixed electromagnet based on visual observations,
guiding the moving ferrofluid toward prescribed geometries.
The learned policies repeatedly attain a variety of shapes spanning polygons,
asterisks and pentominoes. These results demonstrate that learning directly from
physical interaction enables reliable fluid shaping,
opening new possibilities for controlling ferrofluid-based soft robots.
introduction:
Ferrofluids are liquids that contain magnetic nanoparticles and deform
under applied magnetic fields [1]. Their ability to
stretch, branch and reorganize supports their use in soft
robotics. Ferrofluid robots form structures that capture and transport objects
[2], split and recombine to negotiate confined passages
[3], and exploit wetting to create mobile droplets and
reconfigurable liquid structures [4].
Controlled changes in ferrofluid geometry can
generate locomotion through cycles of elongation and contraction
[5] or through the nonreciprocal strokes of liquid cilia
[4].
These capabilities motivate control of the liquid’s
geometry for soft robotic interactions with the surroundings.
Additional examples are reviewed in Appendix A.

Existing shape-control methods connect magnetic commands to geometric
descriptors or desired contours. Visual feedback regulates elongation and
orientation [6], as well as deformation ratio
[5]; Bayesian optimization also tunes feedback controllers for
three-dimensional position, stretch direction and stretch radius
[7]. For full silhouettes, learned models of water–ferrofluid
interfaces guide the selection of coil currents by predicting the target match
at steady state [8]. Related work shapes
nonmagnetic droplets supported by an air–ferrofluid interface: electromagnet
arrays produce convex, concave and time-varying contours
[9], learned models predict shape sequences and
infer successive actuations [10], and physical
Bayesian optimization selects coil settings for requested outlines
[11]. These studies establish several routes to geometric
control, including configurations maintained under selected magnetic fields.

Fluid motion offers a further source of attainable geometry,
much as learned dynamic maneuvers extend the reach of soft robot arms
[12]. A moving
interface can pass through shapes that it cannot sustain at equilibrium.
In immersed drops, interfacial tension supplies a restoring stress, inertia
sustains motion and viscosity damps the response
[13, 14].
Magnetic actuation influences both how the fluid deforms
and which geometries emerge. Deformation followed by field removal produces
oscillation and relaxation [15], while magnetic preparation
selects spreading patterns [16] and a bottom electromagnet produces
noncircular thin-drop geometries [17].
Prescribed magnetic pulses also drive confined ferrofluid drops
through transient nonelliptical outlines to pump surrounding liquid
[18]. Mechanically excited
ferrofluid puddles exhibit star-shaped modes whose frequencies can be tuned
magnetically [19]. These results motivate using the evolving
fluid response to create chosen silhouettes. The control problem is to select
magnetic commands as the fluid moves so that a prescribed shape appears
along its trajectory, even if only briefly.

Machine learning offers tools for controlling the
nonlinear, time-dependent behavior of soft robots
[20, 21]. Reinforcement learning, in
particular, improves control policies through interaction guided by task
rewards [22]. It has been used to exploit viscous coiling to deposit prescribed curves,
with nozzle motions learned in simulation and executed physically
[23], and to control plasma shape in a tokamak with
policies trained in simulation [24].
Simulation pretraining followed by physical adaptation
enables ultrasound-driven microrobot navigation [25], while
learning directly from camera observations regulates interface position and
droplet size in microfluidic experiments [26].

For ferrofluids, the challenge of modeling coupled
magnetic and fluid dynamics [8] motivates learning directly
from physical interaction, avoiding the need to construct a fluid simulator
and the challenges of sim-to-real transfer.
DreamerV3 supports data-efficient learning by
fitting a world model to collected experience and training a policy through
imagined interaction with that model [27]. Learning through
such models has been demonstrated in simulated visual-control tasks
[28] and directly on physical robots [29],
on a physical labyrinth game [30], and in active-flow-control
experiments [31, 32, 33].

Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning
to exploit the dynamics of ferrofluid immersed in water for prescribed shape
control (Fig. ). We learn a dynamics model from physical
experience and use it to train policies, which select current
commands for a single fixed electromagnet (Figs. 2 and 3).
The same approach to learning
directly on hardware could be explored for ferrofluid locomotion and
manipulation.

Contributions.
We introduce a physical platform
designed to be easy to reproduce and operate, combining a single fixed
electromagnet and visual feedback.
We integrate DreamerV3 [27] with the platform to learn
shape-control policies directly through physical interaction. We formulate
a reward for improvements in the best window-averaged silhouette overlap
and demonstrate its effectiveness for learning transient shape control.
We evaluate transient shape control for 20 silhouettes
spanning polygons, asterisks with three to six rays and pentominoes.
We compare trained and untrained policies in shape accuracy,
attainment frequency and time to attainment, and characterize persistence
near each episode’s peak intersection-over-union (IoU) score.
