title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash
authors: Yuseon Choi,Sanghyeon Park,Eunjong Lee,Hanseo Lee,Sangjin Kim
abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems.
introduction:
Embodied agents have rapidly advanced with the emergence of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) [1, 2, 3], enabling robots to understand complex environments and execute long-horizon tasks. In particular, Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based VLA and WAMs [4] generate actions and future states through iterative denoising and state prediction. However, existing models often struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, as highlighted by VLABench [5] and LIBERO-Plus [6]. Meanwhile, iterative denoising incurs substantial computational overhead and energy consumption. To mitigate these costs, prior studies have explored computation skipping techniques, such as reducing denoising steps [7, 8] and reusing intermediate results [9, 10]. However, these techniques often introduce a trade-off between inference efficiency and task accuracy.

Building on experience-based inference [11, 12], we develop a unified warm-start framework for VLA and WAMs that retrieves successful experiences to initialize iterative denoising. Rather than directly reusing past outputs, warm-started inference adapts retrieved latent states to current observations, improving task success while reducing redundant computation. Unlike conventional computation skipping, this approach introduces a new design opportunity that trades storage capacity for both task accuracy and inference efficiency. As the experience bank grows, the likelihood of retrieving relevant successful experiences increases, improving retrieval hit rates and enabling greater computation skipping. More importantly, even after retrieval hit rates saturate, larger banks provide better-matched latent states that further improve task accuracy.

However, realizing these benefits in edge environments requires a memory architecture capable of efficiently storing and searching large-scale experience banks. While LPDDR provides low access latency, its limited capacity and power budget constrain the retention of continuously growing experiences [13]. NAND flash offers high storage density and low cost per bit, but large-scale similarity-based key searches incur substantial latency and bandwidth overhead from repeated NAND accesses and data movement [14]. Existing Compute-in-Flash (CIF) architectures mitigate data movement by performing search operations within NAND [15, 16], yet their search throughput remains constrained by sensing latency and limited computational parallelism. Furthermore, as robotic agents continuously accumulate new experiences, efficient physical organization becomes essential to maintaining search parallelism and minimizing unnecessary key accesses.

In this work, we propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. By directly integrating CMOS logic with NAND arrays, CBA enables high-bandwidth internal data access and in-flash computation, reducing search-related data movement. FlashX leverages low-latency pSLC regions for parallel key search, supported by interleaved CIF engines on the CBA CMOS die, while retaining dense TLC regions for latent value storage. Furthermore, FlashX introduces proprioception-aware experience clustering to reduce the search space through selective key retrieval. Online experience placement further eliminates the overhead of frequent global reclustering while maintaining efficient experience organization. Together, these techniques enable capacity-scalable experience reuse, improving task accuracy and inference efficiency under edge memory and power constraints.

title: Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation
authors: Junghoon Seo,Hakjin Lee,Jaehoon Sim
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen
instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware
reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible
surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their
distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSE-Pose, which
derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations.
We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those
inside a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is
consistent across camera frames and metric
scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope
conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance
selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive
keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and
HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at
both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and
viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across
benchmarks.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation requires a stable object-centered reference frame for
reasoning about grasps, placements, contacts, and tool motion. Instance-level
pose estimation obtains this frame by aligning an observation to a known object
model [1, 2]. Category-level 6D pose estimation addresses a
broader setting by predicting rotation, translation, and metric size for an
unseen instance of a known category in a shared canonical
frame [3, 4, 5]. A successful estimator
must establish the same semantic axes across substantial variation in shape,
appearance, viewpoint, and visibility. This capability allows a robot to
transfer an interaction strategy to a novel mug, bottle, or tool without first
acquiring its exact geometry.

Category-level pose estimation is both a geometric estimation problem and a
representation learning problem. An RGB-D crop records the object surface
visible from one viewpoint and can include points from supporting surfaces
or the background. Organizing the visible geometry in a category-consistent
frame helps relate corresponding parts across instances. Adaptive 3D
keypoints provide an effective interface for this
purpose [6, 7, 8, 9], aggregating dense observations
into a compact, instance-conditioned structure that supports
correspondence-based reasoning across intra-category shape variation.

Object-aware reconstruction provides complementary supervision by encouraging
this intermediate representation to retain the measured structure from which
pose is inferred, and its target determines which points in the RGB-D crop are
treated as object evidence. A registered instance mesh provides a precise
reference for selecting points near the object surface. Standard annotations
also describe where to select points for reconstruction. Pose defines the
canonical frame, and metric size gives the extent along each axis.

We use these annotations to construct a pose-and-size envelope. Each
observed 3D point is mapped to normalized object coordinates using the
annotated pose and size, and it contributes to reconstruction when it lies
inside the annotated extent after each face is dilated by an object-normalized
tolerance. The support follows the orientation and
anisotropic extent of the instance, and canonicalization gives the tolerance a
consistent meaning across camera frames, categories, and metric scales. When
the annotated extent bounds the object
surface, the dilated envelope contains every point a surface-distance
criterion selects, extending support to nearby measurements around concavities
and interiors.

MORSE-Pose, short for Mesh-free Object-aware Reconstruction via
pose-and-Size Envelopes, integrates this supervision with an adaptive RGB-D
keypoint estimator in which multi-level visual features, geometric evidence,
and learnable category prototypes shape keypoints that support correspondence
prediction, pose and size estimation, and observed-surface reconstruction,
while inference uses only the RGB-D crop and category
label. Our evaluation connects the supervision geometry to
the final task through point-level audits, matched target substitutions,
robustness and cross-view studies, ablations, and efficiency comparisons.
At the 10∘​5​cm10^{\circ}5\,\mathrm{cm} threshold in Fig. 1,
MORSE-Pose reaches 88.888.8 AP on REAL275 and 63.263.2 AP on HouseCat6D.

Our contributions are threefold: a pose-and-size envelope with containment and
invariance properties that derives object-aware reconstruction support
directly from category-level pose and metric-size annotations, its integration
with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learned category
context in a unified estimator, and an evaluation connecting selector geometry
to task behavior and strong pose accuracy on REAL275 and HouseCat6D.

title: TuringPAI: A Foundation for On-Device Physical AI
authors: Qiman Wu,Hanlin Chen,Yuhua Wei,Mingyuan Wang,Shaman Tang,Minghao Li,Rui Xin,Xingye Liu,Zhichao Yang,Yiqi Yu,Hongyan Pei,Xiaowen Tian,YingYing Liu,Shiwen Liu,Jiahui Hu,Yizhao Wang,Yuheng Zhang,Anhua Liu,Yue He,Shuang Su,Da Zhu,Hua Zhou,Pengfei Diao,Haojie Yang,Weichao Huang,Hang Zhang,Honggou Yang,Xianming Liu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12 Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.
introduction:
Physical AI systems must understand changing environments and translate observations into decisions and actions under real-world computational and latency constraints Shukor et al. (2025); Black et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026). Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a reusable foundation by connecting visual perception with language instructions and reasoning Liu et al. (2023a); Wang et al. (2024a); Bai et al. (2025). Autonomous driving, a mature and practically important application of Physical AI, serves as a major setting for developing and evaluating such models Foundation Model Team and XPeng Inc. (2026); Tian et al. (2024). It requires spatial understanding, reasoning over observations across cameras and time, and timely responses within limited onboard resources. Robotic manipulation presents complementary demands on object geometry, interaction state, and instruction following Black et al. (2024).

Visual inputs in Physical AI applications often consist of high-resolution observations collected across multiple cameras and time steps Caesar et al. (2020); Khazatsky et al. (2024).
These observations contain substantial redundancy, yet local geometry and small temporal changes can affect downstream actions.
VLM pipelines that encode each observation as a dense patch sequence can spend substantial computation on spatially correlated content Bolya et al. (2023); Shang et al. (2025).
Forwarding separate visual sequences for successive frames further expands the language-model context with overlapping scene information Huang et al. (2025); Shen et al. (2025).
Under limited onboard compute and strict latency constraints, this redundancy increases the cost of using rich observation histories.
These requirements motivate VLM designs that aggregate local evidence before global modeling and integrate complementary information across spatial scales and time, while retaining the cues needed for downstream action.

Architecture alone, however, does not ensure that a VLM learns the physical information required by these tasks.
General image–text alignment and instruction learning support broad semantic understanding, but do not necessarily provide explicit supervision for metric geometry or temporal changes.
For example, a caption may identify a vehicle ahead without specifying its distance or whether the gap is closing, although both quantities matter for driving decisions.
Prior work shows that explicit spatial and temporal training tasks can strengthen the corresponding capabilities of VLMs Chen et al. (2024a); Ren et al. (2024).
Architecture and training data thus play complementary roles:
the architecture organizes observations efficiently, while the data guide the learning of information relevant to physical interaction.

To address these challenges, we present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI built around a shared vision-language foundation.
At its core, TuringPAI-VL combines HybridViT-MLQ with a training mixture tailored to Physical AI.
TuringPAI-VL provides the pretrained foundation for TuringPAI-Drive and TuringPAI-Embodied, which adapt it to autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, respectively.

HybridViT-MLQ organizes local features, scene context, and observation history into a multi-scale representation of the current observation.
HybridViT first uses a convolutional front end to form locally condensed patch tokens, over which the visual Transformer models global relationships.
We then introduce Multi-scale Latent Queries (MLQ), a hierarchy of feature-conditioned queries that aggregates visual evidence within the same Transformer.
The queries occupy spatial grids at multiple resolutions and share a spatiotemporal positional encoding with patch tokens.
For video, one query hierarchy is initialized from the current frame and aggregates evidence from both current and preceding frames.
Only the updated query features are passed to the language model.
For a fixed query layout, this interface incorporates observation history without increasing the output sequence length.
HybridViT thus reduces the sequence length used for visual encoding, while MLQ organizes multi-scale and temporal evidence within a controlled language-model input budget.
MLQ can also be adapted to other ViT backbones with compatible feature, positional, and attention interfaces.
As an additional deployment benefit, the convolutional front end supports heterogeneous execution on NVIDIA Orin-X hardware NVIDIA (n.d.), including DLA and GPU overlap in our implementation.

To train TuringPAI-VL, we complement general vision–language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal tasks.
Following the data-construction approach of VLM3 Cai et al. (2026), we use pixel-depth questions and camera-conditioned 3D object localization to supervise distance, position, size, and orientation, providing geometric cues for driving clearance and object placement. Cross-view correspondence and relative camera-pose data support associations across observations, while multi-frame driving and manipulation examples provide signals about motion and state changes.

We evaluate TuringPAI-VL on general multimodal benchmarks and spatial
and geometric understanding tasks relevant to Physical AI.
Driving evaluations of TuringPAI-Drive cover open-loop trajectory
prediction and XPeng’s in-house simulation.
For deployment, we use XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT), our in-house inference
runtime that combines mixed-precision execution with hardware-aware
optimization, enabling 12 Hz trajectory generation on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC.
TuringPAI-Drive is scheduled for rollout to XPeng vehicles equipped with NVIDIA Orin-X as part of the VLA 2.0 system.
Beyond driving, TuringPAI-Embodied, initialized from TuringPAI-VL,
achieves a 96.8% average success rate across the four LIBERO Liu et al. (2023b) suites.
These results support TuringPAI-VL as a shared vision-language
foundation for driving and manipulation under practical deployment
constraints.

title: MIR-Depth: Multi-Range Refinement for Single-View RGB-D Depth Completion of Transparent Objects
authors: Xinzhe Fu,Qi Shao,Yuanfei Xie,Taoyu Wu,Zhihao Cao,Long Hu,Hong Liang,Xianzhi Li,Anh Nguyen,Baoru Huang,Rongsheng Li
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects.
Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors.
Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution.
To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth.
Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU.
Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints.
Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.
Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.
introduction:
Transparent objects are common in household and laboratory settings, yet recovering their surface geometry remains challenging for robotic manipulation (Fig. MIR-Depth: Multi-Range Refinement for Single-View RGB-D Depth Completion of Transparent Objects).
Accurate visible-surface depth supports grasp planning [1], but reflection and refraction cause missing or erroneous nonzero RGB-D measurements that may correspond to background surfaces [2, 3, 4].
Opaque-scene depth completion often uses observed depths as geometric anchors [5, 6, 7], whereas transparent-region readings may lie behind the surface a gripper must contact [8].
An object mask localizes the target but cannot establish the reliability of nonzero readings, so single-view completion must fill missing depth and correct corrupted measurements without treating them as reliable surface constraints.

Single-view networks predict dense depth from RGB-D inputs in one forward pass [9, 10, 11], while prior-guided methods incorporate monocular depth estimates [12, 13, 14], as in ReMake, which combines a relative-depth prior with an object mask [8].
Despite providing a useful metric reference, prior-guided predictions can have residual errors ranging from a few millimeters along thin rims to tens of centimeters in strongly refracted interiors.
With a fixed per-pixel sampling budget, narrow search intervals miss large refraction offsets, whereas workspace-wide intervals reduce local sampling resolution.
Multi-range disparity volumes address a similar trade-off in stereo matching [15, 16], but single-view RGB-D completion lacks epipolar correlation and must score candidates using monocular context and unreliable raw depth.

MIR-Depth (Fig. 2) iteratively refines single-view depth across multiple inverse-depth volumes using metric initialization and multi-scale context from RGB, raw depth, the object mask, and a frozen Depth Anything V2 prior [14].
Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses combines one shared global volume with two pixel-wise local volumes around the initial reference inverse depth, using validity-masked raw-depth residuals as soft evidence.
Since global bins share scene-wide planes while local bins shift per pixel, a 3D hourglass aggregates the global volume spatially, whereas depth-axis convolutions filter local volumes without cross-pixel depth mixing.
Selective Recurrent Refinement uses out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to combine fine local detail and wide global corrections through a multi-scale ConvGRU.
Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial regions without clamping to raw depth.
Together, these designs reduce depth error on TransCG and four unseen zero-shot benchmarks while supporting reliable 6-DoF grasping on a physical robot.

Our main contributions are:

We propose Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses, pairing a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume with depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes to cover large refraction offsets and fine surface detail.

We design Selective Recurrent Refinement, introducing out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update single-view inverse depth from monocular context and soft raw-depth residuals.

We introduce Spatially Gated Correction, learning a full-resolution per-pixel spatial gate to blend recurrent depth residuals into the initial estimate without treating nonzero raw depth as a hard constraint.

1. We propose Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses, pairing a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume with depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes to cover large refraction offsets and fine surface detail.

2. We design Selective Recurrent Refinement, introducing out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update single-view inverse depth from monocular context and soft raw-depth residuals.

3. We introduce Spatially Gated Correction, learning a full-resolution per-pixel spatial gate to blend recurrent depth residuals into the initial estimate without treating nonzero raw depth as a hard constraint.

title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation
authors: Clinton Enwerem,Saleh Kemal,John S. Baras,Calin Belta
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy’s action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.
introduction:
Residual reinforcement learning (RL) improves a policy trained by imitation without retraining it: the imitation-trained base policy is typically fixed, and a residual policy learns a bounded correction to its actions from additional interaction with the environment (Ankile et al., 2024; Ankile et al., 2025). The interaction available for this second stage is limited. For instance, many robotic manipulation tasks typically consist of multiple, ordered phases, such as grasping, transporting, inserting, and releasing a part Liu et al. (2026); Lei et al. (2025); Enwerem et al. (2026a). For such tasks, the designer must decide in which phases the residual policy is trained and which components of the action, for example which joints, it corrects. We study how to make this decision under a fixed interaction budget.

A natural choice is to train the residual policy in the phases where the base policy fails. However, the phase in which a failure is detected identifies where the episode ended, and not necessarily where a different action would have prevented the failure, because an error made in an early phase can leave the system in a state from which the later phases cannot be completed. Fig. 1(a) shows an example. A point mass with limited braking must pass through a channel and cross a dock line below a speed limit. Under the base policy, the mass enters the dock phase too fast for braking to reduce its speed to the limit, and the failure is detected at the dock line; when a state-feedback controller replaces the base policy during the channel phase only, the episode is completed. Similar behavior can appear in higher-dimensional systems such as the bimanual robotic manipulator depicted in Fig. 1(b,c) charged with contact-rich tasks with multiple phases. In this example, substituting the state-feedback controller during release improved task completion.

Existing work on improving imitation policies falls into two groups. The first group specifies how the policy is updated. RL can start from demonstrations (Rajeswaran et al., 2018; Ball et al., 2023) or use human corrections (Luo et al., 2025). Residual RL trains corrections to a frozen behavior-cloning policy using on-policy (Ankile et al., 2024) or off-policy updates (Ankile et al., 2025), following earlier residual corrections to conventional controllers (Johannink et al., 2019); other methods steer the denoising inputs of a diffusion policy (Wagenmaker et al., 2025) or use other policy updates (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Lei et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). These methods do not address how limited interaction should be divided among the phases of a task. The second group accounts for the phase structure. Sequential Dexterity improves the states passed between sub-policies (Chen et al., 2023), Foresight residual RL shapes local rewards using predictions of downstream success (Liu et al., 2026), and RL Token and PARTS restrict learning to selected phases (Xu et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026), which PARTS obtains from bottlenecks identified by a human. To our knowledge, none of these methods estimates, before training, how much a correction restricted to one phase and one group of action components would change full-task completion, or uses such an estimate to divide an interaction budget.

In this paper, we estimate the effect of a correction in each phase on completion of the entire task before residual training begins, using the state-feedback controller that generated the demonstrations for the base policy. We compare two episodes that start from the same initial condition (Fig. 2): in the first, the base policy supplies every action; in the second, the state-feedback controller replaces selected action components during one phase. We call the resulting change in full-task completion probability the completion gain. Our contributions are as follows. First, we define the completion gain and show that it factors into the probability of reaching the phase and the mean improvement in completion probability from the start of the phase. Unlike the failure frequency of a phase, it credits a phase with the failures that a correction in the phase prevents in later phases. Second, we propose gain-based allocation, which uses paired estimates of completion gain to select the action components that the residual policy corrects in each phase and the probability with which training episodes start in each phase, with the cost of estimation charged to the same interaction budget. Compared with Foresight (Liu et al., 2026), which changes the reward of the RL update, and PARTS (Su et al., 2026), which relies on a human to choose the phases, gain-based allocation leaves the RL update unchanged and chooses the phases from data, using the state-feedback controller. Third, we evaluate the approach in simulated point-mass docking, against four other allocation strategies under the same budget, and in simulated bimanual assembly.

title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
authors: Zirui Song,Jiadong Zhang,Zheng Lu,Xiaosong Ma,Xiaojun Chang,Xiuying Chen
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure.
Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task.
Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way.
A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure).
In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions.
SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker.
Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction.
Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict.
Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures.
Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0.
These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
introduction:
Task success rate is the primary metric for comparing robot manipulation policies in simulation.
Each episode is scored by a success checker, a hand-written rule that uses simulator state to determine whether the robot completed the task specified by the instruction.
Evaluating generalist manipulation models, including vision-language-action models (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026b; Lu et al., 2026b) and world action models (Li et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026), on physical robots is costly and difficult to reproduce across laboratories (Zhou et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026a).
Recent simulated benchmarks such as RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025), RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), and RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026b) therefore play a central role in model evaluation.
They aggregate checker verdicts into the success rates used to rank policies.
Prior work has shown that these rates can be affected by memorization of training configurations (Zhou et al., 2026b; Fei et al., 2025), task shortcuts and overfitting to fixed test sets (Jiang et al., 2026), and artifacts in the physics engine (Zhou et al., 2026a).
The reliability of the success checkers that produce these rates has
received less attention.
This raises a basic question: do checker verdicts
accurately reflect whether a robot’s execution satisfies the task instruction?

Expert demonstrations can establish that a success checker accepts a reference execution.
RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025), for example, retains an evaluation seed only if the scripted expert passes the checker on that seed.
A learned policy can reach states outside those covered by the demonstrations by stopping before the task is complete or by completing it in a different way.
Figure 1 illustrates two errors that can arise in these states.
The first task illustrates a phantom success.
The checker reports success when the robot lifts the bottle 3 cm off the table without shaking it.
A phantom success occurs when the checker marks an execution as successful even though it does not satisfy the instruction.
The second task illustrates a silent failure.
The robot picks up one bottle with each arm as instructed, but the checker reports failure because it additionally requires both bottles to be at the centre of the table.
A silent failure occurs when the checker marks an execution as failed even though it satisfies the instruction.

Validation with scripted experts can miss checker errors because expert trajectories may never expose discrepancies between the instruction and the conditions the checker tests.
To uncover these errors, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers on states that scripted experts never reach.
Given a task instruction and its checker code, an LLM agent compares the requirements in the instruction with the conditions tested by the checker. It uses discrepancies between the two to propose states that the checker may misclassify.
For each proposed state, the agent predicts from the code whether the checker will return success or failure. The agent then constructs the state in simulation, using robot motion governed by simulated physics wherever possible. The pipeline runs the unmodified checker on the resulting state and renders the scene from multiple camera views. A candidate is retained only if the rendered views establish that the execution’s outcome under the instruction differs from the checker verdict.
Across 142 tasks in the three benchmarks, the agent proposed 568 candidate states.
The actual checker verdict matched the agent’s prediction in 183 cases.
Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct checker defects.

We identify 61 defects across 49 tasks in RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. RoboCasa365 has 17 phantom successes and one silent failure, while RoboDojo has three phantom successes and nine silent failures. Both types are common in RoboTwin 2.0, with 20 phantom successes and 11 silent failures.
These patterns reflect the conditions each benchmark’s checkers enforce. RoboCasa365 checkers often omit conditions required by the instruction, allowing incomplete executions to pass. RoboDojo checkers often impose conditions beyond those in the instruction, causing executions that satisfy the instruction to fail.
These errors can inflate or depress reported success rates. To measure their effect on released policies, we repair the defects identified by SimAudit and score the same policy rollouts with the original and repaired checkers. We count a verdict change whenever the two checkers disagree on an episode.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we define two types of success checker errors, phantom success and silent failure, and illustrate both with rendered examples from states outside expert trajectories. Second, we introduce SimAudit, an agentic pipeline that proposes candidate error cases from task instructions and checker code, constructs them in simulation, and verifies errors by comparing the unmodified checker’s verdict with renders from multiple camera views. Third, we report 61 visually verified defects across three benchmarks, with different proportions of the two error types. After repairing the defects, we score the same rollouts from released policies with both checkers. The original and repaired checkers disagree on up to 9.1% of a policy’s rollouts.

title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
authors: Amani Kiruga,Mark Hamilton,Joshua B. Tenenbaum,William T. Freeman,Vincent Sitzmann,Yilun Du,Ayush Tewari
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Includes references and appendices. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy.
In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site
introduction:
The human visual system exhibits a remarkable ability to parse the 3D world from 2D projections. Crucially, this capability is not brittle: humans can readily understand the 3D structure of objects and scenes even when viewed from highly unconventional angles (Yildirim et al., 2015), under strange lighting (Adelson, 2000), or under different compositional arrangements (Lake et al., 2017). A central challenge in perception theory is explaining how human vision can be so robust. A rich body of literature in cognitive science and developmental psychology suggests that this robustness arises because human vision is not merely a passive, bottom-up filter but also includes an active, top-down generative process. By
maintaining an internal mental model of the physical world, the mind can
continuously predict and match sensory inputs, allowing it to reliably resolve
ambiguities in unseen environments (Spagna et al., 2024; Clark, 2013; Friston, 2010; Tenenbaum et al., 2011).

This cognitive perspective heavily influenced classical computational theories,
which formalized perception as “vision as inverse graphics” (Yuille & Kersten, 2006).
In this paradigm, visual understanding is cast as Bayesian inference over a
generative model of image formation and scene
structure (Knill & Richards, 1996; Kersten et al., 2004). Rather than simply
recognizing 2D patterns, the visual system performs
analysis-by-synthesis, actively searching for the underlying 3D scene
representation that best explains the observed 2D image.

In contrast, modern monocular 3D reconstruction systems have largely abandoned
this generative top-down inference in favor of amortized, feedforward architectures (Szymanowicz et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2021; Charatan et al., 2024; Wewer et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2023) that directly map a
2D input image to a 3D output.
While this pattern-matching approach enables very fast inference, it
fundamentally lacks the robustness of generative inference. As we demonstrate
in this paper, feedforward networks degrade in unpredictable ways when faced
with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training, such
as unconventional camera viewpoints (see Fig. 2).

Inspired by the generative nature of human vision and classic analysis-by-synthesis methods (Blanz & Vetter, 2023a; Yuille & Kersten, 2006), we propose Infer3D. Rather than trusting a feedforward encoder on OOD data, Infer3D formulates perception as an inverse generative problem. We search for the scene geometry 𝒮\mathcal{S} and rendering parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} that maximize the explanatory likelihood of the input observation. To ensure our optimization remains constrained to plausible, multi-view-consistent 3D structures, we couple a 2D generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network. This encourages the optimized latent variables to always decode to a valid representation on the training manifold, effectively synthesizing an internal hypothesis that best matches the confusing sensory input. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process ambiguous stimuli (Kar et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2018; Tschantz et al., 2023), we introduce an adaptive inference strategy. Because our generative framework leverages an encoder for initialization, we show that the initial reconstruction error provides a very reliable and efficient signal for OOD detection.
This allows Infer3D to dynamically route standard inputs through fast feedforward passes while reserving expensive test-time optimization exclusively for OOD images.

Overall, our work makes the following contributions: (1) we introduce Infer3D, a modular analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines a learned 2D generative model with a feedforward 3D lifter to enable multi-view-consistent, OOD-robust inference from single images; (2) we propose an adaptive inference and OOD detection strategy that leverages the initial reconstruction error of the generative prior, requiring no external classifiers; and (3) through a controlled experimental setup, we demonstrate that Infer3D successfully generalizes to unseen viewpoints, non-linear lens distortions, and unobserved textures where state-of-the-art feedforward methods collapse (see Fig. 1).
